GIT Final Summary

🏁 One exam away from freedom 🎉

1PDH & Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) Cycle›

Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) Complex — Overview

  • Function: Converts pyruvate → Acetyl-CoA by oxidative decarboxylation (irreversible reaction)
  • Location: Mitochondria only — enzyme is present ONLY in the mitochondria
  • Significance: Links glycolysis (cytoplasm) to TCA cycle (mitochondria) — "gateway" reaction
  • N.B: Glucose → Pyruvate (glycolysis in cytoplasm) → Acetyl CoA (PDH in mitochondria)
  • Under aerobic conditions: Pyruvate is oxidized in the mitochondria to form Acetyl CoA

PDH Complex — Enzymes & Cofactors

  • Requires 3 enzymes (multienzyme complex) and 5 cofactors (coenzymes)
  • Cofactor 1: TPP (Thiamine pyrophosphate) — from Vitamin B1
  • Cofactor 2: FAD (Flavin adenine dinucleotide) — from Vitamin B2
  • Cofactor 3: CoA-SH (Coenzyme A) — from Pantothenic acid (Vitamin B5)
  • Cofactor 4: NAD⁺ (Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) — from Vitamin B3
  • Cofactor 5: Lipoic acid
  • Reaction: Pyruvate + CoA-SH + NAD⁺ → Acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH

PDH Regulation

  • Regulated by phosphorylation: Most ACTIVE in dephosphorylated state
  • PDH Kinase (inactivates PDH by phosphorylation):
  • → ACTIVATED by: ATP, NADH, Acetyl-CoA (high energy state = products)
  • → INHIBITED by: Pyruvate, NAD⁺, CoA-SH (low energy state = substrates)
  • PDH Phosphatase (activates PDH by dephosphorylation): Activated by Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
  • Clinical note: PDH deficiency (often TPP/B1 deficiency) → lactic acidosis + neurological symptoms

TCA Cycle — Location & Entry Point

  • Also known as: Krebs cycle or Citric Acid Cycle
  • Location: Mitochondrial matrix
  • Entry point: Acetyl-CoA (2-carbon compound)
  • Primary function: Final common pathway for oxidation of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins

TCA Cycle — 8 Steps in Detail

  • Step 1 — Citrate Synthase: Acetyl-CoA + Oxaloacetate → Citrate. Condensation reaction.
  • Step 2 — Aconitase: Citrate → Isocitrate. Isomerization reaction.
  • Step 3 — Isocitrate Dehydrogenase: Isocitrate → α-Ketoglutarate + CO₂ + NADH. FIRST oxidative decarboxylation.
  • Step 4 — α-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase Complex: α-KG → Succinyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. SECOND oxidative decarboxylation. Requires SAME 5 cofactors as PDH.
  • Step 5 — Succinyl-CoA Synthetase: Succinyl-CoA → Succinate + GTP. ONLY step producing GTP directly. Example of substrate-level phosphorylation.
  • Step 6 — Succinate Dehydrogenase: Succinate → Fumarate + FADH₂. Located on inner mitochondrial membrane. Also = Complex II of ETC.
  • Step 7 — Fumarase: Fumarate → L-Malate. Hydration reaction (addition of water).
  • Step 8 — Malate Dehydrogenase: L-Malate → Oxaloacetate + NADH. Regenerates OAA for next cycle.
  • N.B: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex requires the SAME cofactors as PDH complex.

TCA Cycle — Overall Products & Energy

  • Per 1 Acetyl-CoA (one turn): 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP = 12 ATP
  • Per 1 Glucose (two turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 GTP = ~24 ATP from TCA alone
  • Regulatory enzymes of TCA (3 key sites):
  • Citrate synthase: stimulated by Acetyl-CoA, Oxaloacetate, ADP, NAD⁺; inhibited by ATP, NADH
  • Isocitrate dehydrogenase: inhibited by ATP; activated by ADP
  • α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase: inhibited by ATP, NADPH, Succinyl-CoA
  • Principle: TCA cycle is INHIBITED when cell has excess ATP; ACTIVATED when ATP is needed

Importance of TCA Cycle — Amphibolic Functions

  • The cycle is AMPHIBOLIC = has both catabolic AND anabolic functions
  • A. Catabolic: Final common oxidative pathway for carbohydrates, fats, proteins → major ATP source
  • B. Anabolic — Amino acids: α-Ketoglutarate + transamination → Glutamate; Oxaloacetate + transamination → Aspartate
  • B. Anabolic — Heme synthesis: Succinyl-CoA → heme synthesis + ketolysis (breakdown of ketone bodies)
  • B. Anabolic — Fatty acids & cholesterol: Citrate diffuses to cytoplasm → Acetyl-CoA → fatty acid synthesis & cholesterol
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1PDH complex is located in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — PDH is found ONLY in the mitochondria. This is why pyruvate must be transported from cytoplasm into mitochondria before it can be converted to Acetyl-CoA.
2How many cofactors are required by PDH complex?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — PDH requires 5 cofactors: TPP (B1), FAD (B2), CoA-SH (B5), NAD⁺ (B3), and Lipoic acid. Plus 3 enzymes.
3PDH kinase is ACTIVATED by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — PDH kinase is activated by products of high energy state: Acetyl-CoA, ATP, NADH → phosphorylates (inactivates) PDH.
4Which TCA step produces GTP directly (substrate-level phosphorylation)?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Step 5: Succinyl-CoA Synthetase produces GTP directly. This is the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle.
5α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires the same cofactors as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Both PDH and α-KG dehydrogenase are multi-enzyme complexes requiring the same 5 cofactors: TPP, FAD, CoA, NAD⁺, lipoic acid.
6Succinate dehydrogenase (TCA step 6) is also known as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Succinate dehydrogenase = Complex II of ETC. It is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane and reduces FAD → FADH₂.
7How many NADH molecules are produced per one turn of TCA?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — 3 NADH per turn: at steps 3 (isocitrate DH), 4 (α-KG DH), and 8 (malate DH).
8TCA cycle is "amphibolic" meaning:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Amphibolic = catabolic (final oxidative pathway → ATP) + anabolic (intermediates for AAs, heme, fatty acids, cholesterol).
9Which TCA intermediate is the starting material for heme synthesis?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Succinyl-CoA + Glycine → δ-ALA (first step of heme synthesis) by ALA synthase.
10Isocitrate dehydrogenase is INHIBITED by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by ATP (energy surplus → no need for more ATP → slow down TCA) and activated by ADP (energy deficit).
2Overall Nitrogen Metabolism›

I. Nitrogen Intake

  • Major source: Dietary proteins — each 100g protein contains 16g nitrogen
  • Average daily intake: 90g protein/day → provides ~14.5g nitrogen/day
  • Minor sources: Phospholipids, nucleic acids, inorganic nitrite and nitrate

II. Nitrogen Output — Routes of Excretion

  • 1. Urine (MAJOR route) — in form of non-protein nitrogenous compounds (NPN):
  • → Urea: 20-40 g/day (most important)
  • → Uric acid: 0.7 g/day
  • → Ammonia: 0.7 g/day
  • → Hippuric acid: 0.7 g/day
  • → Creatinine: 1 g/day (Female) | 1.5 g/day (Male)
  • 2. Stool: 1 g/day — undigested protein, mucin, digestive enzymes
  • 3. Sweat: 0.3 g/day — in form of urea
  • 4. Other routes: milk, hair, menstruation, nails

III. Nitrogen Balance — Definition & States

  • Definition: Balance between nitrogen intake and output = balance between protein anabolism and catabolism
  • A. Nitrogen Equilibrium: Intake = Output → healthy adult on adequate diet
  • B. Positive Nitrogen Balance (anabolism — intake > output):
  • → Pregnancy, during growth, muscular training, convalescence from disease
  • C. Negative Nitrogen Balance (catabolism — output > intake):
  • → Catabolic diseases: diabetes mellitus, thyrotoxicosis, cancer, Cushing syndrome, fevers, infectious diseases
  • → Inadequate protein intake: malnutrition, starvation, malabsorption
  • → Protein loss: albuminuria, haemorrhage, burns, lactation on inadequate diet

Catabolic Pathways of Amino Acids — Overview

  • Amino acids are catabolized via:
  • 1. Removal of amino group (NH₂) as NH₃ → deamination
  • 2. The resulting carbon skeleton → enters metabolic pathways
  • Fate of carbon skeleton:
  • 1. Reamination → α-keto acid + NH₃ → non-essential amino acids
  • 2. Glucogenic pathway → pyruvate or TCA intermediates → gluconeogenesis → glucose (all AAs except leucine)
  • 3. Ketogenic pathway → acetoacetyl-CoA → ketone bodies (leucine only — purely ketogenic)
  • 4. Glucogenic + ketogenic (both glucose and ketone bodies): Phe, Tyr, Ile, Trp

3Deamination, Transamination & Transdeamination›

Deamination — Definition & Types

  • Definition: Removal of amino group (–NH₂) from amino acid in the form of NH₃
  • Types: I. General methods (oxidative deamination, transamination, transdeamination); II. Specific methods

1. Oxidative Deamination

  • Definition: Removal of amino group accompanied by oxidation
  • Site: Liver, kidney
  • Three enzymes:
  • A. L-amino acid oxidase: Acts on L-amino acids EXCEPT glutamic acid; needs FMN as coenzyme; not widely distributed
  • B. D-amino acid oxidase: Acts on D-amino acids; needs FAD as coenzyme; present in animals and bacteria
  • C. L-glutamate dehydrogenase: Acts ONLY on glutamic acid; needs NAD⁺ as coenzyme; HIGHLY ACTIVE inside the body; most important enzyme

2. Transamination

  • Definition: Transfer of amino group (–NH₂) from α-amino acid to an α-keto acid → forming new amino acid + new keto acid
  • Site: Liver, muscle, heart (in both mitochondria and cytoplasm)
  • Enzymes: Transaminases (aminotransferases)
  • Coenzyme: Vitamin B6 — pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
  • All amino acids EXCEPT 4 undergo transamination: Lysine, Threonine, Proline, Hydroxyproline
  • Reactions are REVERSIBLE — important for biosynthesis of non-essential amino acids
  • Induction: Transaminase synthesis is induced by glucocorticoids, thyroxine, growth hormone; inhibited by insulin
  • GPT (ALT) — Glutamate Pyruvate Transaminase: ↑ in liver disease specifically
  • GOT (AST) — Glutamate Oxaloacetate Transaminase: ↑ in myocardial infarction AND liver disease

3. Transdeamination

  • Definition: Combination of transamination + oxidative deamination
  • Why it is needed:
  • → Transamination ALONE does not release NH₃ (just transfers the group)
  • → L-amino acid oxidase has LOW activity and limited distribution
  • → L-glutamate dehydrogenase is HIGHLY ACTIVE but acts only on glutamate
  • Mechanism: Step 1: Amino acid + α-ketoglutarate → Glutamic acid (by transaminase); Step 2: Glutamic acid → NH₃ + α-ketoglutarate (by L-glutamate dehydrogenase)
  • Importance: This system is widely distributed and highly active; L-glutamate dehydrogenase INDIRECTLY deaminates ALL amino acids
  • Conclusion: Transdeamination is the ONLY mechanism for net deamination of all amino acids in the body

Fate of End Products of Deamination

  • Fate of NH₃ → see Topic 4 (Ammonia & Urea Cycle)
  • Fate of carbon skeleton:
  • 1. Reamination: α-keto acid + NH₃ → non-essential amino acids
  • 2. Glucogenic pathway: pyruvate or TCA intermediates → gluconeogenesis → glucose
  • 3. Ketogenic pathway: acetoacetyl-CoA → ketone bodies

4Metabolism of Ammonia & Urea Cycle›

Sources of Ammonia

  • 1. Deamination of amino acids (major source)
  • 2. Bacterial action on proteins of diet in GIT
  • 3. Catabolism of purine and pyrimidine bases
  • Blood ammonia level: 10-20 μg/dL (highly toxic even at low concentrations)
  • Note: Ammonia is HIGHLY TOXIC because it is a highly diffusible substance

Transport of Ammonia in Blood

  • Two mechanisms for transport of NH₃ from peripheral tissues to liver:
  • 1. Glutamine pathway (MOST TISSUES): NH₃ + Glutamic acid → Glutamine (by glutamine synthetase — mitochondrial enzyme in kidney and brain)
  • → In BRAIN: Glutamine formation is the MAJOR mechanism for removal of NH₃; glutamine is a storage form of NH₃
  • → In KIDNEY: Glutamine → NH₃ + glutamic acid (by glutaminase); NH₃ is excreted as NH₄⁺; accounts for 60% of urinary ammonia
  • 2. Alanine pathway (MUSCLE primarily): Transamination of pyruvate to form alanine; alanine is transported to liver → converted back to pyruvate by transamination (glucose-alanine cycle)

Fate of Ammonia

  • A. ANABOLIC fate (NH₃ is used to synthesize):
  • 1. Biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine bases → DNA, RNA, coenzymes (NAD, FAD, CoASH), nucleotides (ATP, CTP)
  • 2. Biosynthesis of amino sugars (e.g., glucosamine) → important for mucopolysaccharides
  • 3. Biosynthesis of non-essential amino acids
  • B. CATABOLIC fate (NH₃ is detoxified/excreted):
  • 1. Direct excretion in urine (40% of urinary ammonia — from kidney deamination)
  • 2. Glutamine pathway in kidney → NH₄⁺ (60% of urinary ammonia)
  • 3. Urea cycle in LIVER → Urea (main catabolic pathway)

Urea Cycle — Steps (Detailed)

  • Site: Liver ONLY. First 2 steps: mitochondria. Steps 3-5: cytoplasm.
  • Step 1 (MITO): NH₃ + CO₂ + 2ATP → Carbamoyl phosphate. Enzyme: CPS-I. Needs N-acetyl glutamate as activator. IRREVERSIBLE. CO₂ fixation reaction.
  • Step 2 (MITO): Carbamoyl phosphate + Ornithine → Citrulline. Enzyme: Ornithine Transcarbamoylase (OTC). Citrulline is transported to cytoplasm.
  • Step 3 (CYTO): Citrulline + Aspartate → Argininosuccinate. Enzyme: Argininosuccinate synthetase. Requires ATP.
  • Step 4 (CYTO): Argininosuccinate → Arginine + Fumarate. Enzyme: Argininosuccinase. Fumarate enters TCA cycle.
  • Step 5 (CYTO): Arginine → Ornithine + UREA. Enzyme: Arginase. Ornithine is recycled back to mitochondria.

CPS-I — Key Enzyme Details

  • Full name: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I
  • Present in: Mitochondria of the liver
  • Requires: 2 ATP + N-acetyl glutamate (activator)
  • Reaction is IRREVERSIBLE
  • Key enzyme for regulation of urea cycle (along with L-glutamate dehydrogenase)
  • N-acetyl glutamate: Increases affinity between CPS-I and ATP

Urea — Properties & Clinical Factors

  • Urea is the main NPN (non-protein nitrogenous) compound
  • Synthesized by: Liver; Excreted by: Kidney
  • Blood urea: 20-40 mg/dL
  • Urinary urea: 20-40 g/day
  • ↑ Blood urea: High protein diet; Renal failure; Obstruction of urinary tract by stones
  • ↓ Blood urea: Low protein diet; Liver disease (e.g., viral hepatitis, bilharzial liver) → diseased liver cannot make urea → ↑ blood NH₃
  • ↑ Blood NH₃ in liver disease: NH₃ is not converted to urea → hepatic encephalopathy

Relations Between TCA Cycle and Urea Cycle

  • 1. CO₂ used in urea cycle is PRODUCED by TCA cycle (Krebs)
  • 2. ATP needed by urea cycle is PRODUCED by TCA cycle
  • 3. Fumarate produced by urea cycle (step 4) enters TCA cycle → Malate → Oxaloacetate

Inborn Errors of Urea Cycle

  • Common result: NH₃ not converted to urea → NH₃ intoxication
  • 1. Hyperammonemia Type I: CPS-I deficiency → lethargy, convulsions, coma, death
  • 2. Hyperammonemia Type II: OTC deficiency (MOST COMMON — 1:30,000 live births) → ↑ glutamine in blood; manifests in first weeks of life → mental retardation
  • 3. Citrullinemia: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency → excess citrulline in plasma and urine
  • 4. Argininosuccinic aciduria: Argininosuccinase deficiency → ↑ argininosuccinic acid in plasma and urine
  • 5. Hyperargininemia: Arginase deficiency → ↑ arginine in blood + urine; also ↑ excretion of lysine and cystine (compete with arginine for renal reabsorption)

NH₃ Intoxication — Mechanism & Management

  • Mechanism of toxicity:
  • 1. NH₃ crosses blood-brain barrier and combines with α-ketoglutarate → glutamic acid → DEPLETES α-KG from TCA → ↓ ATP production in brain
  • 2. Excess NH₃ → ↑ glutamine synthesis → astrocyte swelling → CEREBRAL OEDEMA
  • Symptoms: Flapping tremors, slurring of speech, blurring of vision, disturbance in sleep, vomiting (infancy), coma in late cases
  • Management — Dietary: Adequate protein but ↓ high-risk proteins; BCAA supplementation; Vegetable-based proteins (↑ fiber → ↑ colonic motility → ↓ NH₃ absorption; ↓ colonic pH)
  • Management — Drugs:
  • → Non-absorbable disaccharides (lactulose, lactiol): convert NH₃ → NH₄⁺ (non-absorbable), ↓ bacterial NH₃ production, ↑ bowel transit
  • → Antibiotics: Neomycin, Metronidazole (↓ NH₃ by gut bacteria); Rifaximin (non-absorbable, safer)
  • → L-ornithine + L-aspartate (LOLA): convert NH₃ to urea

5Amino Acids Metabolism›

Classification of Amino Acids by Metabolic Fate

  • Glucogenic AAs (give glucose via gluconeogenesis): Give pyruvate or TCA intermediates → ALL amino acids EXCEPT leucine
  • Ketogenic only (leucine): Gives acetoacetyl-CoA → ketone bodies ONLY; CANNOT produce glucose
  • Both glucogenic + ketogenic: Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, Isoleucine, Tryptophan
  • Essential AAs (cannot be synthesized, must be taken in diet): Mnemonic PVT TIM HaLL: Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine (semi), Arginine (semi), Leucine, Lysine

Glycine Metabolism

  • Non-essential: Synthesized from serine, threonine, or by glycine synthase
  • Importance of Glycine:
  • 1. Formation of purine bases (→ DNA, RNA)
  • 2. Formation of bile salts
  • 3. Formation of creatine (from 3 AAs: glycine + arginine + methionine; in liver and muscle)
  • 4. Acts as inhibitory neurotransmitter in spinal cord and medulla
  • 5. Glutathione formation (glutamic acid + cysteine + glycine)
  • 6. Heme production: glycine + succinyl-CoA → δ-ALA (first step of heme synthesis)
  • 7. Collagen formation: glycine = 1/3 of collagen amino acid content
  • Inborn errors: Primary hyperoxaluria (↑ oxalate → renal stones); Glycinuria (renal tubular defect)

Serine Metabolism

  • Non-essential; glucogenic AA (gives pyruvic acid)
  • Synthesis: From glycine (by serine hydroxymethyltransferase) OR from 3-phosphoglycerate
  • Importance of Serine:
  • 1. Synthesis of cysteine (serine + homocysteine → cysteine)
  • 2. Ethanolamine and choline synthesis: Serine → ethanolamine → choline (by addition of 3 CH₃ groups via SAM)
  • 3. Formation of sphingosine base (→ sphingomyelin of myelin sheath)
  • 4. Formation of C2 and C8 of purine ring (→ nucleotide synthesis)

Methionine Metabolism

  • Essential, sulphur-containing, glucogenic AA (gives succinyl-CoA)
  • Activation: Methionine → S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) — active methyl donor
  • SAM importance (methyl donor for):
  • → N-acetylserotonin → Melatonin
  • → Ethanolamine → Choline
  • → Nor-epinephrine → Epinephrine
  • → Uracil → Thymine (DNA synthesis)
  • → Carnosine → Anserine

Cysteine & Cystine Metabolism

  • Cysteine: Non-essential, glucogenic (gives pyruvate); synthesized from homocysteine + serine
  • Importance of cysteine: Glutathione formation; CoA-SH synthesis; Taurine synthesis (→ bile salts); Detoxification; PAPS (active sulfate donor)
  • Homocystinuria: Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency → ↑ homocysteine in urine
  • → Manifestations: Thrombosis, osteoporosis, dislocation of lens (ectopia lentis), mental retardation
  • → Two forms: Vitamin B6-responsive and B6-unresponsive
  • → Tx: Low methionine + high cysteine diet
  • Cystinuria: Genetic defect in renal tubular reabsorption of dibasic AAs (cystine, lysine, arginine, ornithine) → cystine stones (rotten egg smell)
  • Cystinosis: Lysosomal disorder → cystine accumulates in RES → renal failure

Aspartic Acid (Aspartate) Metabolism

  • Non-essential; glucogenic AA (gives oxaloacetate via transamination)
  • Synthesis: From oxaloacetic acid (OAA) by transamination
  • Importance of Aspartic Acid:
  • 1. Synthesis of purine base (contributes N1 of purine ring → DNA and RNA)
  • 2. Synthesis of pyrimidine (contributes N1, C4, C5, C6 of pyrimidine ring)
  • 3. Carrier of NH₃ in the Urea Cycle (aspartate donates its amino group to form argininosuccinate)
  • 4. By decarboxylation: Aspartate → β-alanine → formation of CoA-SH (so both cysteine and aspartate contribute to CoA-SH synthesis)

Glutamic Acid (Glutamate) Metabolism

  • Non-essential; glucogenic AA (gives α-ketoglutarate)
  • Synthesis: From α-ketoglutaric acid by transamination or reductive amination
  • Importance of Glutamic Acid:
  • 1. Enters in protein structure (abundant in many proteins)
  • 2. Acts as EXCITATORY neurotransmitter in the CNS
  • 3. Formation of GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid): glutamate → GABA by decarboxylation (requires vitamin B6/PLP)
  • → In Vit B6 deficiency: GABA formation is inhibited → convulsions, especially in infants after stress
  • 4. Glutathione formation (glutamic acid + cysteine + glycine = GSH)
  • 5. N-acetyl glutamate: cofactor activator for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) in Urea Cycle
  • 6. Formation of ornithine → arginine (in the urea cycle)
  • 7. Formation of glutamine: glutamate + NH₃ → glutamine (by glutamine synthetase) — principal mechanism for NH₃ removal from BRAIN; glutamine is hydrolyzed in kidney by glutaminase → NH₃ excreted as NH₄⁺

Histidine Metabolism

  • Semi-essential AA; glucogenic (gives glutamic acid)
  • Catabolism product: FIGLU (formiminoglutamate) → accumulates in urine in FOLIC ACID DEFICIENCY (FIGLU test)
  • Specialized products:
  • 1. Histamine (by decarboxylation): vasodilator + neurotransmitter
  • 2. Ergothioneine: antioxidant in RBCs, liver, semen → protects from free radicals

Arginine Metabolism

  • Basic, semi-essential, glucogenic AA (gives ornithine → glutamate semialdehyde → α-ketoglutarate)
  • Importance of arginine:
  • 1. Formation of creatine and creatinine
  • 2. Intermediate in urea cycle
  • 3. Formation of Nitric Oxide (NO): neurochemical transmitter → cGMP → vasodilatation + smooth muscle relaxation
  • 4. Agmatine synthesis (by decarboxylation): novel neurotransmitter/neuromodulator in brain

Phenylalanine & Tyrosine Metabolism

  • Phenylalanine: Essential; glucogenic + ketogenic (gives fumarate + acetoacetate)
  • Tyrosine: Non-essential (from Phe by phenylalanine hydroxylase); glucogenic + ketogenic
  • Importance of tyrosine:
  • 1. Thyroid hormones (T3, T4, rT3): from 2 tyrosines + 4 iodine atoms in follicular cells
  • 2. Catecholamines: Adrenaline + noradrenaline (in adrenal medulla); catabolized by MAO → VMA (↑ in urine in pheochromocytoma)
  • 3. Melanin: Tyrosinase → DOPA → dopaquinone → melanin; in melanocytes
  • PKU (Phenylketonuria): Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency
  • → ↑ phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, phenylacetate in plasma/urine
  • → CNS: mental retardation, seizures, hyperactivity, microcephaly
  • → Hypopigmentation: ↑ Phe inhibits tyrosinase → ↓ melanin
  • → Diagnosis: 24-48h after birth (Guthrie test); Tx: low Phe + high Tyr diet; AVOID aspartame
  • Alkaptonuria: Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency → homogentisic aciduria (urine turns BLACK on standing), arthritis, ochronosis (dark cartilage)
  • Albinism: Tyrosinase deficiency → no melanin → hypopigmentation, photophobia, ↑ skin cancer risk
  • Hypertyrosinemia: Tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT) deficiency → ↑ tyrosine in blood and urine

Tryptophan Metabolism

  • Essential AA; glucogenic + ketogenic (gives alanine + acetoacetate)
  • Tryptophan is precursor for:
  • 1. Serotonin: hydroxylation + decarboxylation → serotonin (vasoconstrictor + neurotransmitter); highest in platelets + GIT; catabolized to 5-HIAA (↑ in carcinoid tumor)
  • 2. Melatonin: serotonin → acetylation → methylation (in pineal gland); regulates sleep-wake cycle; ↑ in darkness
  • 3. Nicotinic acid (Niacin/B3): 60mg tryptophan = 1mg niacin; deficiency → pellagra
  • Hartnup disease: Impaired renal tubular reabsorption of tryptophan (+ histidine, lysine) → aminoaciduria + pellagra-like rash; treated with nicotinic acid
  • Putrefaction products: Indole and skatol → give stool characteristic odor/color

Lysine & Branched-Chain AAs (BCAA)

  • Lysine: Essential, PURELY KETOGENIC (gives acetoacetate)
  • → Important for: collagen/elastin (hydroxylysine), carnitine synthesis (for FA transport into mitochondria)
  • BCAAs (Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine): Essential; metabolized mainly in MUSCLE, brain, adipose — NOT liver (liver lacks BCAAs transaminases)
  • → Valine: glucogenic → succinyl-CoA
  • → Leucine: PURELY KETOGENIC → acetoacetate
  • → Isoleucine: glucogenic + ketogenic → succinyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA
  • Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): Deficiency of branched-chain α-keto acid decarboxylase → accumulation of BCAA keto acids → maple syrup/burnt sugar urine odor, ketoacidosis, mental retardation, death after 1 year if untreated
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Which is the ONLY purely ketogenic amino acid?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Leucine is the ONLY purely ketogenic amino acid → gives only acetoacetyl-CoA → ketone bodies. Cannot contribute to gluconeogenesis.
2PKU (phenylketonuria) is caused by deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → ↑ Phe → phenylpyruvate, mental retardation, musty urine, hypopigmentation.
3Alkaptonuria is characterized by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Alkaptonuria: homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency → homogentisic acid in urine turns BLACK on air exposure. Also: joint arthritis, ochronosis.
4Tryptophan is the precursor for which vitamin?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — 60mg tryptophan → 1mg nicotinic acid (niacin). Tryptophan or B6 deficiency → impaired niacin synthesis → pellagra.
5Homocystinuria presents with:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase deficiency): ↑ homocysteine → lens subluxation, thromboembolism, mental retardation, Marfan-like body.
6FIGLU (formiminoglutamate) accumulates in urine in deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — FIGLU is a catabolite of histidine. In folic acid deficiency, FIGLU cannot be further processed → ↑ FIGLU in urine (FIGLU test).
7MSUD (Maple Syrup Urine Disease) is caused by deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — BCKAD deficiency → accumulation of BCAA keto acids → maple syrup/burnt sugar urine odor, ketoacidosis, mental retardation.
8S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) from methionine acts as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — SAM is the active methyl donor: NE → epinephrine, ethanolamine → choline, uracil → thymine, serotonin → melatonin.
9Glycine contributes to heme synthesis by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Glycine + Succinyl-CoA → δ-aminolevulinic acid (δ-ALA) by ALA synthase (requires PLP) — first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.
10BCAAs (Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine) are primarily metabolized in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Liver lacks BCAA transaminases → BCAAs are metabolized in MUSCLE (mainly), brain, and adipose tissue. This is why they are spared in liver disease.
6Xenobiotics Metabolism›

Definition & Overview

  • Xenobiotics (Greek: xenos = foreign, bios = life): Chemical substances foreign to biological systems
  • Examples: Drugs, environmental pollutants, food additives, pesticides, industrial chemicals
  • Routes of entry: Ingestion, inhalation, or skin absorption
  • Primary goal: Convert lipophilic (fat-soluble) → hydrophilic (water-soluble) compounds for excretion via urine or bile
  • Important concept: Metabolism usually = detoxification; BUT sometimes produces REACTIVE/TOXIC metabolites (BIOACTIVATION) — e.g., CCl₄ → CCl₃ radical (more toxic)

Sites of Xenobiotic Metabolism

  • 1. Liver (PRIMARY site): Highest concentration of metabolic enzymes (Phase I and II)
  • 2. Intestine: First-pass metabolism — very important for oral drugs
  • 3. Kidneys: Excretion + limited metabolism
  • 4. Lungs: Metabolism of inhaled compounds
  • 5. Skin: Minor metabolic activity

Phase I Reactions — Functionalization

  • Definition: Introduce or expose functional groups (–OH, –NH₂, –SH, –COOH) → slightly increase polarity → prepare for Phase II
  • Key concept: Phase I products may be MORE or LESS toxic than parent compound
  • A. OXIDATION (Most common Phase I reaction):
  • → Enzyme: Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) — heme-containing monooxygenases
  • → Location: SMOOTH endoplasmic reticulum (SER)
  • → Requires: NADPH + O₂ + CYP450 reductase
  • → Reaction: Drug + O₂ + NADPH → Drug-OH + H₂O + NADP⁺
  • → CYP450 is a SUPERFAMILY of enzymes with many isoforms (CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP3A4, etc.)
  • → Subject to enzyme INDUCTION (e.g., rifampicin, phenobarbitone) and INHIBITION (e.g., cimetidine, ketoconazole)
  • B. REDUCTION:
  • → Under LOW O₂ conditions (anaerobic)
  • → By reductases in liver microsomes AND intestinal microflora
  • → Example: nitro reduction, azo reduction
  • C. HYDROLYSIS:
  • → Cleavage of ester or amide bonds
  • → By esterases and amidases
  • → Example: aspirin (ester) → salicylate + acetic acid

Phase II Reactions — Conjugation

  • Definition: Conjugation of xenobiotic (or Phase I metabolite) with endogenous substrate → HIGHLY POLAR, usually INACTIVE compounds → EASILY EXCRETED
  • Characteristics of Phase II: ↑ Water solubility significantly; Usually DETOXIFYING; Mainly in liver cytosol; Require high-energy cofactors
  • A. GLUCURONIDATION (MOST COMMON Phase II reaction):
  • → Enzymes: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs)
  • → Cofactor: UDP-glucuronic acid
  • → Examples: bilirubin, morphine, paracetamol metabolites, chloramphenicol
  • → Glucuronides excreted in urine OR bile
  • B. SULFATION:
  • → Enzymes: Sulfotransferases (SULTs)
  • → Cofactor: PAPS (3-phosphoadenosine-5-phosphosulfate)
  • → Important for: steroid hormones, phenolic drugs
  • C. GLUTATHIONE (GSH) CONJUGATION:
  • → Enzymes: Glutathione-S-transferases (GSTs)
  • → Protects cells from reactive ELECTROPHILIC metabolites
  • → GSH depletion (e.g., paracetamol overdose) → toxic metabolite (NAPQI) damages liver
  • D. ACETYLATION:
  • → Enzymes: N-acetyltransferases (NATs)
  • → Cofactor: Acetyl-CoA
  • → Example: isoniazid (INH) for TB — genetic polymorphism → fast vs. slow acetylators
  • E. METHYLATION:
  • → Enzymes: Methyltransferases
  • → Cofactor: SAM (S-adenosylmethionine)
  • → UNIQUE: decreases biological activity but does NOT significantly increase water solubility (unlike other Phase II reactions)

Phase III — Transport & Excretion

  • Active transport of Phase II metabolites out of cells into bile or urine
  • Transporters: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (e.g., P-glycoprotein, MRP)
  • Clinical: Mutations in ABC transporters → drug resistance in cancer cells

Clinical Pharmacology Concepts

  • First-pass effect: Oral drug → absorbed from gut → portal vein → liver (+ intestinal wall) → metabolized before reaching systemic circulation → ↓ bioavailability
  • Enzyme induction: Certain drugs induce CYP450 synthesis → ↑ metabolism of other drugs → ↓ drug levels → therapeutic failure (e.g., rifampicin induces CYP3A4)
  • Enzyme inhibition: Drugs inhibit CYP450 → ↓ metabolism → ↑ drug levels → toxicity (e.g., ketoconazole inhibits CYP3A4)
  • Genetic polymorphism: Fast acetylators (INH): rapid drug inactivation; Slow acetylators: drug accumulation → more side effects (peripheral neuropathy with INH)
  • Paracetamol toxicity: At normal doses: NAPQI (reactive metabolite) detoxified by GSH; Overdose: GSH depleted → NAPQI accumulates → hepatocellular necrosis (zone 3)
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Primary goal of xenobiotic metabolism is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The main aim is to make foreign lipophilic compounds water-soluble for excretion via urine or bile.
2Principal organ for xenobiotic metabolism is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Liver is the principal site due to highest concentration of Phase I (CYP450) and Phase II (UGTs, GSTs) enzymes.
3CYP450 enzymes are located in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CYP450 = heme-containing monooxygenases embedded in the SMOOTH ER of hepatocytes.
4The most common Phase II reaction is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Glucuronidation (by UGTs using UDP-glucuronic acid) is the most common Phase II conjugation reaction.
5Cofactor for glucuronidation reactions:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — UDP-glucuronic acid is the cofactor for UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs).
6Glutathione (GSH) conjugation protects against:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — GSH conjugates reactive electrophilic intermediates. In paracetamol overdose, NAPQI depletes GSH → uncoupled NAPQI damages hepatocytes (zone 3 necrosis).
7First-pass metabolism of oral drugs occurs in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Oral drug → absorbed → portal vein → liver + intestinal wall metabolism before entering systemic circulation. This reduces bioavailability.
8Methylation differs from other Phase II reactions because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Methylation decreases biological activity but DOES NOT markedly increase water solubility — unique among Phase II reactions.
9A patient on rifampicin starts the oral contraceptive pill. She gets pregnant. The reason is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Rifampicin is a potent CYP450 inducer → ↑ metabolism of estrogen in OCP → ↓ circulating estrogen → contraceptive failure.
10In slow acetylators taking isoniazid (INH):
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Slow acetylators have low NAT activity → INH accumulates → INH competes with Vitamin B6 (PLP) → peripheral neuropathy. Also more hepatotoxic metabolites.
