📝 Practice MCQs 157 Questions
1Carbon dioxide is a product of the following enzyme:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — α‑Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation of α‑ketoglutarate to succinyl‑CoA, releasing CO₂.
2The following enzyme participates in substrate‑level phosphorylation:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Succinyl‑CoA synthetase (succinate thiokinase) directly generates GTP (or ATP) from the high‑energy thioester bond of succinyl‑CoA — substrate‑level phosphorylation.
3Thiamine is important for conversion of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a cofactor for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.
4Conversion of succinyl‑CoA to succinate requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Succinyl‑CoA synthetase phosphorylates GDP to GTP (coupled with release of succinate from succinyl‑CoA).
5Dehydrogenation of succinic acid to fumaric acid requires the following hydrogen carrier:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Succinate dehydrogenase uses FAD (tightly bound, becoming FADH₂) to oxidize succinate to fumarate.
6The Krebs cycle occurs in which cellular location in eukaryotic cells?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — All Krebs cycle enzymes (except succinate dehydrogenase, which is membrane‑embedded) are located in the mitochondrial matrix.
7The enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA before entry into the Krebs cycle is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle.
8Which enzyme of the Krebs cycle is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Succinate dehydrogenase is unique among TCA enzymes in being an integral inner mitochondrial membrane protein, also serving as Complex II of the electron transport chain.
9How many NADH molecules are generated per turn of the Krebs cycle (per acetyl‑CoA)?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Three NADH molecules are produced per turn: at isocitrate dehydrogenase, α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase.
10The Krebs cycle is described as amphibolic because it:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Amphibolic means serving both catabolic (oxidative energy production) and anabolic roles (intermediates feed gluconeogenesis, heme synthesis, amino acid synthesis, etc.).
11Which step produces CO₂?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to α‑ketoglutarate, releasing CO₂ (one of the cycle's two decarboxylation steps).
12An infant with developmental delay and lactic acidosis has pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency. Which metabolite cannot effectively enter the Krebs cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — With PDH deficiency, pyruvate cannot be converted to acetyl‑CoA, so it cannot effectively enter the TCA cycle and instead accumulates and is reduced to lactate.
13A 3‑month‑old infant with developmental delay, hypotonia, and seizures has elevated fumarate levels due to fumarase deficiency. Which step is impaired?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Fumarase normally catalyzes hydration of fumarate to malate; its deficiency blocks this step, causing fumarate to accumulate.
14What is the product formed by malate dehydrogenase?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Malate dehydrogenase oxidizes malate to oxaloacetate, regenerating the molecule needed to combine with the next acetyl‑CoA.
15A patient with prolonged starvation has low protein intake. Which TCA intermediate is most dependent on amino acid metabolism for replenishment?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — α‑Ketoglutarate is the transamination product of glutamate and is the TCA intermediate most directly replenished by amino acid catabolism.
16Malate dehydrogenase produces:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Malate dehydrogenase reduces NAD⁺ to NADH while oxidizing malate to oxaloacetate.
17A chronic alcoholic with confusion and lactic acidosis improves after thiamine (TPP). Which combined metabolic processes were impaired?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Both pyruvate dehydrogenase and α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase require TPP; thiamine deficiency impairs both, contributing to lactic acidosis that improves with thiamine repletion.
18Acetyl‑CoA is formed from pyruvate by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA via oxidative decarboxylation, releasing CO₂ and generating NADH.
19Which is important in transferring energy from the glycolytic pathway to the TCA cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Acetyl‑CoA, generated from glycolytically derived pyruvate, is the molecule that physically carries carbon/energy into the TCA cycle.
20CO₂ is NOT produced in the reaction catalyzed by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Succinate dehydrogenase catalyzes a simple dehydrogenation (succinate→fumarate) without decarboxylation, unlike the other three enzymes listed.
21How many ATP molecules are produced on complete oxidation of acetyl‑CoA in the citric acid cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — One turn of the TCA cycle yields 3 NADH (×~2.5 ATP), 1 FADH₂ (×~1.5 ATP), and 1 GTP, totaling approximately 12 ATP per cycle from the textbook count used here — but oxidation of one acetyl‑CoA together with its entry products is conventionally tallied at 15 ATP in many classic biochemistry texts using older (P/O ratio 3 and 2) conventions.
22The following cofactor is NOT associated with the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The PDH complex requires TPP, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD⁺, and CoA — biotin is not one of its cofactors (biotin is used by pyruvate carboxylase instead).
23All of the following are intermediates of the citric acid cycle EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Pyruvate is the substrate that is converted to acetyl‑CoA before entering the cycle; it is not itself a TCA cycle intermediate.
24The TCA cycle to be continued requires regeneration of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Oxaloacetate must be regenerated at the end of each turn so it can condense with a new acetyl‑CoA molecule via citrate synthase, allowing the cycle to continue.
25How many ATP molecules are produced on complete oxidation of pyruvic acid in the citric acid cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Including the NADH generated by pyruvate dehydrogenase plus the full turn of the TCA cycle, complete oxidation of one pyruvate is classically tallied at about 15 ATP.
26How many ATP molecules are produced on complete oxidation of glucose?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Using the classic (older textbook) accounting, complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule yields about 38 ATP (more recent estimates using updated P/O ratios give ~30–32, but 38 is the answer used by this source).
27The following cofactor is NOT associated with the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — NADP⁺ is not a PDH cofactor; the complex instead uses NAD⁺, along with FAD, lipoic acid, TPP, and CoA.
28The only enzyme of the TCA cycle that produces FADH₂ is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Succinate dehydrogenase is the sole TCA enzyme that reduces FAD to FADH₂; the other dehydrogenases use NAD⁺.
29The only enzyme of the TCA cycle attached to the inner mitochondrial membrane is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Succinate dehydrogenase is the only TCA cycle enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (also functioning as ETC Complex II).
30The only enzyme of the TCA cycle that produces GTP is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Succinyl‑CoA synthetase generates GTP directly via substrate‑level phosphorylation as succinyl‑CoA is converted to succinate.
31Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is located in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The PDH complex is a large multi‑enzyme assembly located in the mitochondrial matrix.
32Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is active in the ________ state:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — PDH kinase phosphorylates (inactivates) the complex, while PDH phosphatase dephosphorylates (activates) it — so the dephosphorylated form is active.
33All of the following are key enzymes of the TCA cycle EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The classic rate‑limiting/regulatory enzymes of the TCA cycle are citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; succinate dehydrogenase is not considered one of the key regulatory steps.
34Malonate inhibits:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Malonate is a classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, structurally resembling succinate.
35________ is used in heme synthesis:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Succinyl‑CoA condenses with glycine (via ALA synthase) as the first step of heme (porphyrin) biosynthesis.
36Which condition decreases the oxidation of acetyl‑CoA by the citric acid cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — A high acetyl‑CoA/CoA ratio signals abundant fuel and high energy charge, which slows further oxidation through the cycle (e.g., reduced free CoA limits citrate synthase activity).
37An amphibolic pathway among the following is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The citric acid cycle is amphibolic, serving both catabolic (oxidation for energy) and anabolic (precursor supply) functions.
38The TCA cycle does NOT take place in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria, so they cannot run the TCA cycle and rely on anaerobic glycolysis.
39Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex require the following for oxidative decarboxylation:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Both multi‑enzyme complexes share the same five cofactors: NAD⁺, FAD, CoA‑SH, TPP, and lipoic acid.
40Substrate‑level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle occurs in which step?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The conversion of succinyl‑CoA to succinate, catalyzed by succinyl‑CoA synthetase, directly generates GTP — the cycle's only substrate‑level phosphorylation step.
41Which enzyme is thiamine‑dependent (TPP) and essential for glucose oxidation in the brain?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Both pyruvate dehydrogenase and α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are TPP‑dependent and essential for oxidative glucose metabolism in the brain, which is why thiamine deficiency severely impairs cerebral energy production.
42Positive nitrogen balance occurs in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Pregnancy is an anabolic state with net protein/tissue synthesis, producing positive nitrogen balance, unlike the catabolic states of starvation, burns, and cancer.
43Negative nitrogen balance is seen in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus promotes protein catabolism, producing negative nitrogen balance, in contrast to the anabolic states listed.
44Oxidative deamination mainly occurs in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Oxidative deamination (mainly via glutamate dehydrogenase) is most active in the liver and kidney, the principal sites of nitrogen disposal.
45L‑amino acid oxidase requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — L‑amino acid oxidase is a flavoprotein that uses FAD as its coenzyme.
46Transamination requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Transaminases require pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B₆, as coenzyme.
47GPT is also called:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — GPT (glutamate‑pyruvate transaminase) is the older name for ALT (alanine aminotransferase).
48Transdeamination is a combination of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Transdeamination couples transamination (amino acid → glutamate) with oxidative deamination of glutamate (by glutamate dehydrogenase), allowing most amino groups to be funneled into free ammonia.
49The predominant amino‑group acceptor in human intermediary metabolism is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — α‑Ketoglutarate is the principal amino‑group acceptor, being converted to glutamate during most transamination reactions.
50Which reaction does NOT liberate NH₃?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Transamination simply transfers an amino group between molecules without releasing free ammonia; oxidative deamination (and hence transdeamination) does release NH₃.
51The coenzyme of transaminases is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), derived from vitamin B₆, is the coenzyme for all transamination reactions.
52Free NH₃ is released during:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate, releasing free ammonia and regenerating α‑ketoglutarate.
53D‑amino acid oxidase needs ________ as a coenzyme:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — D‑amino acid oxidase is an FAD‑dependent flavoprotein (unlike L‑amino acid oxidase, which some sources also link to FAD, the distinguishing answer here is FAD).
54L‑glutamate dehydrogenase needs ________ as a coenzyme:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Glutamate dehydrogenase uses NAD⁺ (or NADP⁺) as coenzyme for the oxidative deamination of glutamate.
55Positive nitrogen balance occurs in all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Diabetes mellitus is catabolic, producing negative (not positive) nitrogen balance, unlike pregnancy, growth, and convalescence.
56Negative nitrogen balance occurs in all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Pregnancy is anabolic (positive nitrogen balance), unlike the catabolic states of starvation, thyrotoxicosis, and diabetes mellitus.
57Positive nitrogen balance can occur:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Growth states such as infancy involve net protein synthesis exceeding breakdown, producing positive nitrogen balance.
58An amino acid that cannot undergo transamination is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Lysine lacks a suitable α‑amino group arrangement for standard transamination and is catabolized by a different route (via saccharopine).
59________ is increased in blood in liver disease (hepatitis):
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — ALT (GPT) is relatively liver‑specific and is the more sensitive/specific marker elevated in hepatocellular disease such as hepatitis.
60________ is increased in blood in case of myocardial infarction:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — AST (GOT) is found in high concentration in cardiac muscle and rises markedly after myocardial infarction.
61Transamination reaction is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Transamination reactions are readily reversible, allowing interconversion between various amino acids and their corresponding keto acids.
62________ biosynthesis is catalyzed by an enzyme that converts ATP to ADP and Pi:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Glutamine synthetase uses ATP (hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi) to add ammonia to glutamate, forming glutamine.
63Ammonia is transported from muscle to liver in the form of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Muscle uses the glucose‑alanine cycle, transaminating pyruvate to alanine to safely carry amino groups to the liver.
64NH₃ is detoxified in the brain in the form of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — In the brain, glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine, the main non‑toxic carrier of ammonia.
65The organ which is extremely sensitive to ammonia toxicity is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The brain is exquisitely sensitive to hyperammonemia, which underlies the neurological symptoms of urea cycle disorders and hepatic encephalopathy.
66What is the site of the urea cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The urea cycle operates mainly in the liver, the principal site of ammonia detoxification into urea.
67What is the normal level of blood urea?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Normal blood urea is approximately 20–40 mg/dL.
68Deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthase 1 leads to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — CPS‑1 deficiency, the first urea cycle enzyme defect, is classified as hyperammonemia type 1.
69The number of ATP utilized for synthesis of one molecule of urea is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Synthesis of one urea molecule consumes the equivalent of 4 ATP (2 used by CPS‑1, 1 by argininosuccinate synthetase using ATP→AMP, counted as 2 high‑energy bonds, totaling 4 ATP equivalents).
70The following enzyme of the urea cycle is present in cytosol:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinase (lyase), and arginase are all cytosolic enzymes of the urea cycle.
71Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CPS‑1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that uses free ammonia (NH₃) as its nitrogen source (not aspartate), consuming 2 ATP, and is activated (not inhibited) by N‑acetylglutamate.
72Hydrolysis of which amino acid yields urea?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Arginase hydrolyzes arginine to release urea and regenerate ornithine.
73Which compound is shared by the TCA cycle and the urea cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Fumarate, released when argininosuccinate is cleaved to arginine, links the urea cycle back into the TCA cycle.
74Which proteins are given to hyperammonemic patients?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Plant proteins are generally lower in the amino acids that heavily burden ammonia‑detoxifying pathways, making them preferable in hyperammonemic patients on protein‑restricted diets.
75The major site of urea synthesis is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The liver is the major (essentially sole) site of complete urea cycle activity and urea synthesis.
76The enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, like many ATP‑utilizing enzymes, requires Mg²⁺ as a cofactor.
77The nitrogen atoms of urea are provided by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — One nitrogen of urea comes from free NH₃ (via carbamoyl phosphate) and the other from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase).
78Enzymes of the urea cycle are found in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CPS‑1 and ornithine transcarbamylase are mitochondrial, while the remaining three urea cycle enzymes are cytosolic.
79A compound serving as a link between the citric acid cycle and the urea cycle is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Fumarate generated by argininosuccinase links the urea cycle to the TCA cycle (this connection is sometimes called the Krebs bicycle).
80Carbamoyl phosphate required for urea synthesis is formed in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 is a mitochondrial enzyme, so carbamoyl phosphate for the urea cycle is formed in mitochondria.
81The major end product of protein catabolism in humans is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Urea is the principal nitrogenous waste product of amino acid/protein catabolism in humans.
82NH₃ is detoxified in brain mainly as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The brain lacks a complete urea cycle, so it detoxifies ammonia mainly by forming glutamine via glutamine synthetase.
83The amino acid NOT involved in the urea cycle is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Arginine, ornithine, and citrulline are direct urea cycle intermediates; histidine plays no role in the cycle.
84NH₃ is detoxified in liver as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The liver, possessing the complete urea cycle, detoxifies ammonia mainly by converting it to urea.
85The metabolite which sustains the urea cycle is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Ornithine is regenerated at the end of each turn (by arginase) and is required to combine with carbamoyl phosphate to keep the cycle running.
86Citrulline is an intermediate of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Citrulline is formed from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate as an intermediate of the urea cycle.
87NH₃ toxicity and hepatic encephalopathy occur in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Cirrhosis impairs hepatic urea cycle function, leading to ammonia accumulation and hepatic encephalopathy.
88Uremia occurs in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Uremia (elevated blood urea due to impaired excretion) occurs with renal disease such as nephritis.
89Low blood urea occurs in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Severe liver disease impairs urea synthesis, lowering blood urea, in contrast to renal disease or high protein intake which raise it.
90Flapping tremors are seen in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Asterixis (flapping tremor) is a classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy caused by ammonia toxicity.
91The standard drug in treatment of NH₃ intoxication is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia as ammonium, reducing its absorption — the standard treatment for hyperammonemia/hepatic encephalopathy.
92Helpful in prevention of hyperammonemia:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Branched‑chain amino acid supplementation is used in hepatic disease to help correct amino acid imbalances and reduce ammonia‑generating aromatic amino acid metabolism.
93________ is the key enzyme of the urea cycle:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS‑1), which commits ammonia to the urea cycle and is activated by N‑acetylglutamate, is regarded as the key/regulatory enzyme.
94Aspartate contributes a nitrogen atom in which cycle?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Aspartate donates its amino group to citrulline (via argininosuccinate synthetase), supplying the second nitrogen atom of urea.
95Which compound is NOT formed from glycine?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Serotonin is synthesized from tryptophan, not glycine; glycine instead contributes to serine, heme, creatine, glutathione, and purines.
96Cysteine can be synthesized from methionine and ________:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The transsulfuration pathway combines homocysteine (from methionine) with serine to form cystathionine, which is then cleaved to yield cysteine.
97Dislocation of the eye lens is a manifestation of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Homocystinuria classically presents with ectopia lentis (lens dislocation), along with skeletal abnormalities and thromboembolism.
98Cysteine becomes essential in cases of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — In homocystinuria, the pathway converting methionine/homocysteine to cysteine is impaired, making cysteine conditionally essential.
99Aspartate is directly synthesized from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Transamination of oxaloacetate (accepting an amino group, typically from glutamate) directly produces aspartate.
100The conversion of glutamate to GABA requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Glutamate decarboxylase, which converts glutamate to GABA, requires PLP as its coenzyme.
101Which amino acid is a direct precursor for ergothionine?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Ergothioneine is synthesized from histidine (via a trimethylated histidine derivative).
102Glutamine synthetase uses glutamate to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Glutamine synthetase adds ammonia to glutamate (using ATP) to form glutamine, a key ammonia‑detoxification and nitrogen‑transport molecule.
103Branched‑chain amino acids (BCAAs) are primarily metabolized in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Unlike most amino acids, BCAAs are predominantly catabolized in skeletal muscle (and other peripheral tissues) rather than the liver, since the liver lacks significant branched‑chain aminotransferase activity.
104Which BCAA is exclusively ketogenic?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Leucine is degraded entirely to acetyl‑CoA and acetoacetate, making it purely ketogenic among the BCAAs.
105Which enzyme converts glutamate to GABA?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Glutamate decarboxylase (a PLP‑dependent enzyme) converts glutamate to the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
106Maple syrup urine disease leads to accumulation of which amino acids in plasma?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — MSUD is caused by deficient branched‑chain α‑ketoacid dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine (and their keto acids).
107Which BCAA is both ketogenic and glucogenic?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Isoleucine's carbon skeleton yields both acetyl‑CoA (ketogenic) and propionyl‑CoA → succinyl‑CoA (glucogenic), making it the only BCAA with both fates.
108Transamination reactions involving glutamate usually produce:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — When glutamate donates its amino group in transamination, it is converted back to α‑ketoglutarate.
109The first step in BCAA catabolism is catalyzed by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — BCAT transaminates the branched‑chain amino acids to their corresponding α‑keto acids as the first catabolic step.
110The following amino acid is not found normally in proteins:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Ornithine is a urea cycle intermediate and is not one of the 20 standard amino acids incorporated into proteins.
111The primary metabolic defect in Maple syrup urine disease is a deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — MSUD results from deficiency of branched‑chain α‑ketoacid dehydrogenase, blocking further oxidative decarboxylation of the BCAA‑derived keto acids.
112Cystinuria results from inability to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Cystinuria is a renal transporter defect that prevents reabsorption of cystine (and dibasic amino acids) in the renal tubules, leading to cystine stones.
113All of the following can be formed from tryptophan EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Melanin is derived from tyrosine, not tryptophan; niacin, serotonin, and melatonin are all tryptophan derivatives.
114Maple syrup urine is characterized by all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — MSUD is a disorder of branched‑chain (not aromatic) amino acid metabolism.
115The carbon skeleton of which amino acid(s) can form glucose as well as fatty acids?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are all both glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids.
116A low‑phenylalanine diet is recommended in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Phenylketonuria, caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, is managed with dietary restriction of phenylalanine.
117Glyoxylate is formed from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Glyoxylate is produced from glycine via the action of glycine oxidase/transaminase, and excess glyoxylate is linked to primary hyperoxaluria.
118High levels of VMA are present in urine in case of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), a catecholamine metabolite, is elevated in urine in pheochromocytoma.
119All of the following compounds are derived from glycine EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Collagen contains abundant glycine as a structural amino acid but is not biosynthetically 'derived from' glycine the way heme, glutathione, and purines/pyrimidines are.
120A patient with phenylketonuria is unable to convert:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — PKU results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, blocking conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
121Cysteine is a non‑essential amino acid; its carbon skeleton is derived from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The carbon skeleton of cysteine comes from serine, while the sulfur is donated by methionine (via homocysteine) in the transsulfuration pathway.
122SHIAA is present in urine in case of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — 5‑Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5‑HIAA), a serotonin metabolite, is markedly elevated in urine in carcinoid tumors (argentaffinoma).
123Increased risk for skin cancer is present in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Albinism results from defective melanin synthesis, removing the skin's main UV‑protective pigment and increasing skin cancer risk.
124Renal stone is present in all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Lesch‑Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency) causes hyperuricemia and gout but is not primarily associated with renal stone formation in the same classic way as the others; note hyperoxaluria, cystinuria, and homocystinuria are all stone‑forming conditions.
125Histamine is formed from histidine by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Histidine decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group of histidine to form histamine.
126In cases of phenylketonuria, the patient is advised to consume a diet rich in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Since PKU patients cannot make tyrosine from phenylalanine, tyrosine becomes conditionally essential and should be supplemented while phenylalanine is restricted.
127Maple syrup urine is an inborn error of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — MSUD is a disorder of branched‑chain amino acid (leucine, isoleucine, valine) catabolism.
128The pellagra‑preventing factor is synthesized from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Niacin (the pellagra‑preventing vitamin) can be endogenously synthesized from tryptophan.
129Dopamine is synthesized in two steps from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Tyrosine is hydroxylated to DOPA and then decarboxylated to dopamine — a two‑step pathway.
130Branched‑chain amino acids are NOT catabolized in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The liver lacks significant branched‑chain aminotransferase activity, so BCAAs largely bypass hepatic catabolism and are instead processed in muscle and other peripheral tissues.
131Cysteine is required to synthesize:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Cysteine is a precursor for taurine, coenzyme A (via pantetheine), and glutathione.
132Cysteine can be synthesized from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — As above, serine provides the carbon skeleton of cysteine in the transsulfuration pathway.
133The coenzyme required for most reactions of amino acids is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the coenzyme for the majority of amino acid reactions, including transamination, decarboxylation, and deamination.
134The following amino acid is essential in adult humans:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Tryptophan is one of the essential amino acids that must be obtained from the diet, unlike tyrosine, serine, and cysteine which can be synthesized endogenously.
135Which amino acid does NOT need tetrahydrofolate for its metabolism?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Tyrosine metabolism does not involve one‑carbon transfer via tetrahydrofolate, unlike glycine and histidine, whose metabolism generates one‑carbon units handled by THF.
136The diet of a child with Maple syrup urine disease should be low in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Since MSUD blocks branched‑chain amino acid catabolism, dietary leucine, isoleucine, and valine must be restricted.
137The following compounds are derived from glutamic acid:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Glutamate is a precursor for proline, ornithine, and GABA, among other compounds.
138Phenylketonuria is due to deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — PKU results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, which normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine.
139Alkaptonuria is due to deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Alkaptonuria results from deficient homogentisic acid oxidase, causing accumulation of homogentisic acid (which darkens urine and tissues).
140The purely ketogenic amino acid is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Leucine is the only amino acid that is purely ketogenic, being degraded entirely to acetyl‑CoA/acetoacetate with no glucogenic contribution.
141NO is derived from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Nitric oxide synthase converts the guanidino nitrogen of arginine into nitric oxide, with citrulline as a byproduct.
142DOPA is an intermediate in the synthesis of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — DOPA is a shared intermediate in both catecholamine synthesis (→ dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and melanin synthesis.
143Carnitine, essential for β‑oxidation, is derived from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Carnitine is synthesized from lysine (with methyl groups donated by SAM, and a contribution from methionine).
144β‑Alanine results from decarboxylation of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Decarboxylation of aspartic acid yields β‑alanine, a component of coenzyme A and carnosine.
145A protein rich in hydroxyproline is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Collagen is uniquely rich in hydroxyproline, formed by post‑translational hydroxylation of proline residues (a vitamin C‑dependent step).
146Arginine is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Arginine is semi‑essential (essential during growth/stress), serves as a precursor for creatine and nitric oxide, and is also a urea cycle intermediate.
147Which amino acid is both glucogenic and ketogenic?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Isoleucine yields both glucogenic (succinyl‑CoA) and ketogenic (acetyl‑CoA) products upon catabolism.
148The smell of rotten egg is characteristic of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Cystinuria is associated with a sulfurous, rotten‑egg‑like odor due to excess sulfur‑containing cystine in the urine.
149The smell of burnt sugar is characteristic of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Maple syrup urine disease classically produces a sweet, burnt‑sugar (maple syrup) odor in urine and sweat.
150The smell of burnt sugar is due to the presence of ________ in urine:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The characteristic maple syrup odor of MSUD urine is attributed to elevated leucine and its keto‑acid derivatives.
151The main enzyme responsible for activation of xenobiotics is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Cytochrome P‑450 (phase I) often converts relatively inert xenobiotics into more reactive intermediates, sometimes 'activating' them before phase II conjugation.
152In metabolism of xenobiotics, all of the following occur in phase I EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Conjugation reactions belong to phase II metabolism; phase I consists of oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions that expose or introduce functional groups.
153Which organ has the greatest xenobiotic metabolism capability?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The liver has by far the highest capacity for xenobiotic (drug/toxin) metabolism, owing to its rich cytochrome P‑450 and conjugating enzyme content.
154The cofactor for methylation reactions is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — S‑adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the universal methyl donor for methylation (phase II) reactions.
155The cofactor for sulfation reactions is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — 3'‑Phosphoadenosine‑5'‑phosphosulfate (PAPS) is the active sulfate donor for sulfation (phase II) reactions.
156Cytochrome P450 has all the following characteristics EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Cytochrome P450s constitute a large, diverse superfamily of many distinct gene families, not a single uniform gene family shared with all other cytochromes.
157Phase I reactions include:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Monooxygenation (hydroxylation) by cytochrome P450 is a classic phase I reaction, while conjugation (e.g., glucuronidation, hippuric acid formation) belongs to phase II.
✍️Biochemistry Written›

1 — Differences Between Glucokinase and Hexokinase

GlucokinaseHexokinase
SiteLiver and pancreatic β cellsAll tissue
Affinity to glucoseLow affinity (high Km)High affinity (low Km)
SubstrateGlucose onlyGlucose & galactose & fructose
Effect of insulinInduces synthesis of glucokinaseNo effect
Effect of glucoseNo effectAllosterically inhibits hexokinase

2 — Lactic Acidosis

  • Conditions that cause decreased oxygenation of tissues force excessive dependence on anaerobic glycolysis for energy production, with lactic acid buildup in tissues and blood
  • Conditions that interfere with circulatory function and cause lactic acidosis: convulsions, shock, uncontrolled hemorrhage

3 — Synthesis and Importance of 2,3-Biphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in RBCs

  • Synthesis:
  • → Some of the 1,3-BPG is converted to 2,3-BPG by action of bisphosphoglycerate mutase
  • → 2,3-BPG is found in only trace amounts in most cells & in high concentration in RBCs
  • Importance:
  • → Interaction of 2,3-BPG with β-chain hemoglobin → decreases hemoglobin affinity for O₂ → release of O₂ to tissues (protects against hypoxia)
  • → In high altitudes & hypoxic states, O₂ tension is low → stimulates synthesis of BPG

4 — Differences Between Liver and Muscle Glycogen

Liver glycogenMuscle glycogen
Amount120 gm (6% of liver weight)300 gm (1% of muscle weight)
SourceHexoses & gluconeogenesisBlood glucose
FunctionSource of blood glucoseSource of energy to muscle
FateGlucoseGlucose 6-phosphate
StarvationReduces liver glycogenNo effect on muscle glycogen
ExerciseHas no effectReduced
InsulinIncrease
GlucagonDecreaseNo effect
GlucocorticoidsIncreaseNo effect

5 — Von Gierke's Disease

  • Cause: due to glucose 6-phosphatase enzyme deficiency in liver
  • Manifestations:
  • 1- Fasting hypoglycemia
  • 2- Hepatomegaly
  • 3- Hyperlipidemia
  • 4- Lactic acidosis
  • 5- Hyperuricaemia
  • 6- Short stature
  • Pathogenesis:
  • 1- Deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase → 2 dual effects:
  • → Glucose 6-P can't pass to blood → hypoglycemia during fasting
  • → Deficiency affects the last steps of gluconeogenesis → more fasting hypoglycemia
  • → Inability to utilize glucose → lipolysis & increased fatty acids oxidation
  • → Accumulated glucose 6-P enters glycolysis → increases formation of lactic acid → lactic acidosis
  • → Glucose 6-P is converted to ribose 5-P via the HMP-pathway → stimulates PRPP synthetase enzyme → increases biosynthesis of purine bases and hyperuricemia

6 — Cori's Disease

  • Cause: due to debranching enzyme deficiency
  • Manifestations: mild hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly

7 — McArdle's Disease

  • Cause: due to deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme → muscle cramps & weakness on exercise
  • Very low blood lactate after exercise

8 — Complex I and II

  • Complex I:
  • → Contains NADH dehydrogenase enzyme, FMN as hydrogen carrier, iron-sulfur center
  • → Takes 2e⁻ & 2H⁺ from NADH+H⁺ → pass to FMN → 2e⁻ pass to iron-sulfur center → coenzyme Q
  • Complex II:
  • → Contains FAD, succinate dehydrogenase (the only enzyme attached to the inner mitochondrial membrane) & iron-sulfur center
  • → Electrons move from succinate to FAD → iron-sulfur center → to coenzyme Q → produce coenzyme QH₂

9 — Mobile Carriers

  • Coenzyme Q: receives electrons from both complex I and complex II
  • Cytochrome C:
  • → Complexes with cytochrome c1 of complex III
  • → Diffuses through the inner mitochondrial membrane, shuttling electrons from c1 of complex III to Cu of complex IV

10 — Uncoupling Agents

  • Increase permeability of membrane → decrease the proton gradient. ATP synthesis stops, but electron transport continues
  • Allow oxidation to occur but prevent phosphorylation (ATP formation)
  • Examples: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (used for weight loss), Aspirin (overdose), Thyroxine in large doses, Thermogenin in brown fat (more mitochondria than white fat)

11 — Importance of Glycine

  • 1. Formation of purine bases
  • 2. Formation of bile salts
  • 3. Formation of creatine
  • 4. Formation of other amino acids as serine
  • 5. Formation of collagen
  • 6. Production of Heme

12 — Phenylketonuria

  • Cause: deficiency in phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme
  • Manifestations:
  • 1- Elevated blood levels of phenylpyruvate, phenyl-lactate and phenylacetate in tissues, plasma and urine
  • 2- Mental retardation, failure to walk, talk, seizures, hyperactivity, tremors, microcephaly and failure to grow
  • 3- Hypopigmentation
  • Treatment:
  • 1. Diet low in phenylalanine, high in tyrosine
  • 2- Avoid aspartame
  • 3- Gene therapy

13 — Importance of Tryptophan

  • 1. Synthesis of serotonin (catabolized to 5-HIAA → increased in urine → intestine cancer); a VC and neurotransmitter
  • 2. Synthesis of melatonin (increased during dark period); hormone synthesized from serotonin via acetylation & methylation
  • 3. Nicotinic acid formation: 60 mg of tryptophan → 1 mg of nicotinic acid
  • → Tryptophan deficiency or vit. B6 deficiency impairs nicotinic acid synthesis → Pellagra

14 — Hartnup Disease

  • Hereditary disorder of tryptophan metabolism → impaired renal tubular reabsorption of tryptophan, basic amino acid histidine and lysine
  • The condition is also associated with a pellagra skin rash, and improves with nicotinic acid administration

15 — Regulation of Heme Synthesis

  • δ-ALA synthase is the key enzyme
  • Stimulation:
  • → Drugs (Phenobarbital, griseofulvin)
  • → Excess porphyrin production → worsen symptoms
  • Inhibition:
  • → Iron
  • → Steroids
  • → Glucose
  • → Lead poisoning → decreases synthesis
  • → Feedback inhibition → increased heme
  • → Increased hemin → suppresses δ-ALA synthase

16 — Importance of Heme

  • • Hemoglobin (O₂ transport)
  • • Myoglobin (O₂ carrying in muscle)
  • • Cytochromes (electron transport & cytochrome P450)
  • • Catalase and peroxidase (H₂O₂ utilization)

17 — Causes, Clinical Evaluation and Management of Physiological Jaundice

  • Causes:
  • → Short life span of fetal red blood cells
  • → Insufficient albumin
  • → Sterile gut
  • → Poor peristalsis
  • → Immature liver
  • → Decreased UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity
  • Clinical evaluation:
  • 1- History: infection, drugs, Rh, birth trauma, feeding pattern
  • 2- Lab: blood culture, liver function tests, direct Coombs test, total serum bilirubin, osmotic fragility
  • Management:
  • → Most of physiological jaundice → no treatment
  • → Phototherapy if total bilirubin > 21 mg/dL → blue light converts trans-bilirubin to cis-bilirubin
1Tongue›

Overview — Tongue Structure

  • Definition: Muscular organ occupying floor of mouth; has apex, base, and two surfaces (dorsal upper + ventral lower)
  • Apex (tip): Lies behind the incisor teeth
  • Base: Directed backwards — attached to mandible by genioglossus and to hyoid bone by hyoglossus

Dorsal Surface — Sulcus Terminalis

  • Directed upwards towards the palate
  • Divided by V-shaped groove called sulcus terminalis into two parts:
  • → Anterior 2/3: oral (mobile) part — lies in oral cavity
  • → Posterior 1/3: pharyngeal part — faces oropharynx
  • Foramen caecum: Narrow pit at the APEX of sulcus terminalis; directed backwards; embryonic remnant of thyroglossal duct (which gives origin to thyroid gland in fetus)
  • Lingual tonsil: Collections of lymphoid follicles in the submucosa of the dorsal surface of the posterior 1/3 of the tongue

Ventral Surface

  • Mucous membrane is smooth and reflected from lower surface of tongue into floor of mouth
  • The mucous membrane forms frenulum in midline

Nerve Supply — Motor

  • All muscles of tongue (intrinsic + extrinsic) are supplied by hypoglossal nerve CN XII
  • EXCEPT palatoglossus muscle — supplied by pharyngeal plexus (vagus CN X)

Nerve Supply — Sensory (Very Important!)

  • Anterior 2/3:
  • → General sensations (touch, pain, temperature): lingual nerve (branch of mandibular nerve V3)
  • → Taste sensations: chorda tympani (branch of facial nerve CN VII)
  • Posterior 1/3:
  • → BOTH general AND taste sensations: glossopharyngeal nerve CN IX
  • Root of tongue (posterior part):
  • → BOTH general AND taste: internal laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X)

Blood Supply of the Tongue

  • Arterial Supply (3 sources):
  • → Lingual artery: carries the MAIN arterial supply of tongue
  • → Tonsillar branch of facial artery: supplies posterior part
  • → Twigs from ascending pharyngeal artery: supply posterior part
  • Venous Drainage:
  • → 2 groups of veins (superficial and deep to hyoglossus muscle)
  • → Join at posterior border of hyoglossus → common lingual veins
  • → End in internal jugular vein OR common facial vein

Lymphatic Drainage

  • Anterior 2/3:
  • → Tip: drains into submental lymph nodes
  • → Margins: drain into submandibular LN of same side
  • → Central part: drains into submandibular LN of BOTH sides
  • Posterior 1/3: drains directly into deep cervical LN of both sides
🏥 Lingual carcinoma spreads first to submental then submandibular LNs. Posterior 1/3 tumor → referred otalgia via CN IX tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) → pain felt in ear.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1All muscles of the tongue are supplied by CN XII EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus CN X). It is the only tongue muscle not supplied by hypoglossal nerve.
2Taste sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Chorda tympani (branch of facial nerve CN VII) carries TASTE from anterior 2/3. Lingual nerve (V3) carries only general sensation from same area.
3The foramen caecum is significant because it is the embryonic remnant of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Foramen caecum marks the site where the thyroglossal duct began. The thyroid gland descends from this point to its final cervical position.
4General sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue travels via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Lingual nerve (branch of mandibular V3) carries general sensation (touch, pain, temperature) from the anterior 2/3.
5Both general AND taste sensation from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue are carried by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — CN IX (glossopharyngeal) carries BOTH modalities from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue.
6The main arterial supply of the tongue is from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Lingual artery (branch of external carotid) is the main supply. Tonsillar branch of facial and ascending pharyngeal supply mainly the posterior part.
7The sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The V-shaped sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into oral part (ant 2/3) and pharyngeal part (post 1/3). Its apex points backwards.
8The lingual tonsil is located in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Lingual tonsil = lymphoid follicles in submucosa of the dorsal surface of the posterior 1/3.
9Venous drainage of the tongue ultimately flows into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Common lingual veins drain into either the internal jugular vein or the common facial vein.
10A patient has a tumor in the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and complains of ear pain. This referred otalgia is via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — CN IX supplies posterior 1/3. Its tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) supplies the middle ear mucosa → referred pain felt as otalgia.
2Parotid Gland›

Overview — Three Major Salivary Glands

  • Parotid: Largest salivary gland; purely serous secretion; pre-auricular
  • Submandibular: Mixed (mainly serous); weight 10-20g; submandibular fossa
  • → Submandibular duct (Wharton's duct): 5 cm long; opens on sublingual papilla in floor of mouth
  • → Parasympathetic: from superior salivary nucleus (pons) → facial nerve → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → relays in submandibular ganglion
  • Sublingual: Smallest; mainly mucous; weight 3-4g; lies in floor of mouth
  • → Opens by ~15 small ducts on sublingual fold
  • → Same parasympathetic pathway as submandibular gland (relay in submandibular ganglion)

Parotid Gland — Site & Shape

  • Largest salivary gland; purely SEROUS secretion
  • Site: Below external acoustic meatus; between angle of mandible and sternomastoid muscle
  • Shape: Roughly pyramidal with 2 ends (upper, lower), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), 3 surfaces
  • Surface anatomy: Represented by 4 points: A (tragus of auricle), B (midpoint of anterior border of mastoid), C (midpoint of mandibular notch), D (anterior border of SCM 2cm below angle of mandible)

Parotid Capsule

  • True (inner) capsule: Formed by condensation of connective tissue of the gland
  • False (outer) capsule: From deep cervical fascia splitting into 2 layers (one superficial, one deep to gland)
  • Deep layer → stylomandibular ligament: Separates parotid from submandibular gland
  • Clinical: In mumps, enlarged parotid is enclosed by firm false capsule → severe pain

Parotid Duct (Stensen's Duct)

  • Length: 2 inches (5 cm)
  • Emerges from anterior border of gland → passes forwards on masseter muscle, one finger-breadth below zygomatic arch
  • At anterior border of masseter → curves INWARDS and pierces: buccal pad of fat → buccopharyngeal fascia → buccinator muscle → mucous membrane of mouth
  • Opens into: Vestibule of mouth OPPOSITE the upper 2nd molar tooth
  • N.B: Short oblique passage between buccinator and mucosa acts as valve-like mechanism preventing inflation of duct during blowing

Structures Inside Parotid — Superficial to Deep

  • 1. Facial nerve CN VII — MOST SUPERFICIAL (enters through postero-medial surface → divides into 5 terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, cervical)
  • 2. Retromandibular vein (posterior facial vein) — formed inside gland by union of superficial temporal vein + maxillary vein; divides into anterior and posterior divisions
  • 3. External carotid artery — DEEPEST (enters through postero-medial surface → divides into superficial temporal artery + maxillary artery)
  • 4. Auriculotemporal nerve (enters through anteromedial surface)
  • 5. Deep parotid lymph nodes

Accessory Parts of Parotid

  • 1. Accessory parotid gland: Anterior border of gland may separate from main gland → lies superficial to masseter muscle above parotid duct
  • 2. Mandibular fossa extension: Upper part of gland may extend behind TMJ into mandibular fossa → patient with mumps feels severe pain DURING MASTICATION as jaw movement compresses inflamed gland

Blood Supply & Lymphatics

  • Arterial: Branches from external carotid artery and its terminal branches
  • Venous: Drains into retromandibular vein
  • Lymph: Parotid LN → upper deep cervical LN

Nerve Supply of Parotid (Very Important — Parasympathetic Pathway)

  • Sensory: Auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3)
  • Sympathetic: Plexus around external carotid artery
  • Parasympathetic (secretomotor) — Step by step:
  • Step 1: Preganglionic fibres arise from INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS in medulla oblongata
  • Step 2: Pass with glossopharyngeal nerve CN IX
  • Step 3: In jugular foramen → CN IX gives TYMPANIC BRANCH (Jacobson's nerve) → enters middle ear → forms tympanic plexus → gives LESSER PETROSAL NERVE
  • Step 4: Lesser petrosal nerve enters infratemporal fossa → relays in OTIC GANGLION
  • Step 5: Postganglionic fibres from otic ganglion → travel with AURICULOTEMPORAL NERVE → reach parotid gland
🏥 (1) Parotid tumor → compresses CN VII → unilateral facial paralysis. (2) Surgical incisions must be TRANSVERSE (terminal branches of CN VII run horizontally). (3) Frey's syndrome (auriculotemporal syndrome): sweating while eating after parotidectomy — regenerating auriculotemporal nerve mistakenly innervates sweat glands instead of parotid.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Stensen's duct opens opposite:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The parotid duct opens into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth.
2Structures inside the parotid from most superficial to deepest:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — From superficial to deep: Facial nerve CN VII (most superficial) → Retromandibular vein → External carotid artery (deepest).
3Parasympathetic supply to parotid relays in which ganglion?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The lesser petrosal nerve (from CN IX via tympanic branch) carries preganglionic fibres to the OTIC GANGLION. Postganglionic fibres travel with the auriculotemporal nerve.
4A parotid tumor causes facial palsy because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — CN VII is the most superficial content of the parotid gland. A tumor growing in the gland will compress CN VII first → facial palsy.
5Why must surgical incisions in the parotid region be transverse?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The 5 terminal branches of CN VII fan out horizontally in the parotid gland. Transverse incisions are parallel to these branches, minimising risk of facial nerve injury.
6Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the parotid travel with:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Inferior salivary nucleus → CN IX → tympanic branch → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion. NOT the facial nerve (which supplies submandibular + sublingual).
7The parotid gland is histologically:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Parotid = purely serous. Submandibular = mixed (mainly serous). Sublingual = mainly mucous.
8Mumps causes severe pain on eating because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The upper part of the parotid gland may extend behind the TMJ into the mandibular fossa. Inflammation (mumps) + jaw movement during chewing → increased pressure → severe pain.
9The retromandibular vein is formed inside the parotid by union of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The retromandibular vein is formed inside the parotid gland by the union of the SUPERFICIAL TEMPORAL VEIN and MAXILLARY VEIN.
10Frey's syndrome after parotidectomy is caused by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Frey's syndrome: after parotid surgery, the auriculotemporal nerve regenerates and mistakenly supplies sweat glands of the overlying skin → sweating and flushing during eating (gustatory sweating).
3Peritoneum›

Definition & Layers

  • Definition: Large thin serous membrane lining the interior of the abdominopelvic cavity; forms the LARGEST SEROUS SAC of the body
  • Visceral peritoneum: Covers the organs
  • Parietal peritoneum: Lines the abdominal wall
  • Peritoneal cavity (peritoneal sac): Potential space between the two layers containing a film of serous fluid (peritoneal fluid)
  • Completely closed sac EXCEPT for the opening of the uterine tube in FEMALE → clinical significance: ascending pelvic infection can reach peritoneal cavity

Peritoneal Coverage of Organs

  • Some organs invaginate peritoneum fully → covered completely except at line of mesenteric attachment
  • Other organs invaginate to a lesser degree → covered on front and sides only
  • Some organs (e.g. duodenum) barely invaginate → covered anteriorly only
  • Intraperitoneal organs (covered completely, have mesentery): jejunum, ileum, transverse colon, stomach, spleen, 1st part duodenum, appendix, sigmoid colon
  • Retroperitoneal organs — Primary: Kidneys, adrenals, aorta, IVC — never had peritoneum
  • Retroperitoneal organs — Secondary: Duodenum (2nd–4th parts), ascending colon, descending colon, pancreas (except tail) — originally intraperitoneal but became retro during development

Peritoneal Folds — Classification

  • Rule: Each peritoneal fold = 2 layers EXCEPT greater omentum = 4 layers (reflected on itself)
  • A. Omenta:
  • → Lesser omentum: between lesser curvature of stomach and porta hepatis of liver; its right free border = anterior boundary of epiploic foramen; contains portal triad
  • → Greater omentum: between greater curvature of stomach and transverse colon; 4 layers; descends into pelvis then reflects upwards; acts as "policeman of abdomen"
  • B. Mesenteries:
  • → Mesentery of small intestine
  • → Transverse mesocolon
  • → Pelvic (sigmoid) mesocolon
  • C. Ligaments: Falciform, gastrosplenic, gastrophrenic, phrenicocolic, lienorenal

Peritoneal Spaces — Subdivisions

  • Greater sac: Main peritoneal cavity
  • Lesser sac (omental bursa): Situated BEHIND the stomach and lesser omentum
  • Epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow): Communication between lesser and greater sac
  • → Height: 3 cm in adults
  • → Boundaries: Anterior = thickened right edge of lesser omentum (containing portal vein posteriorly, hepatic artery left, CBD right); Posterior = peritoneum covering IVC; Above = caudate lobe of liver; Below = 1st inch of 1st part of duodenum

Subphrenic & Other Clinically Important Spaces

  • Subphrenic spaces: Right and left; between diaphragm and liver; common sites for abscess (right more common)
  • Bare area of liver: Area on posterior diaphragmatic surface NOT covered by peritoneum; bounded by coronary ligaments (right & left); allows direct spread of infection/tumour between liver and right pleural cavity — clinically important
  • Hepatorenal pouch (Morrison's pouch): Between right lobe of liver and right kidney; most dependent part in supine position → fluid collects here first
  • Rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas): In females; most dependent peritoneal space in erect/sitting position
  • Paracolic gutters: Lateral to ascending and descending colon; allow spread of fluid/pus up and down abdomen
⚠️ Greater omentum = "policeman of abdomen": migrates to sites of infection/inflammation and walls off the process, preventing generalised peritonitis. Also stores fat and has immune cells.
🏥 Peritonitis: inflammation (perforated viscus → generalised). Ascites: fluid in peritoneal cavity (causes: liver cirrhosis, malignancy, hypoalbuminaemia). Paracentesis: drain fluid through needle. Ectopic pregnancy can implant in peritoneal cavity (secondary to tubal rupture).
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1The peritoneal cavity communicates with the lesser sac via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow) is the ONLY communication between the greater sac and lesser sac (omental bursa).
2The greater omentum is unique because it has:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Greater omentum = 4 layers (peritoneum covers anterior and posterior of stomach, descends, then reflects back). All other peritoneal folds = 2 layers.
3Which is an INTRAPERITONEAL organ?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Transverse colon is intraperitoneal (suspended by transverse mesocolon). Duodenum (2nd-4th), ascending colon, and kidneys are retroperitoneal.
4Contents of the free right border of the lesser omentum (portal triad):
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Free right border of lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) = portal triad: Portal vein (posterior), Hepatic artery proper (left), CBD (right and anterior).
5The peritoneal cavity is NOT completely closed in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — In females, the uterine tube opens directly into the peritoneal cavity → ascending genital infection can cause peritonitis (PID) and ectopic peritoneal pregnancies can occur.
6The most dependent peritoneal space in the supine position:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Morrison's pouch (hepatorenal pouch, between right lobe of liver and right kidney) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the SUPINE position → fluid and blood collect here first.
7The "policeman of abdomen" refers to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Greater omentum migrates to sites of inflammation/infection and walls off the process → nickname "policeman of abdomen."
8Which is a SECONDARY retroperitoneal organ?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Pancreas (except tail) is secondary retroperitoneal — it was originally intraperitoneal but became retroperitoneal during embryonic development. Kidney = primary retroperitoneal.
9Inferior boundary of epiploic foramen is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The inferior boundary of the epiploic foramen is the 1st inch of the 1st part of the duodenum.
10In right-sided perforated duodenal ulcer, fluid tracking through paracolic gutter would go to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The right paracolic gutter connects the right iliac fossa to the right subphrenic space and Morrison's pouch. Duodenal fluid tracks superiorly to these spaces.
4Liver›

Site & Shape

  • Occupies: Right hypochondrium + upper epigastrium + part of left hypochondrium (up to left lateral/midclavicular line)
  • Lies mostly under cover of ribs and costal cartilages immediately below diaphragm
  • Shape: Wedge-shaped, resembles a four-sided pyramid on its side; base directed to right, apex to left
  • Surfaces: Diaphragmatic (smooth, dome-shaped) and Visceral (relatively flat/concave, facing down and back)
  • Inferior border: Thin and sharp medially; has notch for ligamentum teres (slightly to right of median plane); cystic notch on right

Lobes — Anatomical Division

  • Two main lobes: Right (6× larger) and Left — divided by:
  • → Falciform ligament: on diaphragmatic surface
  • → Fissure for ligamentum venosum: on posterior surface
  • → Fissure for ligamentum teres: on inferior surface
  • Caudate lobe: On posterior surface; bounded by IVC groove (right), fissure for ligamentum venosum (left), porta hepatis (below)
  • Quadrate lobe: On inferior surface; bounded by gallbladder fossa (right), fissure for ligamentum teres (left)
  • Functional/Surgical division (Cantlie line): Line from gallbladder fossa to IVC → divides liver into right and left functional lobes (each with independent blood supply, bile drainage, lymphatics)

Visceral Surface — H-shaped Arrangement

  • Right limb of H: IVC groove (posterior) + gallbladder fossa (anterior)
  • Left limb of H: Fissure for ligamentum venosum (posterior) + fissure for ligamentum teres (anterior)
  • Crossbar of H = PORTA HEPATIS (transverse fissure — "gate of the liver")
  • Contents of porta hepatis (front to back): Hepatic ducts (right and left) — FRONT; Hepatic artery branches — MIDDLE; Portal vein branches — POSTERIOR

Blood Supply

  • DUAL blood supply:
  • → Portal vein (~80%): venous, nutrient-rich blood from GIT; formed behind neck of pancreas at L1 (SMV + splenic vein)
  • → Hepatic artery proper (~20%): oxygenated blood; branch of common hepatic artery (from celiac trunk)
  • Venous drainage: 3 hepatic veins (right, middle, left) → drain into IVC just below diaphragm
  • N.B: Hepatic veins have no valves and drain directly into IVC

Peritoneal Attachments

  • Falciform ligament: Connects liver to anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm; contains ligamentum teres (obliterated left umbilical vein)
  • Bare area: Area on posterior diaphragmatic surface NOT covered by peritoneum; bounded by coronary ligaments (right and left); allows direct spread of infection between liver and thorax
  • Coronary ligaments: Reflect peritoneum from liver to diaphragm
  • Triangular ligaments: Left and right, at extremities of coronary ligaments
  • Ligamentum teres: Obliterated left umbilical vein (in falciform ligament)
  • Ligamentum venosum: Obliterated ductus venosus (fetal bypass of liver)

Relations of the Liver — All Surfaces

  • Superior surface: Related to the diaphragm, which separates it from: corresponding lungs and pleura (on each side); pericardium and heart (in the centre)
  • Anterior surface: Xiphoid process and anterior abdominal wall (in median plane); diaphragm and costal margin (on each side)
  • Right lateral surface: Related to diaphragm (intervening), then: Rt. lung and pleura (upper ⅓); Costo-diaphragmatic recess (middle ⅓); 10th and 11th ribs (lower ⅓)
  • Posterior surface (4 areas):
  • → Bare area proper: to the right of IVC groove, related to diaphragm and Rt. suprarenal gland
  • → Groove for IVC: lodges the IVC; pierced by hepatic veins
  • → Caudate lobe: related to the lesser sac (omental bursa)
  • → Oesophageal impression: just to the left of fissure for lig. venosum; related to abdominal oesophagus
  • Visceral (inferior) surface:
  • → Left lobe: Gastric impression (stomach); lesser omentum (omental tuberosity)
  • → Quadrate lobe: Lesser omentum; pyloric end of stomach; 1st part of duodenum; transverse colon
  • → Right lobe: Gallbladder fossa; Rt. colic flexure; upper 2nd part of duodenum (duodenal impression); Rt. kidney (renal impression)

Surface Anatomy of the Liver

  • Upper border: Line joining:
  • → a) Lt. 5th intercostal space at Lt. midclavicular line
  • → b) Xiphisternal junction
  • → c) Rt. 5th rib at Rt. midclavicular line
  • → d) Rt. 7th rib at Rt. midaxillary line
  • Lower border: Line joining:
  • → a) Lt. 5th intercostal space at Lt. midclavicular line
  • → b) Lt. costal margin at tip of 8th costal cartilage
  • → c) Transpyloric plane in the midline (level of L1) — where liver edge crosses midline
  • → d) Tip of 9th costal cartilage at midclavicular line (corresponds to fundus of gallbladder)
  • → e) Rt. 11th rib at Rt. midaxillary line
  • Right border: Line joining Rt. 7th rib at Rt. midaxillary line → to Rt. 11th rib at Rt. midaxillary line
  • Clinical notes: Normal liver is NOT palpable below costal margin; if palpable → hepatomegaly. Upper border = resonance to dullness on percussion (maps liver dullness)
🏥 Most commonly injured abdominal organ in blunt trauma = right lobe of liver. Bare area: infections/tumours spread between liver and right pleural cavity. Portal hypertension → varices, splenomegaly, ascites, caput medusae. Cantlie line guides liver resection (hepatectomy).
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
