✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Portal vein = Superior Mesenteric Vein + Splenic Vein. Formed at level L1, behind the neck of the pancreas. The IMV drains into the splenic vein.
2Percentage of liver blood supplied by portal vein:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Portal vein provides ~80% (venous, nutrient-rich from GIT). Hepatic artery provides ~20% (oxygenated).
3The caudate lobe is bounded by which structure on its left?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Caudate lobe boundaries: right = IVC groove; left = fissure for ligamentum venosum; below = porta hepatis.
4Contents of porta hepatis from FRONT to BACK:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — From front to back at porta hepatis: Bile ducts (most anterior), Hepatic artery branches (middle), Portal vein branches (most posterior).
5Ligamentum teres is the obliterated:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Ligamentum teres = obliterated left umbilical vein (carried oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus). Ligamentum venosum = obliterated ductus venosus.
6The bare area of the liver is clinically important because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The bare area has no peritoneal covering → direct communication between liver and thorax (right pleural cavity). Subphrenic abscess can erode into pleural space.
7The functional/surgical division of liver is along:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Cantlie line (a vertical plane from gallbladder fossa to IVC) divides the liver into right and left functional lobes with independent blood supply and bile drainage.
8Anatomical division of liver into right and left lobes on diaphragmatic surface:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Falciform ligament divides the diaphragmatic surface into right (large) and left (small) anatomical lobes.
9Hepatic veins drain into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Three hepatic veins (right, middle, left) drain directly into the IVC just inferior to the diaphragm (at approximately T8).
10The crossbar of the H-shaped arrangement on the visceral surface of the liver is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The porta hepatis forms the horizontal crossbar of the H-shape on the visceral surface, separating anterior structures (gallbladder fossa + ligamentum teres) from posterior (IVC groove + ligamentum venosum).
5Extrahepatic Biliary Apparatus›

Components of Extrahepatic Biliary Apparatus

  • 1. Right and left hepatic ducts: Drain bile from right and left lobes of liver respectively; join to form common hepatic duct
  • 2. Common hepatic duct: 1 inch (2.5 cm) long; joins cystic duct to form CBD
  • 3. Cystic duct: From gallbladder; joins common hepatic duct
  • 4. Bile duct (CBD — Common Bile Duct): ~3 inches (7.5 cm) long; most important duct
  • 5. Gallbladder: Pear-shaped sac

Gallbladder — Anatomy

  • Shape: Elongated pear-shaped sac
  • Capacity: 30-50 mL
  • Dimensions: ~10 cm long × 3 cm wide
  • Location: Gallbladder fossa on inferior surface of right lobe of liver
  • Function: Stores and concentrates bile (absorbs water and electrolytes); discharges bile into duodenum by muscular contraction

Parts of Gallbladder

  • 1. Fundus: Projects below inferior border of liver at tip of right 9th costal cartilage; related to anterior abdominal wall (Murphy's point); completely surrounded by peritoneum (all surfaces free)
  • 2. Body: Upper surface lies against gallbladder fossa of liver (no peritoneum — attached); lower surface related to transverse colon and superior part of duodenum
  • 3. Neck: Joins cystic duct; related inferiorly to 1st part of duodenum
  • → Hartmann's pouch: Posteromedial dilatation of neck; gallstones commonly lodge here; may adhere to 1st part of duodenum → cholecystoduodenal fistula (Bouveret syndrome)

Common Bile Duct (CBD) — Detailed Course

  • Length: ~3 inches
  • Formation: Common hepatic duct + cystic duct
  • Position in hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum): CBD is to the RIGHT; Hepatic artery proper to the LEFT; Portal vein POSTERIOR
  • CBD then passes: Posterior to 1st part of duodenum → groove on posterior surface of head of pancreas → joins main pancreatic duct (Wirsung)
  • Opens: Into 2nd part of duodenum at MAJOR DUODENAL PAPILLA via AMPULLA OF VATER
  • Sphincter of Oddi: Smooth muscle sphincter controlling flow through ampulla; keeps sphincter closed between meals; relaxes with CCK

Blood Supply, Lymphatics & Nerves

  • Arterial (Gallbladder): Cystic artery — branch of RIGHT hepatic artery (in Calot's triangle)
  • Calot's triangle: Bounded by cystic duct (below-right), common hepatic duct (below-left), liver (above); cystic artery crosses this triangle → important surgically
  • Venous: Cystic vein → portal vein; small veins directly to liver
  • Lymph: → Cystic and hepatic nodes → upper deep cervical nodes
  • Nerve: Sympathetic (T7-T9) via cystic plexus; Parasympathetic (vagus) → stimulate contraction and bile release
🏥 Murphy's sign: pain on deep inspiration during palpation of RUQ at 9th costal cartilage tip = acute cholecystitis. Courvoisier's sign: painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = pancreatic cancer (NOT gallstones — because in gallstone disease, GB is fibrotic/non-distensible). Cholelithiasis: stones lodge in Hartmann's pouch, cystic duct, or ampulla of Vater → obstructive jaundice if CBD obstructed.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Common bile duct is formed by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CBD = Common hepatic duct + Cystic duct. The CBD then travels down to join the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater.
2Position of CBD in the hepatoduodenal ligament:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — In the hepatoduodenal ligament: CBD is RIGHT; Hepatic artery is LEFT; Portal vein is POSTERIOR. Mnemonic: "Bill's at the Right, Harry's at the Left, Pete's at the Back."
3CBD opens into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — CBD + pancreatic duct → Ampulla of Vater → Sphincter of Oddi → Major duodenal papilla in the 2nd part of duodenum (medial wall).
4Gallbladder fundus is palpable at:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — GB fundus projects below the inferior liver border at the TIP of the right 9th costal cartilage — Murphy's point; the basis of Murphy's sign.
5The cystic artery is usually a branch of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Cystic artery = branch of RIGHT hepatic artery in most people. It crosses Calot's triangle to supply the gallbladder. Important in cholecystectomy.
6Which part of the gallbladder is COMPLETELY surrounded by peritoneum?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The fundus is the only part completely surrounded by peritoneum on all surfaces. The body's upper surface lacks peritoneum (attached to liver).
7Hartmann's pouch in relation to adjacent structures:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Hartmann's pouch is the posteromedial dilatation of the gallbladder neck, related inferiorly to the 1st part of duodenum → chronic inflammation/stone can cause cholecystoduodenal fistula.
8Sphincter of Oddi controls flow at:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla of Vater where CBD and pancreatic duct open into the 2nd part of duodenum. It stays contracted between meals and relaxes with CCK.
9Courvoisier's sign (painless jaundice + palpable GB) indicates:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — In gallstone disease, the GB is usually chronically inflamed and fibrotic (cannot distend). Pancreatic cancer causes gradual CBD obstruction → gallbladder distends (non-tender) = Courvoisier's sign.
10Calot's triangle is bounded by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Calot's triangle: cystic duct (below-right), common hepatic duct (below-left), inferior surface of liver (above). The cystic artery is found within this triangle → must be identified in cholecystectomy.
6Portal Vein›

Important Features of Portal Vein

  • Length: ~3 inches (7.5 cm)
  • Feature 1: Provides approximately 80% of blood that flows through the liver
  • Feature 2: Its tributaries and branches contain up to 1/3 of total blood volume in the entire body
  • Feature 3: Portal vein and ALL its tributaries are DEVOID OF VALVES throughout (unlike systemic veins)

Formation & Course

  • Formation: Behind neck of pancreas at level L1 — union of SUPERIOR MESENTERIC VEIN (SMV) + SPLENIC VEIN
  • N.B: Splenic vein itself receives the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV)
  • Three parts:
  • → 1. Infra-duodenal: behind neck of pancreas; in front of IVC
  • → 2. Retro-duodenal: posterior to 1st part of duodenum; anterior to IVC
  • → 3. Supra-duodenal: in the RIGHT FREE MARGIN OF LESSER OMENTUM (hepatoduodenal ligament), along with hepatic artery and CBD
  • End: Divides at right end of porta hepatis into right and left branches

Tributaries of Portal Vein

  • 1. Splenic vein (which receives inferior mesenteric vein)
  • 2. Superior mesenteric vein
  • 3. Superior pancreaticoduodenal vein
  • 4. Right gastric vein
  • 5. Left gastric vein (receives oesophageal veins from lower oesophagus — IMPORTANT for varices)
  • 6. Cystic vein → drains into right branch before entering liver
  • 7. Para-umbilical veins of Sappey → drain into left branch

Portocaval Anastomoses — All 5 Sites

  • Definition: Sites where portal tributaries communicate with systemic (caval) veins; normally small and collapsed; dilate in portal hypertension
  • 1. LOWER OESOPHAGUS (most important clinically): Left gastric v. (portal) ↔ Oesophageal tributaries of azygos/hemiazygos v. (systemic) → OESOPHAGEAL VARICES → life-threatening bleeding
  • 2. UMBILICUS (caput medusae): Para-umbilical veins of Sappey (portal, left branch) ↔ Superficial epigastric veins (systemic) → dilated peri-umbilical veins radiating outward = caput medusae
  • 3. ANAL CANAL (haemorrhoids): Superior rectal v. (portal, from IMV) ↔ Middle and inferior rectal v. (systemic, from internal iliac) → HAEMORRHOIDS (internal, above dentate line, painless)
  • 4. RETROPERITONEUM (Veins of Retzius): Portal tributaries ↔ Renal and lumbar veins (systemic)
  • 5. BARE AREA OF LIVER: Portal tributaries ↔ Phrenic/IVC tributaries through diaphragm
🏥 Portal hypertension (>12 mmHg) causes: oesophageal varices (life-threatening haemorrhage), splenomegaly (→ hypersplenism), ascites, caput medusae, haemorrhoids, hepatic encephalopathy. TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) = artificial portosystemic connection to decompress portal hypertension.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Portal vein is formed at level L1 by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Portal vein = SMV + Splenic vein, formed behind neck of pancreas at L1. The IMV drains into the splenic vein (not directly into portal vein usually).
2Portal vein is devoid of valves. What is the clinical consequence?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Absence of valves means blood can flow in either direction. In portal hypertension, portal blood is diverted retrograde through anastomoses to systemic circulation → varices.
3Most clinically dangerous portocaval anastomosis:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Oesophageal varices carry risk of life-threatening torrential haemorrhage (mortality >30% per bleed) — most dangerous portocaval anastomosis.
4Caput medusae is formed by dilation of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Para-umbilical veins of Sappey (portal → left branch) anastomose with superficial epigastric veins (systemic) → dilate → visible dilated veins radiating from umbilicus = caput medusae.
5The supra-duodenal part of portal vein lies in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Supra-duodenal part = in the hepatoduodenal ligament (right free margin of lesser omentum) along with hepatic artery proper and CBD.
6IMV drains into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — IMV typically drains into the splenic vein before it joins the SMV to form the portal vein.
7Haemorrhoids in portal hypertension occur because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Superior rectal vein (IMV → portal) anastomoses with middle and inferior rectal veins (internal iliac → systemic). In portal HTN this site dilates → internal haemorrhoids (above dentate line).
8How much of total blood volume is contained in portal tributaries?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Portal vein tributaries and branches contain up to 1/3 of total body blood volume — clinically important in portal hypertension and bleeding.
9The left gastric vein receives tributaries from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Left gastric vein receives oesophageal tributaries from the lower oesophagus — these form the PORTAL side of the oesophageal portocaval anastomosis.
10TIPS procedure (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt) treats portal hypertension by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — TIPS: a stent is passed via jugular vein → IVC → hepatic vein → tunnelled through liver parenchyma → into portal vein → decompresses portal hypertension.
7Blood Supply of GIT›

Arterial Territories — Overview

  • The GIT is supplied by 3 unpaired branches of abdominal aorta:
  • 1. Celiac trunk → FOREGUT: Lower oesophagus, stomach, duodenum (superior part + proximal half of 2nd part up to entry of bile duct)
  • 2. Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) → MIDGUT: Rest of duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, right 2/3 of transverse colon
  • 3. Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) → HINDGUT: Left 1/3 transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, most of rectum

Celiac Trunk — Branches

  • Origin: Aorta at T12 level; short stump (1-2 cm) immediately below aortic hiatus
  • Three branches:
  • 1. Left gastric artery: Smallest; runs along lesser curvature of stomach; anastomoses with right gastric artery
  • 2. Splenic artery (LARGEST celiac branch): Tortuous; runs along upper border of pancreas; branches: short gastric arteries (to fundus of stomach) + left gastroepiploic artery (greater curvature)
  • 3. Common hepatic artery: Runs to right → divides into:
  • → Hepatic artery proper (to liver via hepatoduodenal ligament)
  • → Gastroduodenal artery (→ right gastroepiploic artery for greater curvature + superior pancreaticoduodenal artery for duodenum/pancreas)
  • → Right gastric artery (to pyloric end of lesser curvature; anastomoses with left gastric)

Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA)

  • Origin: Aorta at L1; emerges from behind neck of pancreas; in front of left renal vein; right of superior mesenteric vein
  • Supplies: Distal duodenum, entire jejunum and ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, right 2/3 transverse colon
  • Branches:
  • → Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (anastomoses with superior → supplies duodenum and pancreas)
  • → Intestinal (jejunal and ileal) arteries — 12-15 branches forming arcades
  • → Ileocolic artery → appendicular artery (supplies appendix)
  • → Right colic artery → supplies ascending colon
  • → Middle colic artery → supplies transverse colon

Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA)

  • Origin: Anterior surface of aorta at L3; just above aortic bifurcation
  • Supplies: Left 1/3 transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, most of rectum
  • Branches:
  • → Left colic artery → descending colon
  • → Sigmoid arteries (2-4) → sigmoid colon
  • → Superior rectal artery (terminal branch) → upper and middle rectum; anastomoses with middle rectal (internal iliac) and inferior rectal (internal pudendal) arteries
  • Watershed zone: Splenic flexure = junction between SMA and IMA territories → most vulnerable area to ischaemia

Venous Drainage — Portal System

  • All GIT veins drain into PORTAL SYSTEM → liver → hepatic veins → IVC
  • SMV: Drains small intestine and right colon
  • Splenic vein: Drains spleen, pancreas, left stomach; receives IMV
  • IMV: Drains left colon, sigmoid, upper rectum → usually into splenic vein
  • Left gastric vein: Drains lesser curvature of stomach + lower oesophagus
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Celiac trunk supplies which embryological gut segment?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Celiac trunk = foregut: lower oesophagus, stomach, duodenum (up to entry of bile duct into 2nd part = embryological foregut-midgut junction).
2Appendix is supplied by a branch of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Appendicular artery = branch of posterior cecal artery, which branches from the ileocolic artery, which is a branch of the SMA.
3IMA originates from the aorta at:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — IMA arises from the ANTERIOR surface of the abdominal aorta at L3, just above the aortic bifurcation (L4).
4Superior rectal artery is the terminal branch of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Superior rectal artery = terminal branch/continuation of the IMA. It supplies upper and middle rectum and anastomoses with middle and inferior rectal arteries.
5Greater curvature of stomach is supplied by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Greater curvature = right gastroepiploic (from gastroduodenal → common hepatic) + left gastroepiploic (from splenic artery). Lesser curvature = left + right gastric arteries.
6Gastroduodenal artery branches from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Gastroduodenal artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery. It passes behind the 1st part of duodenum.
7"Watershed" zone most vulnerable to ischaemia between SMA and IMA:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Splenic flexure is the watershed zone between SMA territory (right 2/3 transverse colon) and IMA territory (left 1/3 transverse colon) → most vulnerable to ischaemia in hypotensive states.
8Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery is a branch of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery = branch of gastroduodenal artery (celiac territory). It anastomoses with inferior pancreaticoduodenal (SMA territory) at the level of the bile duct entry.
9All venous blood from the GIT drains via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — All GIT venous blood (from oesophagus to upper rectum) drains via the portal venous system to the liver before reaching the IVC.
10Short gastric arteries supply:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Short gastric arteries = 5-7 branches from the splenic artery; they supply the fundus and upper body of the stomach.
8Rectum, Anal Canal & Ischiorectal Fossa›

Anatomy of the Rectum

  • Definition: Terminal part of large intestine
  • Length: ~13 cm (5 inches)
  • Begins: At level S3 as continuation of sigmoid colon
  • Ends: At anorectal junction (1 inch in front of and below tip of coccyx) where it continues as anal canal
  • Width: ~4 cm at beginning; DILATED near end = RECTAL AMPULLA
  • Unlike colon: NO taeniae coli; NO haustrations; NO appendices epiploicae

Flexures of the Rectum

  • Sacral curve (upper): Concave forwards — follows concavity of sacrum
  • Perineal (anorectal) flexure (lower curve): Convex forwards — where rectum bends backwards 80° to pierce pelvic diaphragm; maintained by PUBORECTALIS MUSCLE
  • Three lateral flexures: Upper and lower Convex to RIGHT; middle convex to LEFT
  • → Correspond internally to three transverse folds (Houston's valves) on mucosa

Relations of Rectum

  • Anterior (male): Bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, ductus deferens
  • Anterior (female): Uterus, cervix, posterior vaginal wall (= rectovaginal septum)
  • Posterior: Sacrum, coccyx, piriformis, coccygeus muscles
  • Peritoneum: Covers upper 2/3 anteriorly and upper 1/3 laterally only; reflected anteriorly to form rectovesical pouch (male) or rectouterine pouch/Pouch of Douglas (female)

Blood Supply of Rectum

  • Superior rectal artery: Branch of IMA; supplies upper and middle rectum
  • Middle rectal artery: Branch of internal iliac artery; supplies middle rectum
  • Inferior rectal artery: Branch of internal pudendal artery (from internal iliac); supplies lower rectum and anal canal
  • Venous drainage:
  • → Superior rectal vein → IMV → PORTAL SYSTEM
  • → Middle and inferior rectal veins → internal iliac → IVC (SYSTEMIC)
  • → This is a PORTOCAVAL ANASTOMOSIS → haemorrhoids in portal hypertension

Anal Canal — Structure

  • Length: ~4 cm (from anorectal junction/flexure to anal opening)
  • Divided at the PECTINATE (DENTATE) LINE:
  • ABOVE dentate line (upper half):
  • → Epithelium: columnar (intestinal type)
  • → Blood supply: superior rectal artery (IMA)
  • → Venous drainage: superior rectal vein → IMV → PORTAL
  • → Lymphatics: internal iliac nodes
  • → Innervation: autonomic (visceral) — NOT pain-sensitive
  • → Clinical: internal haemorrhoids here — PAINLESS
  • BELOW dentate line (lower half):
  • → Epithelium: stratified squamous (skin type)
  • → Blood supply: inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal)
  • → Venous drainage: inferior rectal vein → internal pudendal → IVC → SYSTEMIC
  • → Lymphatics: superficial inguinal lymph nodes
  • → Innervation: somatic (inferior rectal nerve, branch of pudendal) — PAIN-SENSITIVE
  • → Clinical: external haemorrhoids here — PAINFUL

Columns of Morgagni & Anal Valves

  • Columns of Morgagni: Longitudinal mucosal folds ABOVE dentate line; each column contains an artery and a vein
  • Anal valves: Connect bases of columns; semilunar folds; above them = ANAL SINUSES
  • Anal sinuses: Contain mucus-secreting anal glands; infection of these glands → perianal abscess → fistula-in-ano

Sphincters of Anal Canal

  • Internal Anal Sphincter (IAS):
  • → Smooth muscle (involuntary)
  • → Thickening of circular layer of muscularis externa
  • → Maintains ~80% of resting anal tone
  • → Innervation: sympathetic (L1-L2) contracts; parasympathetic (S2-S4) relaxes
  • External Anal Sphincter (EAS):
  • → Skeletal muscle (voluntary)
  • → Three parts: subcutaneous, superficial, deep
  • → Innervation: inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve) + perineal branch of S4
  • Puborectalis muscle:
  • → Part of levator ani; passes from pubic bone, slings behind anorectal junction
  • → Creates the ANORECTAL ANGLE (~90° in continent state)
  • → ESSENTIAL FOR CONTINENCE — damage → incontinence

Lymph Drainage & Nerve Supply of Anal Canal

  • Lymph drainage — important division at pectinate (dentate) line:
  • → Upper half of anal canal: Drains into pararectal lymph nodes → inferior mesenteric lymph nodes
  • → Lower half of anal canal: Drains into superficial inguinal lymph nodes
  • Clinical significance: Carcinoma above pectinate line spreads to internal iliac/inferior mesenteric nodes; carcinoma below pectinate line spreads to inguinal nodes (may present as inguinal lymphadenopathy)
  • Nerve supply of sphincters:
  • → Internal sphincter (smooth, involuntary): Sympathetic from L1–L2 (→ contraction, maintains continence); Parasympathetic from S2–S4 via pelvic nerve (→ relaxation during defecation)
  • → External sphincter (striated, voluntary): Pudendal nerve (inferior rectal nerve) from S2–S4 anterior horn cells + Perineal branch of 4th sacral nerve → voluntary contraction/relaxation
  • Sensory: Below pectinate line: somatic (pudendal) — sharp/precise pain sensation; Above pectinate line: autonomic — vague, poorly localised (hemorrhoids above pectinate line are painless)

Ischiorectal (Ischioanal) Fossa

  • Definition: Wedge-shaped fat-filled space on each side of the anal canal
  • Boundaries:
  • → Medially: external anal sphincter + levator ani
  • → Laterally: ischial tuberosity + obturator internus covered by obturator fascia
  • → Base (floor): skin and fascia of perineum
  • → Apex: where levator ani meets obturator fascia
  • → Anteriorly: perineal body
  • → Posteriorly: sacrotuberous ligament
  • Contents:
  • → Fat (perianal fat)
  • → Inferior rectal vessels and nerves
  • → Perineal branch of S4
  • → Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels in ALCOCK'S CANAL (fascial tunnel within obturator fascia on lateral wall)
  • Clinical: Perianal abscess commonly forms here; horseshoe abscess crosses posterior midline to involve both sides; Alcock's canal compression → pudendal neuralgia
🏥 Internal haemorrhoids (above dentate): PAINLESS — autonomic innervation. External haemorrhoids (below dentate): PAINFUL — somatic. Fistula-in-ano: tract from anal gland (at dentate) to perianal skin. Goodsall's rule: posterior fistulae have curved tracts opening in midline posteriorly; anterior fistulae have straight radial tracts.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1The pectinate/dentate line marks the border between:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Dentate line divides: above = columnar epithelium, portal venous drainage, autonomic innervation (painless); below = squamous epithelium, systemic venous drainage, somatic innervation (painful).
2Internal haemorrhoids are painless because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Above the dentate line = autonomic innervation only → visceral pain (vague discomfort) but NOT sharp somatic pain. This is why internal haemorrhoids are painless.
3Lymph drainage from BELOW the dentate line:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Below dentate = perineal skin territory → superficial inguinal LN. Above dentate = internal iliac LN.
4Puborectalis is essential for:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Puborectalis slings behind the anorectal junction creating ~90° angle. Intact puborectalis = continent; damaged puborectalis = incontinence. It is the most important continence muscle.
5Inferior rectal artery is a branch of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Inferior rectal artery = branch of internal pudendal artery, which is a branch of the internal iliac artery.
6The rectum differs from the colon histologically/anatomically by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Rectum lacks all 3 colonic features: taeniae coli, haustra (sacculations), and appendices epiploicae.
7Pudendal nerve in the ischiorectal fossa travels in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels travel in Alcock's canal — a tunnel within the obturator fascia on the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa.
8Venous drainage from the upper anal canal into the PORTAL system is via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Upper anal canal → superior rectal vein → IMV → portal vein. This is the portocaval anastomosis at the anorectal junction.
9The perineal (anorectal) flexure is maintained by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Puborectalis pulls the anorectal junction anteriorly → creates ~90° anorectal angle. If puborectalis relaxes during defecation → angle straightens → facilitates evacuation.
10Columns of Morgagni are located:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Columns of Morgagni = longitudinal mucosal folds above the dentate line, each containing an artery and a vein. Their bases are connected by anal valves.

📝 Practice MCQs 62 Questions
1A 52-year-old woman presents with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging reveals a gallstone impacted in the part of the common bile duct that descends within the right free margin of the lesser omentum, anterior to the portal vein and to the right of the proper hepatic artery. Which part of the common bile duct is most likely affected?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The supraduodenal part of the CBD runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, anterior to the portal vein and to the right of the hepatic artery proper — exactly the relations described.
2A surgeon performing a pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) notes that the common bile duct is running in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas and, in some areas, is completely surrounded by pancreatic tissue. Which part of the common bile duct is being described?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The infraduodenal (pancreatic) part of the CBD lies behind, and is sometimes embedded within, the head of the pancreas before it reaches the duodenal wall.
3A 60-year-old man undergoes endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for evaluation of obstructive jaundice. The endoscopist identifies the opening of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) on the posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum, about 10 cm distal to the pylorus. At this site, which two ducts unite before draining into the duodenum?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct join within the duodenal wall to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), opening at the major duodenal papilla.
4A 45-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness. Ultrasound reveals gallstones. The surgeon notes that the gallbladder is in a fossa on the inferior surface of a liver lobe. Which lobe is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The gallbladder is anatomically situated in a shallow depression known as the gallbladder fossa, which is located on the visceral surface of the liver's right lobe. Therefore, the right lobe is the specific anatomical region that houses the gallbladder.
5During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies the main artery supplying the gallbladder before ligating it. From which artery does the cystic artery most commonly arise?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery, typically within Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle.
6A patient with cholecystitis is found to have inflammation spreading to the liver. The venous drainage of the gallbladder is noted to be dual, with some veins draining directly into the liver. Which vessel drains the main cystic vein into?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The main cystic vein typically drains into the portal vein (commonly its right branch); smaller accessory cystic veins drain directly into the adjacent liver substance.
7A 55-year-old man with chronic liver disease presents with ascites and splenomegaly. Imaging shows a dilated portal vein measuring about 7.5 cm in length. Which of the following statements about the portal vein is correct?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The portal vein supplies roughly 70–80% of total hepatic blood flow (the hepatic artery provides the remainder); it is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins and, like its tributaries, is valveless.
8A patient with portal hypertension develops severe hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals bleeding esophageal varices. Which veins are involved in the portocaval anastomosis at the lower third of the esophagus?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — At the lower esophagus, esophageal branches of the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with esophageal tributaries of the accessory hemiazygos vein (systemic), the basis of esophageal varices in portal hypertension.
9A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with prominent, snake-like veins radiating from his umbilicus. Which veins are responsible for this clinical finding known as caput medusae?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Caput medusae results from dilated paraumbilical veins (portal, running in the falciform ligament) anastomosing with the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall (systemic) around the umbilicus.
10During abdominal surgery, a surgeon observes the formation of the portal vein behind the neck of the pancreas at the level of L1. Which two veins unite to form the portal vein at this location?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein; the inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein before this confluence.
11A patient with portal hypertension develops hemorrhoids due to portocaval anastomosis in the anal canal. Which veins are involved in this anastomosis?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Internal hemorrhoids reflect dilation where the superior rectal vein (portal) anastomoses with the inferior rectal veins (systemic).
12A 50-year-old woman with portal vein thrombosis is found to have a dual system of venous drainage from the gallbladder. The cystic vein drains directly into which vessel before entering the liver?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — As above, the cystic vein drains into the portal venous system (typically its right branch) before its blood passes through the liver.
13A radiologist notes that the portal vein and its tributaries are unique in that they:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Unlike most systemic veins, the portal vein and its tributaries are valveless, which permits retrograde flow and the formation of portosystemic collaterals when portal pressure rises.
14A patient is being evaluated for a liver transplant. The surgeon notes that the portal vein ends at the right end of the porta hepatis by dividing into:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — At the porta hepatis, the portal vein terminates by dividing into right and left branches supplying the corresponding parts of the liver.
15During an anatomy dissection, a student is asked to name a tributary of the portal vein that also receives the inferior mesenteric vein. Which vessel is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein, which then joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
16A patient with advanced liver disease is found to have up to one third of the total blood volume in the body contained within the portal vein and its branches. Which of the following is NOT a direct tributary of the portal vein?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The IVC belongs to the systemic venous system and is not a tributary of the portal vein; the SMV, splenic vein, and gastric veins all drain directly into the portal venous system.
17A 55-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to his back. Imaging reveals a large ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach near the lesser curvature. Which artery is most at risk of being eroded by this ulcer?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature within the lesser omentum, making it the vessel most at risk of erosion by an ulcer in this region.
18A 43-year-old woman undergoes a splenectomy after trauma. During the procedure, the surgeon ligates an artery running along the superior border of the pancreas that gives off several branches to the stomach and pancreas. Which artery is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The splenic artery runs a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas, giving pancreatic branches and gastric branches (short gastric, left gastroepiploic) before reaching the spleen.
19A 30-year-old patient presents with acute appendicitis. Which artery is primarily responsible for supplying blood to the appendix?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The appendicular artery, which supplies the appendix, is a branch of the ileocolic artery (itself a branch of the SMA).
20A 70-year-old man has ischemia of the distal transverse colon. Which major artery is most likely compromised?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon is supplied by the middle colic artery (SMA), but the distal third is supplied by the left colic artery, a branch of the IMA.
21A 25-year-old woman is found to have a congenital anomaly where the right hepatic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery. Normally, the right hepatic artery is a branch of which vessel?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The right hepatic artery normally arises from the hepatic artery proper, the continuation of the common hepatic artery beyond the origin of the gastroduodenal artery.
22A patient develops an infarction of the jejunum. Which branch of the superior mesenteric artery is directly responsible for supplying the jejunum?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The jejunal branches of the SMA directly supply the jejunum, while separate ileal branches supply the ileum.
23A 60-year-old man is found to have a blockage at the origin of the celiac trunk. Which of the following organs would be most affected by this blockage?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The celiac trunk supplies the foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, proximal duodenum); the other listed structures are midgut/hindgut derivatives supplied by the SMA or IMA.
24During surgery for colon cancer, the surgeon ligates an artery that runs in the transverse mesocolon and supplies the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. Which artery is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The middle colic artery, a branch of the SMA, runs in the transverse mesocolon and supplies the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
25A 45-year-old man presents with rectal bleeding. Imaging shows a lesion in the upper rectum. Which artery is the primary source of blood supply to this region?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The superior rectal artery, the terminal continuation of the IMA, is the principal supply to the upper rectum.
26A patient has ischemia affecting the jejunum, ileum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of transverse colon. Which artery is most likely affected?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — All of these structures are midgut derivatives supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
27During a pelvic MRI, a radiologist notes that the rectum follows a curve concave forwards, closely paralleling the sacrum. Which flexure is being described?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The sacral flexure is the anteroposterior curve of the rectum that follows the concavity of the sacrum and coccyx.
28A 49-year-old woman undergoes surgery for a low rectal tumor. The surgeon notes three lateral bends in the rectum. Which statement about these lateral flexures is correct?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The rectum has three lateral curves: the upper and lower are convex to the right, and the middle (most prominent) curve is convex to the left.
29A patient with portal hypertension develops internal hemorrhoids. Which rectal vein is primarily responsible for draining blood into the portal venous system?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Only the superior rectal vein drains into the portal venous system (via the inferior mesenteric vein); the middle and inferior rectal veins are systemic.
30A 58-year-old man presents with rectal bleeding. On examination, the bleeding site is above the pectinate line. Which artery is the main source of blood to this area?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Mucosa above the pectinate line (hindgut-derived) is supplied mainly by the superior rectal artery.
31A 35-year-old woman presents with perianal pain and swelling. The affected area is supplied by a branch of the internal pudendal artery. Which artery is involved?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The inferior rectal artery, a branch of the internal pudendal artery, supplies the lower anal canal and perianal skin.
32A 70-year-old man is found to have a thrombosis in the middle rectal vein. Where does this vein primarily drain?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The middle rectal vein is a systemic vein that drains into the internal iliac vein.
33A patient is undergoing a colectomy. The surgeon must ligate the artery that is a direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and supplies the upper rectum. Which artery is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The superior rectal artery is the direct continuation of the IMA beyond its last sigmoid branch, supplying the upper rectum.
34A 60-year-old male presents with a mass at the anorectal junction, where the rectum bends sharply to form an angle of about 80 degrees. What is the name of this anatomical curve?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The perineal (anorectal) flexure is the sharp posterior angulation, maintained by the puborectalis sling, where the rectum turns to become the anal canal.
35A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with rectal carcinoma. The surgeon notes that the venous drainage of the rectum provides a site for portosystemic anastomosis. Which two veins are primarily involved in this anastomosis?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The classic portosystemic anastomosis of the rectal wall lies between the superior rectal vein (portal) and the inferior rectal vein (systemic).
36A 35-year-old woman with a ruptured appendix was sent to the emergency department for surgery. To cut off the blood supply to the appendix, a surgeon should ligate which of the following arteries?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The appendix is supplied by the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, so the ileocolic artery (or its appendicular branch) is ligated.
37A 60-year-old woman arrived at the emergency room complaining of acute abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with ischemic bowel resulting from obstruction of the superior mesenteric artery. Which of the following is most likely affected by ischemia?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The cecum is a midgut derivative supplied by the SMA (via the ileocolic artery); the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum are supplied by the IMA and rectal arteries instead.
38A 45-year-old man presents with painless bright red rectal bleeding. Examination reveals dilated veins within the anal columns above the pectinate line. Which vein contributes to these structures?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The internal rectal venous plexus within the anal columns, above the pectinate line, drains via the superior rectal vein.
39A surgeon identifies a wavy line in the anal canal that marks the embryological site of attachment of the anal membrane. Which structure is being observed?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The pectinate (dentate) line marks the former site of attachment of the anal membrane and the junction between the hindgut- and ectoderm-derived parts of the anal canal.
40A patient with chronic constipation is found to have thickening of the internal anal sphincter. Which statement regarding this sphincter is correct?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle, a thickened continuation of the circular muscle layer of the rectum, surrounding only the upper two-thirds of the anal canal, and is under autonomic (not inferior rectal nerve) control.
41During pelvic surgery, parasympathetic fibers to the internal anal sphincter are damaged. Which spinal segments give rise to these fibers?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Parasympathetic fibers to the internal anal sphincter (causing relaxation) arise from spinal segments S2–S4 via the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
42A 32-year-old woman has an injury to the inferior rectal nerve. Which muscle is most likely affected?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The inferior rectal nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve, supplies the external anal sphincter, a voluntary striated muscle.
43A patient has a lesion supplied by the inferior rectal artery. The lesion is most likely located in which part of the anal canal?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The inferior rectal artery supplies the lower (ectoderm-derived) part of the anal canal, below the pectinate line.
44A surgeon is operating in the ischiorectal fossa and identifies a wedge-shaped fat-filled space lateral to the anal canal. Which structure forms the medial wall of this fossa?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The medial wall of the ischioanal fossa is formed by the lower anal canal/external anal sphincter together with the sloping levator ani, while obturator internus forms the lateral wall.
45A patient suffers trauma to the coccygeal region affecting the origin of a portion of the external anal sphincter. Which part arises from the tip of the coccyx and the anococcygeal body?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The superficial part of the external anal sphincter attaches posteriorly to the tip of the coccyx via the anococcygeal ligament/body and anteriorly to the perineal body.
46A 58-year-old man undergoes surgery that damages the circular smooth muscle surrounding the upper two-thirds of the anal canal. Which structure has most likely been injured?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The internal anal sphincter, formed of circular smooth muscle, surrounds the upper two-thirds of the anal canal.
47A patient loses voluntary control of defecation after injury to the inferior rectal nerve. Which muscle is primarily affected?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Voluntary control of defecation depends on the external anal sphincter, supplied by the inferior rectal nerve.
48A medical student is asked which anal sphincter is a continuation of the circular muscle layer of the gut. The correct answer is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The internal anal sphincter is the direct continuation of the circular smooth muscle layer of the gut wall.
49During a practical exam, a student is asked which part of the external anal sphincter forms the "true sphincter" and has no bony attachment. Which is correct?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The deep part of the external anal sphincter encircles the upper anal canal as a true sphincteric ring, blending with puborectalis, with no bony attachment.
50A surgeon identifies muscle fibers arising from the tip of the coccyx and passing around the anus to insert into the perineal body. Which part of the external anal sphincter is this?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — This describes the superficial part of the external anal sphincter, an elliptical loop from the coccyx (via the anococcygeal ligament) around the anus to the perineal body.
51A patient with spinal cord injury at L1-L2 experiences altered autonomic control of the anal canal. Which sphincter receives sympathetic fibers from these segments?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Sympathetic fibers from the lower lumbar (L1–L2) segments reach the internal anal sphincter via the hypogastric plexus and cause it to contract.
52Which pair correctly matches muscle type and sphincter?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The internal anal sphincter is smooth (involuntary) muscle, while the external anal sphincter is striated (voluntary) muscle — only this option pairs them correctly.
53A surgeon accidentally damages the perineal branch of the 4th sacral nerve. Which structure may lose part of its motor innervation?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The perineal branch of S4, together with the inferior rectal nerve, supplies motor innervation to the external anal sphincter.
54A surgeon is performing a parotidectomy and needs to identify the most superficial structure within the gland to avoid injuring it. Which of the following is the most superficial?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Within the parotid gland, the facial nerve is the most superficial structure, lying superficial to the retromandibular vein, which itself lies superficial to the external carotid artery.
55A patient is diagnosed with a parotid duct stone (sialolithiasis). The physician plans to examine the opening of the duct in the oral cavity. Where should the physician look?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth.
56During a deep face laceration repair, the doctor notes a severed duct running across the masseter muscle. To locate the duct using surface anatomy, a line is drawn between the tragus and the midpoint of the upper lip. Which part of the line represents the duct?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The parotid duct's surface course corresponds to the middle third of a line drawn from the tragus to the midpoint of the upper lip, crossing the masseter.
57A 55-year-old male patient underwent surgery for the removal of the parotid gland. Which of the following sites does its duct open?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — As above, the parotid duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth.
58A 72-year-old patient has lost taste sensation on the anterior two-third of the tongue. This is probably due to injury to branches of which of the following nerves?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve, which joins the lingual nerve en route to the tongue.
59A 42-year-old patient has lost general sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue following radical resection of a primary tongue tumor. This is probably due to injury to branches of which of the following nerves?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — General sensation (touch, temperature, pain) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
60A 21-year-old woman has suffered a gunshot wound to her abdomen. After examining the patient's angiogram, the surgeon locates the bleeding source from the lesser omentum's free margin. Which of the following structures is most likely to be injured?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The free margin of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad: the portal vein posteriorly, the hepatic artery proper anteriorly on the left, and the common bile duct anteriorly on the right.
61A surgeon enters the peritoneal space located anterior to the stomach during an abdominal operation. This space constitutes the main compartment of the peritoneal cavity. Which space has the surgeon entered?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The greater sac is the main, larger compartment of the peritoneal cavity, lying anterior to the stomach and most abdominal viscera.
62During abdominal surgery, a surgeon passes through the epiploic (omental) foramen and enters a peritoneal compartment located posterior to the stomach. Which space has been entered?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) is the only communication between the greater sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa), the recess lying posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum.
✍️Anatomy Written›

1 — Portosystemic Anastomosis (most important)

Lower Third of OesophagusUmbilicusMid-Anal Canal
PortalOesophageal tributaries of left gastric v.Paraumbilical veinsSuperior rectal veins
SystemicOesophageal tributaries of azygos/accessory hemiazygos v.Superficial veins of anterior abdominal wallMiddle and inferior rectal veins
ClinicallyPortal obstruction → Oesophageal VaricesCaput Medusae (distension of veins around umbilicus)Distension of these vessels leads to Haemorrhoids and piles

2 — Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue

  • Anterior 2/3:
  • → Tip: drains into the submental L.N.
  • → Margins: drain into the submandibular L.N. of its side
  • → Central part: drains into the submandibular L.N. of both sides
  • Posterior 1/3: drains into deep cervical L.N. of both sides

3 — Structures Inside the Parotid Gland (Superficial to deep)

  • 1. Facial nerve CN VII and its branches — MOST SUPERFICIAL
  • → Facial n. & its branches enter through the postero-medial surface → 5 terminal branches:
  • → Temporal: leaves through its upper end
  • → Zygomatic, Buccal, Mandibular: leave through its anterior border
  • → Cervical: leaves through its lower end
  • 2. Retromandibular vein (posterior facial v.) — Lies in between
  • → Formed inside the gland by Superficial temporal v. & Maxillary v.
  • → Divides into anterior & posterior divisions: leave through its lower end
  • 3. External carotid artery — DEEPEST
  • → Enters through postero-medial surface → 2 terminal branches:
  • → The superficial temporal artery leaves through its upper end
  • → The maxillary artery leaves through its antero-medial surface
  • 4. Auriculotemporal nerve
  • → Enters through its anteromedial surface & leaves through its upper end
  • 5. Deep parotid lymph nodes

4 — Contents of Right Free Border of Lesser Omentum (HCP)

  • 1. Portal vein — posteriorly
  • 2. Hepatic artery proper — in front of portal vein and to LEFT of common bile duct
  • 3. Common bile duct — in front of portal vein and to the RIGHT of hepatic artery

5 — Epiploic Foramen of Winslow (Important)

  • Short, vertical slit in upper part of right border of lesser sac → leads into the greater sac
  • Boundaries:
  • → Anterior: thickened right edge of the lesser omentum
  • → Posterior: peritoneum covering the I.V.C.
  • → Above: caudate lobe of liver
  • → Below: 1st inch of 1st part of duodenum

6 — Extrahepatic Biliary Apparatus

  • 1. Rt. & Lt. Hepatic ducts: drain bile from Rt. & Lt. Lobes of the liver
  • 2. Common Hepatic duct: 1-inch duct that joins cystic duct to form CBD
  • 3. Gallbladder
  • 4. Cystic duct
  • 5. Bile duct (CBD)

7 — Bile Duct / Common Bile Duct

  • 1. Supra-duodenal: in Rt. Free margin of lesser omentum — to right of hepatic artery proper and anterior to portal vein
  • 2. Retro-duodenal: behind first part of duodenum
  • 3. Infra-duodenal (pancreatic): groove on posterior surface of head of pancreas
  • 4. Intra-duodenal (Intramural): Main pancreatic & terminal bile ducts join in the posteromedial 2nd part of duodenum (below middle, 10cm from pylorus) forming ampulla of Vater → opens at major duodenal papilla

8 — Portal Vein

  • Formation (BEGAIN): formed behind neck of pancreas by union of superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein at level of L1
  • End: at right end of porta hepatis by dividing into right & left branches
  • Tributaries:
  • 1. Splenic vein
  • 2. Superior mesenteric vein
  • 3. Superior pancreaticoduodenal vein
  • 4. Left and right gastric veins
  • 5. Cystic vein → joins right branch of portal vein before entering liver
  • 6. Paraumbilical veins (of Sappey) → small veins joining left branch of portal vein before it enters left lobe of liver

9 — Anal Sphincters

  • Internal Anal Sphincter:
  • → Ring of circular smooth muscle fibres surrounding upper two thirds of anal canal
  • → Continuous with circular muscle of gut
  • → Thickness ranges from 1.5 to 3.5 mm (thinner in females)
  • → Nerve supply: Sympathetic (lower two lumbar segments) → contraction; Parasympathetic (S2, 3, 4) → relaxation
  • External Sphincter — surrounds lower two thirds; overlaps internal sphincter in middle third; formed from STRIATED VOLUNTARY muscle:
  • → Deep part: thick annular band — true sphincter, no bony attachment
  • → Superficial part: arises from tip of coccyx and anococcygeal body → passes forward around sides of anus → inserted into perineal body
  • → Subcutaneous part: surrounds anal orifice, no bony attachment
  • → Nerve supply: inferior rectal nerve + perineal branch of 4th sacral nerve

10 — Surface Anatomy of The Liver (Repeated)

  • Upper Border:
  • → A: Left 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular
  • → B: Xiphi-sternal Junction
  • → C: Right 5th rib, Mid-clavicular
  • → D: Right 7th rib, Mid-Axillary
  • Right Border:
  • → D: Right 7th rib, Mid-Axillary
  • → E: Right 11th rib, Mid-Axillary
  • Lower Border:
  • → E: Right 11th rib, Mid-Axillary
  • → F: Tip of 9th Costal Cartilage, Mid-clavicular (Gallbladder)
  • → G: Transpyloric L1, Midline
  • → H: Tip of Left 8th Costal Cartilage, Costal Margin
  • → A: Left 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular.
1Esophagus›

Swallowing (Deglutition) — Overview

  • Definition: The propelling of food bolus from mouth to stomach
  • Control: Swallowing center in the medulla oblongata
  • Three phases: Buccal (voluntary) → Pharyngeal (involuntary) → Esophageal (involuntary)

Phase 1 — Buccal (Voluntary)

  • Tongue elevation and retraction against hard palate → propels bolus to pharynx
  • Voluntary initiation — once bolus reaches pharynx, process becomes automatic reflex

Phase 2 — Pharyngeal (Involuntary)

  • Very rapid (1 second) — occurs reflexively via swallowing reflex:
  • Receptor: oropharynx (tonsillar pillars)
  • Afferent: glossopharyngeal nerves (CN IX)
  • Center: medulla oblongata (swallowing center)
  • Efferent: motor fibers of CN V, IX, X, XII
  • Series of protective responses:
  • a. Elevation of soft palate → closes nasal cavity (prevents nasal regurgitation)
  • b. Approximation of palatopharyngeal folds → sagittal slit (only small particles pass)
  • c. Closure of glottis: approximation of vocal cords + elevation of larynx + folding of epiglottis
  • d. Inhibition of breathing (swallowing apnea)
  • e. Relaxation of pharyngoesophageal (upper) sphincter (UES) → rapid pharyngeal peristalsis → forces food into relaxed upper esophagus

Phase 3 — Esophageal (Involuntary)

  • A. Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES): Normally closed by striated muscle tone; relaxes during swallowing then recloses
  • B. Primary peristaltic waves:
  • → Start at upper end of esophagus as continuation of pharyngeal peristalsis
  • → Travel at 2-4 cm/sec (gravity may increase to 4 cm/sec)
  • → Coordinated in upper half by vago-vagal reflex (striated muscle); lower half by local enteric reflex
  • → N.B: Bilateral vagotomy → difficult swallowing in UPPER HALF only
  • C. Secondary peristaltic waves:
  • → Initiated by DISTENSION of esophagus by residual bolus (not by swallowing)
  • → Repeated until all food is cleared

Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) — Detailed

  • Also called: Cardiac sphincter
  • Location: Lower 3-5 cm of esophagus
  • Resting tone: High-pressure zone (15-30 cm H₂O above intra-abdominal pressure) → prevents gastric reflux
  • Its tone is INCREASED (contracted) by: Sympathetic α-adrenergic stimulation; local myenteric plexus; gastrin hormone; drugs that neutralize gastric acid → ↑ gastrin → ↑ LES tone
  • Its tone is DECREASED (relaxed) by: Inhibitory vagal stimulation via VIP secretion; local myenteric plexus; fatty foods; chocolate; coffee
  • N.B: When food bolus reaches LES → relaxes with some delay → allows passage to stomach
  • Mechanisms preventing gastric reflux into esophagus:
  • 1. High-pressure zone of LES
  • 2. Intra-abdominal segment of esophagus is squeezed by increased intra-abdominal pressure
  • 3. Esophagus enters stomach at acute angle (flap valve mechanism)
  • 4. Gastrin hormone increases tone of lower esophagus
🏥 Achalasia (Cardiospasm): ↑ resting LES tone + absent peristalsis due to deficiency of VIP and NO (defective myenteric plexus development). → Food accumulates, esophagus dilates. Dysphagia for BOTH solids and liquids. Barium swallow: "bird-beak" appearance at cardia. GERD: LES incompetence → acid reflux → heartburn, oesophagitis, Barrett's oesophagus.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1The swallowing center is located in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The swallowing (deglutition) center is in the medulla oblongata. It coordinates the complex reflex sequence of swallowing.
2Which phase of swallowing is entirely voluntary?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The buccal (oral) phase is the only voluntary phase. Once the bolus reaches the pharynx, the swallowing reflex takes over involuntarily.
3Secondary esophageal peristalsis is triggered by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Secondary peristalsis is initiated by DISTENSION of the esophagus by residual food (not by swallowing). It clears any food left after primary peristalsis.
4Bilateral vagotomy affects swallowing in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Upper esophagus (striated muscle) is coordinated by vago-vagal reflex → bilateral vagotomy disrupts this. Lower esophagus (smooth muscle) uses local enteric reflex → not affected by vagotomy.
5LES resting pressure is maintained above intra-abdominal pressure by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — LES maintains a resting high-pressure zone of 15-30 cm H₂O above intra-abdominal pressure, preventing gastric contents from refluxing into oesophagus.
6LES tone is DECREASED by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — LES relaxation (decreased tone): inhibitory vagal (VIP), local enteric plexus inhibition, fatty foods, chocolate, coffee. These are the causes of GERD.
7In achalasia, the primary defect is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Achalasia: defective myenteric plexus → deficiency of VIP and NO → LES cannot relax + absent peristalsis → dysphagia for both solids and liquids.
8Protection of airway during swallowing involves:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Three mechanisms protect the airway: (1) vocal cords approximate, (2) larynx elevates (moves under tongue base), (3) epiglottis folds back to cover laryngeal inlet. Plus swallowing apnea.
9Gastrin hormone affects the LES by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Gastrin increases LES tone. This is why antacids (which neutralize acid) → increase gastrin release → increase LES tone → protect against reflux (paradoxical but protective mechanism).
10Speed of primary esophageal peristalsis is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Primary peristalsis travels at 2-4 cm/sec. Gravity can increase the effective speed of the bolus to about 4 cm/sec.
2Gastric Secretion›

Overview of Gastric Secretion

  • Volume: 2.5-3 L/day of acidic juice (pH can reach 1)
  • Gastric glands types: Oxyntic glands (gastric glands) in body/fundus; Pyloric glands in antrum/pylorus
  • Distribution of cells:
  • → Body and fundus: all cell types EXCEPT G cells
  • → Antrum of pyloric area: mucous neck cells, chief cells, G cells, D cells
  • → Pyloric canal and cardiac region: goblet cells only

Gastric Secretory Cells — Complete Table

  • 1. Mucous neck cells (Goblet cells): Secrete soluble thin mucus; lubricate gastric chyme; stimulated by vagal
  • 2. Chief (peptic) cells: Secrete pepsinogen I (large, linked to HCl secretion) + pepsinogen II (less, not linked) + gelatinase + gastric lipase; activated to PEPSIN by HCl; optimal pH 1.8-3.5
  • 3. Parietal (oxyntic) cells: Secrete (a) HCl and (b) intrinsic factor (glycoprotein essential for Vit B12 absorption in ileum)
  • 4. G cells: In antrum; secrete gastrin (G34, G17-most important, G14); acts on stomach (↑ motility + secretion), pancreas (↑ insulin), LES (contraction), ileocecal sphincter (relaxation)
  • 5. D cells: Secrete somatostatin → inhibits HCl + gastrin (negative feedback at pH <2)
  • 6. Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells: Secrete histamine → stimulates parietal cells via H2 receptors → ↑ cAMP → ↑ HCl

Mechanism of HCl Secretion (Detailed)

  • In the parietal cell: CO₂ (from metabolism or blood) + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (by carbonic anhydrase)
  • 1. H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → HCO₃⁻ diffuses to blood in exchange for Cl⁻ (→ post-prandial alkaline tide)
  • 2. H₂O in cytoplasm → H⁺ + OH⁻ → H⁺ secreted into lumen via H⁺-K⁺ ATPase (proton pump)
  • 3. K⁺ recycled by Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase on basolateral membrane
  • 4. Cl⁻ secreted into lumen → unites with H⁺ → HCl
  • 5. Water diffuses to lumen → iso-osmotic HCl
  • Post-prandial alkaline tide: ↑ HCO₃⁻ in blood after gastric secretion → temporarily ↑ blood/urine pH

Factors Affecting HCl Secretion (Receptors on Parietal Cells)

  • ↑ HCl (stimulate):
  • → Histamine: H2 receptors → ↑ cAMP (blocked by cimetidine/ranitidine)
  • → Acetylcholine: muscarinic M3 receptors → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ (blocked by atropine)
  • → Gastrin: gastrin-CCK-B receptors → ↑ Ca²⁺
  • ↓ HCl (inhibit):
  • → Prostaglandin E₂: ↓ cAMP → ↓ HCl (used in treatment of peptic ulcer)
  • → Somatostatin: Gi → ↓ cAMP

Functions of HCl

  • 1. Sterilization: kills bacteria (maintains near-sterile stomach)
  • 2. Activation of pepsinogen → pepsin + provides optimal pH (1.8-3.5) for pepsin action → protein digestion
  • 3. HCl enters duodenum → stimulates secretin release → ↑ bile and pancreatic secretion
  • 4. Produces curdling of milk (casein precipitation)
  • 5. Initiates enterogastric inhibitory reflex → ↓ gastric secretion/evacuation
  • 6. ↑ Absorption of iron (converts ferric Fe³⁺ → ferrous Fe²⁺) and calcium (prevents calcium salt precipitation)

Control of Gastric Secretion — Three Phases

  • 1. Cephalic Phase (~30%):
  • → Stimulated by sight, smell, taste, thought of food (conditioned and unconditioned reflexes)
  • → Cerebral cortex + amygdala + hypothalamus → vagal center (dorsal motor nucleus) → vagus
  • → Vagus stimulates: Direct ACh on gastric glands; Gastrin releasing peptide (GRP) → G cells → gastrin
  • → ↑ with anxiety; ↓ with depression
  • → Proved by sham feeding experiment (esophageal fistula + gastric fistula)
  • 2. Gastric Phase (~60%):
  • → Food in stomach → mechanical distension + chemical (polypeptides, amino acids, caffeine, alcohol)
  • → Via: gastrin secretion; local nerve plexus (Meissner's); vago-vagal long reflex
  • → N.B: Hypoglycemia → ↑ vagal stimuli → ↑ gastric secretion
  • 3. Intestinal Phase (~10%):
  • → EARLY: small amounts of gastrin from duodenal mucosa → slightly ↑ secretion
  • → LATE (INHIBITORY): acid/fat/hyperosmotic solution/distension in duodenum →
  • → A. Enterogastric reflex (nervous: local/ganglionic/vago-vagal) → inhibits motility and secretion
  • → B. Hormonal: CCK, secretin, GIP, VIP → hormonal feedback inhibition of gastric secretion
🏥 H2 blockers (cimetidine, ranitidine): block H2 receptors on parietal cells. PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole): irreversibly block H⁺/K⁺ ATPase — most effective acid suppression. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: gastrinoma → very high gastrin → multiple resistant peptic ulcers. Pernicious anemia: autoimmune gastritis → loss of parietal cells → no intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Parietal cells secrete:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both HCl (via H⁺/K⁺ ATPase proton pump) and intrinsic factor (glycoprotein essential for Vit B12 absorption in terminal ileum).
2HCl concentration in parietal cell secretion is approximately:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Parietal cells secrete ~160 mEq/L HCl (nearly isotonic). The concentration of H⁺ is 3 million times higher than in plasma.
3Which receptor mediates histamine stimulation of HCl secretion?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Histamine acts on H2 receptors on parietal cells → ↑ cAMP → ↑ HCl. H2 blockers (cimetidine, ranitidine) block these receptors.
4Post-prandial alkaline tide refers to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — During HCl secretion, HCO₃⁻ is exchanged into blood for Cl⁻ → temporary ↑ in blood pH (alkaline tide) after meals.
5The cephalic phase of gastric secretion constitutes approximately:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Cephalic phase ≈ 30% of total gastric secretion. Gastric phase ≈ 60%. Intestinal phase ≈ 10%.
6Sham feeding experiment proved the role of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Sham feeding: esophagus cut in neck + gastric fistula → food swallowed passes outside → yet gastric secretion increases → proves cephalic phase via unconditioned vagal reflexes.
7The inhibitory intestinal phase is triggered by presence of what in duodenum?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Duodenal acid, fat, hyperosmotic/hypo-osmotic solutions, and distension → enterogastric reflex + CCK + secretin + GIP + VIP → inhibit gastric secretion and motility.
8Prostaglandin E₂ inhibits HCl secretion by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — PGE₂ acts on parietal cells via Gi-coupled receptors → ↓ cAMP → ↓ HCl secretion. Also stimulates mucus and HCO₃⁻ secretion → used in treatment of peptic ulcers.
9Intrinsic factor deficiency leads to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Intrinsic factor (from parietal cells) is essential for Vitamin B12 absorption in terminal ileum. Loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis) → no IF → no B12 → megaloblastic anemia = pernicious anemia.
10Functions of HCl include all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — HCl does NOT directly digest carbohydrates (that's amylase). HCl functions: sterilization, pepsinogen activation, stimulates secretin, curdling milk, ↑ Fe²⁺ and Ca²⁺ absorption, enterogastric reflex.
3Gastric Motility›

Filling and Storage of Food in Stomach

  • Stomach accommodates up to 1 litre without ↑ intra-gastric pressure because:
  • a. Plasticity of gastric wall (intrinsic property of smooth muscle)
  • b. Receptive relaxation: reflex relaxation of fundus and body triggered by pharyngeal and esophageal movements; mediated by vago-vagal reflex; neurotransmitter = VIP
  • c. Law of LaPlace: P = T/r — as radius increases with food entry, pressure stays low because tension increases little

Gastric Basic Electrical Rhythm (BER) — Slow Waves

  • 3-5 cycles/min due to partial depolarisation of circular smooth muscle cells
  • Origin: Pacemaker at midpoint of GREATER CURVATURE
  • Some slow waves → spike potentials → peristaltic contractions
  • ↑ spike rate (↑ motility): Vagal stimulation, gastrin, motilin
  • ↓ spike rate (↓ motility): Sympathetic stimulation, secretin, GIP
  • N.B: Slow waves: duodenum = 12/min; ileum = 9/min

Types of Gastric Movements

  • 1. Tonic (weak) waves: 3 waves/min; in fundus and body; maintain intra-gastric pressure; mix gastric secretion with food
  • 2. Receptive relaxation: Reflex relaxation of fundus/body to receive bolus; initiated by vago-vagal reflex (pharyngeal/esophageal movements); neurotransmitter: VIP
  • 3. Peristaltic movements: 3-4/min; coordinated by BER; distension → stretch receptors → vago-vagal reflex; leads to:
  • → Grinding of food to fine particles
  • → Emptying of fine particles into duodenum (propulsive)
  • → Antiperistalsis (from pyloric antrum to fundus) = "pyloric mill" or RETROPULSION → mixes food with gastric secretion
  • 4. Hunger contractions: After 12h fasting → hypoglycemia → feeding center → vagus → strong painful contractions near fundus; increase over 3-4 days then disappear
  • → N.B: MMC (Migrating Myoelectric Complexes) during fasting at 90-min intervals → mediated by MOTILIN → clears stomach of residue

Nervous Regulation of Gastric Motility

  • Vagal (Parasympathetic): Excitatory cholinergic effect → ↑ gastric peristalsis and tone; main stimulator of gastric motility
  • Sympathetic: Inhibitory (noradrenergic effect) → ↓ gastric motility; mediates inhibition during pain, stress, fear
  • Myenteric plexus (Enteric NS): Involved in both short local reflexes and long vago-vagal reflexes; coordinates peristaltic movements independently
  • N.B: Bilateral vagotomy → impairs swallowing in upper esophagus + reduces gastric peristalsis → used surgically to ↓ HCl secretion (peptic ulcer treatment)

Factors Affecting Gastric Emptying

  • Pyloric pump regulates rate of emptying with a mixed meal (usually empties in ~3 hours)
  • A. Factors in STOMACH (promoting emptying):
  • → Type of food: carbohydrate (fastest) > protein > fat (slowest)
  • → Consistency: liquids fastest
  • → Volume: moderate volume → ↑ emptying via vago-vagal reflex + gastrin; excessive → over-distension → ↓ emptying
  • B. Factors in DUODENUM (inhibiting emptying via enterogastric reflex + hormones):
  • → Excessive duodenal distension → ↓ emptying
  • → Fat in duodenum: → CCK release → inhibits gastric motility (most potent inhibitor)
  • → Duodenal acidity: → secretin + enterogastric reflex → ↓ emptying
  • → Duodenal osmolality: hyper- or hypo-osmolar → duodenal osmoreceptors → ↓ emptying
  • C. Emotional factors: Pain → reflex inhibition; Depression/fear → sympathetic inhibition; Anxiety/anger → parasympathetic ↑ emptying
  • D. Chemical factors: ↑ emptying: cholinergic drugs, alcohol, bicarbonate, coffee; ↓ emptying: adrenergic drugs, atropine, excessive smoking

Vomiting — Definition, Centers, Mechanism

  • Definition: Expulsion of gastric contents through esophagus, pharynx, and mouth
  • Vomiting center: Medulla oblongata; mediated by CN V, VII, IX, X, XII and spinal nerves to diaphragm/abdominal muscles
  • Preceded by: Nausea, salivation, increased respiration
  • Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ): Area postrema (4th ventricle floor); responds to drugs, toxins, metabolic disorders
🏥 Pyloric stenosis (infant): projectile NON-bilious vomiting + metabolic alkalosis (HCl loss) + hypochloraemia + hypokalaemia. Metoclopramide/domperidone: D2 antagonist → prokinetic → ↑ gastric emptying. Erythromycin: motilin receptor agonist → ↑ gastric motility (also used as prokinetic).
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Receptive relaxation of the stomach is mediated by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Receptive relaxation: pharyngeal/esophageal movements → vago-vagal reflex → VIP release from inhibitory neurons → fundus relaxes to accommodate food.
2The gastric pacemaker (BER origin) is located at:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — The gastric pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal) are located at the midpoint of the greater curvature, generating BER of 3-5/min.
3Migrating Myoelectric Complexes (MMC) are mediated by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — MMC occur during fasting every 90 min, mediated by MOTILIN. They clear stomach and intestine of residue ("housekeeper" function).
4Most potent inhibitor of gastric emptying:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Fat in the duodenum is the most potent inhibitor of gastric emptying. CCK is released → inhibits gastric motility → adequate time for fat digestion.
5Retropulsion (antiperistalsis) in the stomach:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Retropulsion = antiperistalsis from pyloric antrum back to fundus. Acts as a grinding mill (pyloric mill), mixing food with gastric juice and reducing particle size.
6In pyloric stenosis, projectile vomiting of gastric contents causes:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Loss of HCl through vomiting → metabolic alkalosis; HCl loss = Cl⁻ loss → hypochloraemia; K⁺ shifts into cells to compensate alkalosis → hypokalaemia.
7Hunger contractions begin approximately how long after fasting?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Hunger contractions begin about 12 hours after fasting, corresponding to hypoglycaemia → feeding center activation → vagus → strong fundal contractions.
8Erythromycin acts as a prokinetic because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Erythromycin binds motilin receptors → mimics motilin → triggers MMC-like contractions → ↑ gastric emptying. Used as prokinetic when metoclopramide is contraindicated.
9Type of food that empties FASTEST from stomach:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Order of gastric emptying: Carbohydrates (fastest) → Protein → Fat (slowest). Fat is the most potent stimulus for CCK release → delays emptying.
10Excessive duodenal distension inhibits gastric emptying via:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Excessive duodenal distension initiates the enterogastric reflex (via local, ganglionic, and vago-vagal pathways) → ↓ gastric secretion and motility → delays emptying.
4Large Intestine›

Motility of Large Intestine

  • 1. Mixing/Segmenting movement (haustral shuffling):
  • → Predominant movement for water and ion absorption
  • → Teniae coli + circular muscle contractions → bag-like haustrations
  • → Forward and backward shuffling of contents → efficient absorption
  • 2. Peristaltic (propulsive) movements:
  • → A. Weak peristalsis: propels chyme slowly from cecum to transverse colon; colon can store contents for days
  • → B. Antiperistalsis: from transverse to ascending colon to complete water absorption
  • → C. Mass movements: 20-25 cm contract as one unit; pushes contents into rectum; occurs 1-3×/day usually after breakfast
  • → Initiated by: gastrocolic reflex (food in stomach + duodenum → reflex colonic contraction via gastrin + local enteric reflexes)

Functions of Large Intestine

  • 1. Absorption of water, electrolytes, vitamins, and some drugs:
  • → ~2 litres of water absorbed following Na⁺Cl⁻ absorption by osmosis
  • → Large amounts of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are absorbed (K⁺ is SECRETED → severe diarrhoea → hypokalaemia)
  • 2. Secretion of alkaline mucus (pH = 8):
  • → By crypts of Lieberkühn and goblet cells
  • → Protects mucosa from acids produced by bacteria
  • → Emotional stress → pelvic nerve → ↑ mucus secretion + motility → diarrhoea
  • 3. Bacterial flora (normal/beneficial):
  • → Prevention of cecal enlargement (digests macromolecules)
  • → Synthesis of vitamin K, B12, riboflavin, thiamin
  • → Harmful effects of bacteria: ammonia formation, cholesterol → hypercholesterolaemia, histamine/serotonin, utilisation of Vit B12 and ascorbic acid
  • 4. Guanylin: Paracrine from ileum + colon → activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP → ↑ Cl⁻ and water secretion + ↓ Na⁺ absorption (same mechanism as E.coli enterotoxin)

Defecation — Mechanism

  • Sphincter control:
  • → Internal anal sphincter: smooth, involuntary, autonomic
  • → External anal sphincter: striated, voluntary, somatic (pudendal nerve from AHC S2,3,4)
  • Defecation centers: LHC of S2,3,4 (involuntary) — under control of medullary and cortical centers
  • Innervation in defecation:
  • → Pudendal nerve (somatic, AHC S2-4): supplies anal canal + EAS; carries friction sensation
  • → Pelvic nerve (parasympathetic, LHC S2-4): supplies rectal wall + IAS; carries fullness sensation
  • → Sympathetic (LHC L1,2): inhibits defecation
  • Preparatory reflexes: Gastro-colic reflex (stomach distension → colonic contraction); Duodeno-colic reflex (duodenal distension → colonic contraction)
  • Intrinsic defecation reflex: Rectal distension → weak peristaltic waves + IAS relaxation (weak)
  • Spinal defecation reflex: Rectal distension → mechanoreceptors → pelvic nerve + pudendal nerve → S2,3,4 center → pelvic nerve: rectal wall contraction + IAS relaxation; pudendal nerve: EAS relaxation
  • Voluntary control: Rectum fills to 25% → urge to defecate sent to brain; if suitable: cortex → ↑ defecation center + aided by straining (Valsalva); if unsuitable: cortex → ↓ center + sympathetic → IAS contracts + EAS voluntary contraction
🏥 Hirschsprung disease: absence of myenteric ganglia (from IAS extending proximally) → IAS cannot relax → functional obstruction → megacolon proximal to aganglionic segment. Diarrhoea → hypokalaemia (K⁺ secreted in colon). Constipation → megacolon if chronic (especially with opioids → ↓ peristalsis).
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions

✅ C — The large intestine SECRETES K⁺. This is why severe diarrhoea → hypokalaemia.

✅ C — Hirschsprung: congenital absence of enteric ganglia (Auerbach's + Meissner's plexus) in a segment from IAS upward → IAS cannot relax → obstruction.

✅ A — EAS is skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve arising from anterior horn cells (AHC) of S2, S3, S4. Voluntary control via cortical/pyramidal fibres.
