✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Guanylin activates guanylate cyclase → ↑ cGMP in intestinal cells → ↑ Cl⁻ and water secretion + ↓ Na⁺ absorption. E.coli enterotoxin uses the same mechanism.
6The internal anal sphincter is controlled by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — IAS is smooth muscle controlled autonomically: sympathetic (L1-2) maintains tone/contracts it; parasympathetic pelvic nerve (S2-4) relaxes it during defecation.
7Normal large intestine absorbs how much water per day?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Large intestine absorbs approximately 2 litres of water per day (following active Na⁺ absorption by osmosis).
8Emotional stress causing diarrhoea is mediated by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Emotional stress → activates pelvic nerve → ↑ mucus secretion + ↑ colonic motility → diarrhoea.
9Voluntary prevention of defecation when urge is felt:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — When conditions are unsuitable, the cortex sends inhibitory impulses to the defecation center + sympathetic IAS contraction + voluntary EAS contraction (pyramidal fibres via pudendal nerve).
10Antiperistalsis in the large intestine occurs from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Antiperistalsis occurs from the transverse colon back toward the ascending colon and cecum → allows more time for water absorption.
5Pancreas›

Overview of Pancreatic Secretion

  • Volume: 1-1.5 L/day; pH: 7.8-8.3; Osmolarity: Iso-osmotic with plasma
  • Ions: Na⁺ + K⁺ same as plasma; HCO₃⁻ higher (145 mEq/L); Cl⁻ lower than plasma
  • Two components:
  • 1. Aqueous alkaline juice (large volume, rich in HCO₃⁻) — from duct cells; stimulated by secretin
  • 2. Enzymatic juice (small volume, rich in enzymes) — from acinar cells; stimulated by CCK-PZ + vagus

Mechanism of HCO₃⁻ Secretion by Duct Cells

  • 1. CO₂ from blood diffuses into duct cells → combines with H₂O via carbonic anhydrase → H₂CO₃
  • 2. H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; additional HCO₃⁻ enters cell via co-transport with Na⁺ at basolateral membrane
  • 3. HCO₃⁻ exchanged for Cl⁻ by secondary active transport through luminal border → into duct lumen; Cl⁻ recycled back into lumen by chloride channels
  • 4. H⁺ pumped out to plasma (acid tide) in exchange for Na⁺
  • 5. Na⁺ enters by co-transport with HCO₃⁻ across basolateral → then transported to lumen
  • 6. Osmotic gradient → water follows → iso-osmotic bicarbonate solution in duct
  • Acid-tide: ↑ H⁺ in venous blood draining pancreas → neutralises alkaline tide of gastric secretion → acid-base balance maintained

Pancreatic Enzymes — Complete List

  • Carbohydrate-digesting: Pancreatic amylase: starch + glycogen → maltose + dextrins
  • Lipid-digesting:
  • → Lipase: triglycerides → fatty acids + monoglycerides (facilitated by bile salts emulsification)
  • → Phospholipase A: lecithin → lysolecithin
  • → Cholesterol esterase: hydrolysis of cholesterol esters
  • Protein-digesting (ALL secreted as inactive proenzymes):
  • → Endopeptidases: trypsinogen → trypsin; chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin; proelastase → elastase
  • → Exopeptidases: procarboxypeptidases → carboxypeptidases
  • → Activated by ENTEROKINASE (enteropeptidase) on duodenal brush border → activates trypsinogen first → trypsin activates all others
  • → TRYPSIN INHIBITOR in pancreatic juice prevents premature autodigestion
  • Nucleases: Ribonuclease (RNA → nucleotides); Deoxyribonuclease (DNA → nucleotides)

Control of Pancreatic Secretion

  • I. Nervous — Three Phases:
  • → Cephalic phase: conditioned + unconditioned reflexes → vagal stimulation of enzymatic secretion (~20%)
  • → Gastric phase: nervous stimulation continues (~5-10% of enzymes)
  • → Intestinal phase: most copious secretion (~70-80%) — in response to secretin + CCK
  • II. Hormonal:
  • Secretin (27 AA; secretin-glucagon family):
  • → Source: S cells of upper SI
  • → Stimulus: acidic chyme from stomach ↓ duodenal pH
  • → Effect: ↑ aqueous alkaline (HCO₃⁻) juice from ducts; ↑ bile Na-HCO₃ secretion
  • → Negative feedback: HCl → secretin → inhibits gastric HCl
  • CCK-PZ (33 AA; gastrin-CCK family; CCK-A and CCK-B receptors):
  • → Source: I cells of upper SI
  • → Stimulus: digestive products of protein (polypeptides, AA) + fat (FA) in duodenum
  • → Effect: ↑ enzyme secretion from acini; potentiates secretin's HCO₃⁻ effect; ↑ insulin; evacuation of gallbladder
  • → Positive feedback: CCK → more protein digestion → more AA → more CCK
🏥 Acute pancreatitis: gallstones/alcohol → premature trypsin activation inside ducts → autodigestion → epigastric pain radiating to back, ↑ serum amylase and lipase. Cystic fibrosis: CFTR mutation → thick mucus → pancreatic duct obstruction → exocrine insufficiency → malabsorption + steatorrhoea + failure to thrive.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Volume and pH of exocrine pancreatic secretion:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Pancreatic secretion: 1-1.5 L/day, pH 7.8-8.3 (alkaline due to high HCO₃⁻). HCO₃⁻ concentration is 145 mEq/L — higher than plasma.
2Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) activates which proenzyme first?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Enterokinase on duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen → trypsin. Trypsin then activates ALL other pancreatic proenzymes (cascade activation).
3Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Secretin is the "acid hormone" — released specifically by acidic chyme entering the duodenum. It stimulates HCO₃⁻ secretion from pancreatic ducts to neutralise the acid.
4CCK-PZ stimulates:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — CCK (I cell hormone) stimulates: acinar enzyme secretion (main effect), gallbladder contraction, potentiates secretin's HCO₃⁻ effect, and ↑ insulin secretion.
5In acute pancreatitis, which enzyme causes autodigestion?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Premature activation of trypsinogen → trypsin INSIDE pancreatic ducts → activates all other proenzymes → autodigestion → acute pancreatitis.
6Acid-tide in pancreatic secretion refers to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — When HCO₃⁻ is secreted into pancreatic duct, H⁺ is released into blood → acid-tide. This neutralises the post-prandial alkaline tide from gastric HCl secretion → maintains blood pH balance.
7Intestinal phase of pancreatic secretion contributes approximately:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Intestinal phase (CCK + secretin response to duodenal chyme) = 70-80% of total pancreatic secretion after a meal — the most important phase.
8HCO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ in pancreatic juice have an inverse relationship because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — In duct cells, HCO₃⁻ enters the lumen in exchange for Cl⁻ via secondary active transport. As secretin ↑ HCO₃⁻ output, Cl⁻ concentration in juice ↓ → inverse relationship.
9Pancreatic amylase differs from salivary amylase by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Both amylases cleave α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. But pancreatic amylase (optimal pH 7.1) acts on BOTH cooked and uncooked starch, while salivary amylase requires cooked starch (cooking breaks the amylopectin sheath).
10Cystic fibrosis causes steatorrhoea because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CF: CFTR Cl⁻ channel mutation → thick, viscid mucus → blocks pancreatic ducts → exocrine insufficiency → no lipase (and no amylase/protease) → malabsorption → steatorrhoea + failure to thrive.
6Liver & Biliary System›

Functions of the Liver — Complete

  • 1. Metabolic Functions:
  • → CHO: Galactose + fructose → glucose; Glucostat function: glycogenesis, lipogenesis (↑ glucose); glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis (↓ glucose); maintains blood glucose 70-110 mg%
  • → Protein: Deamination of AAs; Conversion of NH₃ → urea (lifesaving); Formation of uric acid; Synthesis of non-essential AAs (transamination); Synthesis of plasma proteins (EXCEPT gamma-globulins)
  • → Fat: Oxidation of FA → energy + ketone bodies; Synthesis of cholesterol, lipoproteins, phospholipids (80% cholesterol → bile salts); Fat synthesis from CHO and protein (lipogenesis)
  • 2. Storage Function:
  • → Glycogen, vitamins A, D, E, K, B12, metals (iron as ferritin, copper)
  • → Iron buffer: if ↓ blood Fe → ferritin releases Fe; if ↑ → liver stores Fe
  • → Blood storage: 10% total blood volume (450 mL) in sinusoids and hepatic veins → can be mobilised in severe haemorrhage
  • 3. Plasma proteins + clotting factors: All plasma proteins EXCEPT gamma-globulins; clotting factors II, VII, IX, X (need Vit K)
  • 4. Vascular function: Blood storage (10% TBV); Blood filtration by Kupffer cells (remove clots + bacteria from portal blood)
  • 5. Drug and hormonal inactivation: Steroid hormones, penicillin, and others
  • 6. Immune response: Part of reticuloendothelial system (Kupffer cells)
  • 7. Bile formation: 0.2g bile salts/day; bile pigments
  • 8. Synthesis of vitamin D: Converts vitamin D₃ to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (first step); kidney completes (→ 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol)
  • 9. Erythropoiesis: Supplies Vit B12, iron, globin for erythropoiesis; RBCs formed in liver during fetal life

Bile — Composition & Volume

  • Volume: 600-1000 mL/day
  • pH: Liver bile: alkaline (7.8-8.5); Gallbladder bile: acidic (7.0-7.4) — due to Na⁺ bicarbonate absorption
  • Liver bile composition: H₂O 97.5%; inorganic (Na⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻); organic: bile salts 1.1%, cholesterol, lecithin, FA, bile pigments, alkaline phosphatase
  • Gallbladder bile: More concentrated (water reduced to 92%), more concentrated organic components Acid-tide (pancreatic): When HCO₃⁻ is secreted by pancreas, H⁺ is released into venous blood → acid-tide; neutralises the post-prandial alkaline tide from gastric HCl secretion

Bile Salts — Types & Functions

  • Primary bile salts: Taurocholate + glycocholate (formed from cholesterol); sodium tauro/glyco-conjugates of cholic and chenodeoxycholic acids
  • Secondary bile salts: Formed in intestine by bacterial action on primary salts
  • Functions of bile salts (6):
  • 1. Fat digestion: reduce surface tension + emulsify fats (with phospholipids) → small particles → ↑ surface area for lipase
  • 2. Fat absorption: combine with FA, cholesterol, fat-soluble vitamins → micelles (water-soluble) → absorbed (hydrotropic effect)
  • 3. Choleretic action: stimulate bile secretion (enterohepatic circulation → most potent choleretic)
  • 4. Solvent action: keep cholesterol and FA in solution → prevent gallstone formation
  • 5. Prevent protein putrefaction: ↑ fat digestion/absorption + ↑ intestinal peristalsis → ↓ protein putrefaction
  • 6. Antibacterial + laxative effect (↑ intestinal motility)

Gallbladder — Functions

  • 1. Storage of bile between meals (sphincter of Oddi closed; liver continuously secretes up to 30-60 mL max)
  • 2. Concentration of bile: Active absorption of Na⁺ → passive absorption of water, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻ (EXCEPT Ca²⁺ stays) → concentrate hepatic bile
  • 3. Continuous flow of hepatic bile by reducing pressure in bile ducts
  • 4. Acidification: Absorption of Na⁺-bicarbonate → pH changes from 7.8 to 7.0 → prevents Ca²⁺ bile stone precipitation
  • 5. Evacuation of bile into duodenum
  • 6. Secretion of white bile (mucus) → protects GB wall + lubricant/buffer in duodenum
  • Gallstone formation: (1) Excess water absorption; (2) ↓ bile salts or lecithin OR ↑ cholesterol → cholesterol stones; (3) Bacterial glucuronidase → free bilirubin + Ca²⁺ → calcium bilirubinate stones

Regulation of Bile Secretion

  • Urogastrone (EGF — Epidermal Growth Factor): Secreted by Brunner's glands of duodenum; also by submandibular glands; inhibits gastric HCl secretion; promotes mucosal healing
  • Post-prandial alkaline tide: After a meal, HCO₃⁻ released into blood from parietal cells during HCl secretion → temporary rise in blood and urine pH
  • Choleretics (↑ bile formation by liver):
  • → Vagal stimulation to liver and gallbladder
  • → Bile salts via enterohepatic circulation (MOST POTENT choleretic — recycled 6-8×/day; total 3.5g/day)
  • → Secretin (hydrocholeretic) — ↑ bile flow via ↑ HCO₃⁻ and water
  • → Vasodilator drugs → ↑ hepatic blood flow → ↑ bile secretion
  • Cholagogues (↑ evacuation of bile from GB): Vagal stimulation; Mg²⁺ sulphate; CCK-PZ
  • Mechanism of bile secretion cycle:
  • → Between meals: sphincter of Oddi CLOSED → hepatic bile stored in GB → concentrated and acidified
  • → During meal: swallowing → reflex vagal relaxation of sphincter; CCK from duodenum → GB evacuation (after fatty meal → GB empties completely in ~1 hour)
  • → After meal: 90-95% bile salts reabsorbed in terminal ileum → portal vein → liver → re-excreted → enterohepatic circulation

Bile Pigments (Bilirubin Metabolism)

  • Source: RES system — Haemoglobin → Bilirubin + Iron + Globin
  • Blood: Bilirubin + Albumin → Haemobilirubin (unconjugated, indirect, insoluble)
  • Liver: Bilirubin + 2 UDP-glucuronate → Bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated, direct, cholebilirubin, soluble) — by glucuronyl transferase
  • Bile → intestine: Bacterial enzymes → urobilinogen → stercobilinogen → stercobilin (50-250 mg/day in faeces — gives brown colour)
  • Enterohepatic circulation: Some urobilinogen reabsorbed from intestine → portal vein → liver (re-excreted in bile) OR excreted in urine
  • In plasma: haemobilirubin + cholebilirubin + urobilinogen
  • In urine: conjugated bilirubin + urobilinogen
  • In faeces: conjugated bilirubin + stercobilinogen
Type of JaundiceUnconj. (indirect)Conj. (direct)Urine BilirubinStool ColourUrine Urobilinogen

Hepatic (hepatocellular)↑↑PresentPale↑ or normal

📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Which plasma proteins are NOT synthesised by the liver?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Liver synthesises ALL plasma proteins EXCEPT gamma-globulins (immunoglobulins), which are made by B lymphocytes/plasma cells.
2The most potent choleretic (stimulates bile formation):
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Bile salts are the MOST POTENT choleretic. As they recycle 6-8× per day via enterohepatic circulation, each pass stimulates more bile formation — positive feedback mechanism.
3Gallbladder concentrates bile by:

✅ A — GB actively absorbs Na⁺ → water follows osmotically, along with Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻ (Ca²⁺ is NOT absorbed — this is clinically important for stone formation).
4In obstructive jaundice, urine is dark and stools are pale because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Complete bile obstruction: conjugated bilirubin (water-soluble) regurgitates into blood → filtered → dark urine. No bile reaches gut → no urobilinogen → no stercobilin → pale/clay-coloured stools.
5Bile salts prevent gallstone formation by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Bile salts (+ phospholipids/lecithin) form mixed micelles that keep cholesterol in solution. ↓ Bile salts or ↑ cholesterol → cholesterol supersaturation → stone formation.
6Enterohepatic circulation of bile salts:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — 90-95% of bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the TERMINAL ILEUM → portal vein → liver → re-secreted into bile. Each molecule cycles 6-8 times per day.
7In haemolytic jaundice:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Haemolytic jaundice: ↑↑ unconjugated bili (albumin-bound → cannot be filtered → no bilirubinuria); liver conjugates excess → more bile pigment → ↑ urobilinogen in stool and urine.
8Clotting factors synthesised by liver that require Vitamin K:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X, and protein C and S. In liver disease or Vit K deficiency → prolonged PT.
9Gallbladder acidifies bile by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Gallbladder absorbs Na⁺-HCO₃⁻ → pH of bile decreases from 7.8 (hepatic bile) to 7.0 (GB bile). This is important to prevent Ca²⁺ stone precipitation.
10After a fatty meal, the gallbladder empties completely in approximately:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — After a fatty meal, CCK (strongest stimulus for GB contraction) is released → GB empties COMPLETELY in about 1 hour. This is why post-cholecystectomy patients are advised to avoid fatty meals.
7Obesity›

Control of Food Intake — Overview

  • Organic sensations:
  • → Hunger: need for food
  • → Appetite: desire for a SPECIFIC type of food
  • → Satiety: sense of fulfilment ("enough")
  • Hypothalamic Appestat Center:
  • → Feeding center (lateral hypothalamic nuclei): continuously active; stimulation → eating; destruction → anorexia
  • → Satiety center (ventromedial hypothalamic nuclei, VMH): inhibits feeding center; stimulation → ↓ food intake; destruction → hyperphagia/obesity

Short-term Regulation of Food Intake

  • A. Afferent impulses from GIT: Distension of stomach and duodenum → vagus → ↓ food intake
  • B. Buccal and esophageal receptors: Amounts of food passing through during chewing/swallowing → signals → stimulate satiety center
  • C. Hormonal factors: Food in stomach/duodenum → CCK + GLP-1 → inhibit feeding center → ↓ food intake

Long-term Regulation of Food Intake

  • Aim: Maintain nutrient stores and blood nutrient levels constant
  • 1. Glucostatic hypothesis: ↓ blood glucose → stimulates feeding center; ↑ blood glucose → stimulates satiety center
  • 2. Lipostatic hypothesis: ↑ fat stores → ↓ food intake
  • Leptin: Protein from adipocytes (ob gene); negative feedback adipose → brain; inhibits NPY → ↓ food intake
  • N.B: Majority of obese humans have ELEVATED leptin → LEPTIN RESISTANCE (abnormal tissue response, not too little hormone)
PeptideSourceEffect
GhrelinStomach↑ Food intake (orexigenic)
NPY + AgRPHypothalamus↑ Food intake (most potent orexigenic)
Orexins (hypocretins)Hypothalamus↑ Food intake + wakefulness
CCKSmall intestine, neurons↓ Food intake (anorexigenic)
GLP-1Small intestine↓ Food intake
PYYSmall intestine↓ Food intake
LeptinAdipose tissue↓ Food intake (long-term)

Obesity — Definition & Causes

  • Definition: Deposition of excess stored fat: >20% of body weight in males; >25% in females (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
  • Direct cause: Increase food intake over energy expenditure (positive energy balance)
  • Hyperphagia types:
  • → Absolute: ↑ food intake
  • → Relative: ↓ energy output with normal food (9.3 kcal excess = 1g fat deposition)
  • Causes of hyperphagia:
  • → Psychogenic obesity: false habits, overeating as tension relief
  • → Hypothalamic abnormalities: lesion in satiety center or tumour
  • Other causes: Genetic factors; hypothyroidism; Cushing syndrome; insulin resistance; leptin deficiency/resistance

Complications of Obesity

  • 1. Musculoskeletal: Flat foot; osteoarthritis of lumbar vertebrae, hip, knee joints
  • 2. Cardiovascular: Cholesterol deposition in arterial wall → atherosclerosis → hypertension + coronary heart disease
  • 3. Gallbladder: Gallstone predisposition (↑ cholesterol in bile)
  • 4. Diabetes mellitus: Inhibits β-cell response to hyperglycaemia; inhibits insulin receptor response; hyperphagia exhausts β-cells
  • 5. Surgical risk: Obese patients are less resistant to surgical operations
  • 6. Mortality: 10% higher than normal persons of same age group

Management of Obesity

  • 1. Decrease energy input: ↓ food intake; emphasise bulk (cellulose, vegetables, salads, fruits) + low CHO + low fat
  • 2. Increase energy output: Muscular exercise
  • 3. Drugs (early treatment only): Amphetamine → ↓ appetite + ↑ metabolic rate; BUT: CNS excitation (insomnia, irritability)
  • 4. Acupuncture: may help inhibit feeding center
  • 5. Massage and surgical interference (bariatric surgery)
  • 6. Psychotherapy
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Site of the satiety center:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Satiety center = ventromedial hypothalamic nuclei (VMH). Feeding center = lateral hypothalamic nuclei. Destruction of VMH → hyperphagia → obesity.
2Most obese patients have ______ leptin levels:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Most obese patients have HIGH leptin levels (proportional to fat mass) but develop leptin resistance — the hypothalamus fails to respond to the satiety signal.
3Ghrelin is an OREXIGENIC hormone secreted from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Ghrelin (orexigenic = stimulates appetite) is secreted by the stomach. Levels rise before meals (signals hunger) and fall after eating.
4NPY (neuropeptide Y) in the hypothalamus:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — NPY is the most potent orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) peptide in the hypothalamus. Leptin acts partly by INHIBITING NPY release → ↓ food intake.
5Obesity predisposes to diabetes mellitus because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Three mechanisms: (1) Obesity → ↓ β-cell response to ↑ glucose; (2) ↓ tissue insulin receptor sensitivity; (3) chronic hyperphagia → β-cell exhaustion → eventual insulin deficiency.
6Destruction of the lateral hypothalamic nuclei (feeding center) causes:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Lateral hypothalamic nuclei = feeding center. Its destruction → anorexia (loss of appetite) and emaciation. VMH destruction → hyperphagia.
7CCK reduces food intake by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — CCK (from SI after food) acts as a short-term satiety signal, partly by inhibiting the hypothalamic feeding center and stimulating the vagus (stretch receptors + hormonal signal).
8Obesity is defined as body fat in EXCESS of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Obesity: excess fat storage >20% body weight in males and >25% in females. BMI ≥30 kg/m² is the international criterion.
9Which is NOT a complication of obesity?
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Obesity increases blood cholesterol (↑ LDL, ↑ VLDL) — not decreases it. All others (HTN, CHD, gallstones) are well-established complications of obesity.
10Energy equivalent of 1g fat deposition:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Every 9.3 kcal consumed in excess of the body's needs results in deposition of 1g of fat. This is the caloric density of fat and the basis of the positive energy balance concept.
8Starvation›

Definition and Causes of Starvation

  • Definition: Severe deficiency in caloric energy intake (partial or complete) for a long time, with water intake maintained
  • Causes: Absence of food; coma; surgical operations; anorexia nervosa (psychopathological — person nauseated by even thinking of food, vomits on seeing food); lesion in feeding center
  • Duration: Variable, may reach 60 days depending on body stores; prolonged starvation >30 days → death from myocardial infarction, pneumonia, or organ failure

General Effects of Starvation

  • 1. Hunger pain starts 12-24h after last meal → maximum after 3-4 days → gradually disappears
  • 2. Mental depression
  • 3. Reduced glandular activity
  • 4. ↓ BMR (due to ↓ hormonal secretion, especially T3)
  • 5. ↓ Cardiovascular activity: bradycardia + hypotension
  • 6. ↓ Respiratory function: ↓ vital capacity
  • 7. General weakness; loss of body weight; negative nitrogen balance
  • 8. ↓ Resistance to infection; ↓ power of regeneration

Metabolic Effects of Starvation — Blood Changes

  • 1. Blood volume, RBCs, Hb: normal at first; decrease later
  • 2. Plasma proteins ↓ → oedema
  • 3. Blood glucose kept at fasting level (70-110 mg/dL) by gluconeogenesis
  • 4. Amino acids kept at fasting level 5-7 mg/dL (from tissue protein)
  • 5. ↑ Fat content (↑ FFA from lipolysis)
  • 6. Ketonaemia (acetoacetate + β-hydroxybutyrate)
  • 7. ↓ Alkali reserve (used for neutralisation of ketone bodies)
  • 8. pH remains constant (respiratory + renal compensation) as long as normal renal/respiratory function

Urine Changes in Starvation

  • 1. Urine volume: variable with water intake
  • 2. N₂ excretion depends on stage of protein catabolism
  • 3. ↑ Creatinine (muscle catabolism → creatinuria)
  • 4. ↓ Urea (to half normal)
  • 5. Ketonuria
  • 6. ↓ Urine pH (keto acids)
  • 7. ↓ Na⁺ + Cl⁻; ↑ K⁺, Mg²⁺, SO₄²⁻ (from tissue autolysis); continuous loss of Ca²⁺ and phosphate (from bone)

Simple Starvation — Adaptive Mechanisms

  • Short-term starvation (<72 hours):
  • → ↓ Insulin + ↑ glucagon + ↑ catecholamines
  • → ↑ Glycogenolysis + lipolysis → FFAs and glycerol released
  • → ↑ Gluconeogenesis from AAs (after glycogen depletion)
  • → Metabolic rate: increases initially then begins to decrease after 2 days
  • Prolonged starvation (>72 hours):
  • → Further ↓ insulin → glycogen stores depleted
  • → ↑ Gluconeogenesis
  • → ↑ β-oxidation of FA + ketogenesis in liver
  • → Brain adapts to using ketones as fuel (reduces protein catabolism — protein sparing)
  • → ↓ Resting metabolic rate by 10-15%
  • → ↓ Physical activity

Stress Starvation

  • Definition: Starvation PLUS a stress condition:
  • Burns, Necrosis (acute pancreatitis, ischaemic necrosis), Severe infection + sepsis, Penetrating/blunt injury, Tumours, Radiation, Allergens, Chronic inflammatory diseases, Environmental pollutants
  • Characteristics (opposite to simple starvation):
  • → Metabolic rate RISES rather than falls
  • → Ketosis is MINIMAL
  • → Protein catabolism ACCELERATES to meet demands for tissue repair and gluconeogenesis
  • → Hyperglycaemia + glucose intolerance
  • → Salt and water retention exacerbated
  • → Hypoalbuminaemia + oedema

Refeeding Syndrome

  • Definition: Fatal/serious disturbances in electrolytes and fluids when severely malnourished/starved patients have nutrients reintroduced
  • Timing: Within first 2-5 days after start of nutrition (oral, enteral, or parenteral)
  • Mechanism:
  • → Rapid shift from fat to carbohydrate metabolism → glucose load → insulin release
  • → Insulin stimulates glycogen + fat + protein synthesis → requires phosphate, magnesium, cofactors (thiamine)
  • → Insulin stimulates K⁺ uptake into cells (via Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase) + glucose uptake
  • → Mg²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ also taken into cells; water follows by osmosis
  • → Result: ↓ serum phosphate + potassium + magnesium (HYPOPHOSPHATAEMIA is most dangerous)
🏥 Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency with adequate calories → ↓albumin → oedema, moon face, fatty liver, dermatitis, depigmented hair. Marasmus: total calorie + protein deficiency → severe wasting, no oedema, "old man face." Anorexia nervosa: psychiatric starvation → hypothalamic amenorrhoea (↓GnRH → ↓LH/FSH → ↓oestrogen), osteoporosis, bradycardia.
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1BMR during prolonged starvation:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — In prolonged starvation, ↓ T3 (thyroid) + ↓ insulin → metabolic rate decreases by 10-15%. This is an adaptive mechanism to prolong survival.
2Which change occurs in STRESS starvation (opposite to simple starvation)?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Stress starvation (starvation + injury/infection): metabolic rate RISES; protein catabolism ACCELERATES; ketosis is minimal (opposite to simple starvation where protein is spared and ketosis is prominent).
3Brain adaptation in prolonged starvation (>72 hrs):
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — After 72 hrs, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies as primary fuel (up to 75% of energy). This reduces glucose demand → reduces protein catabolism (protein sparing) → survival extended.
4In starvation, blood glucose is maintained at fasting levels by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Blood glucose is maintained at 70-110 mg/dL during starvation by gluconeogenesis from: amino acids (muscle protein) + glycerol (lipolysis) + lactate (Cori cycle).
5Ketonuria in starvation is caused by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Starvation → ↓ insulin + ↑ glucagon → lipolysis → ↑ FFAs → ↑ β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity → ketogenesis → ketonaemia → ketonuria.
6Refeeding syndrome is characterised by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Refeeding: glucose → insulin surge → drives K⁺, PO₄³⁻, Mg²⁺ into cells → profound hypophosphataemia (most dangerous — causes haemolysis, respiratory failure, cardiac failure).
7Hunger contractions are maximum after:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Hunger contractions start 12-24h after last meal, reach maximum intensity at 3-4 days of fasting, then gradually disappear (possibly due to ↓ sensitivity of feeding center to hypoglycaemia).
8Prolonged starvation >30 days leads to death from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Prolonged starvation eventually exhausts all fat stores → cardiac + skeletal muscle protein catabolism → myocardial dysfunction → myocardial infarction; also ↓ immunity → pneumonia; organ failure.
9Kwashiorkor differs from marasmus in that kwashiorkor has:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency with ADEQUATE calories → ↓ albumin → osmotic oedema (moon face, ascites, pedal oedema) + fatty liver. No severe wasting (calories adequate). Marasmus = total calorie + protein starvation → severe wasting without oedema.
10In simple starvation, protein catabolism is REDUCED because:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — In prolonged simple starvation: brain uses ketones → less glucose needed → less gluconeogenesis from AAs → protein catabolism ↓ (protein sparing). This is the key adaptive mechanism.

📝 Practice MCQs 102 Questions
1Deglutition is defined as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Deglutition (swallowing) is the process that propels the food bolus from the mouth into the stomach, passing through buccal, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases.
2The swallowing center is located in the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The swallowing center lies in the medulla oblongata, closely related to the respiratory center, which is why breathing is briefly inhibited during swallowing.
3Which phase of swallowing is voluntary?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Only the buccal (oral) phase is voluntary; the pharyngeal and esophageal phases occur as involuntary reflexes once initiated.
4During the buccal phase, the food bolus is propelled by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The tongue is elevated and retracted against the hard palate, pushing the bolus backward into the pharynx to trigger the swallowing reflex.
5The afferent nerve of the swallowing reflex is the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Sensory receptors around the pharynx send afferent impulses mainly via the glossopharyngeal nerve to the swallowing center in the medulla.
6Closure of the glottis during swallowing is aided by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The epiglottis folds backward over the laryngeal opening, helping close the glottis and prevent aspiration of food into the airway.
7Temporary inhibition of breathing during swallowing is called:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — This brief, reflex pause in respiration that accompanies swallowing is specifically termed swallowing apnea, protecting the airway.
8The upper esophageal sphincter is normally closed to prevent:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The UES stays tonically closed between swallows mainly to stop air from being drawn into the esophagus and stomach during breathing.
9Primary peristaltic waves are:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Primary peristalsis is simply the forward continuation of the pharyngeal contraction wave down the entire esophagus, driven by the swallowing center.
10Secondary peristaltic waves are initiated by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Secondary waves arise locally from distension caused by retained bolus in the esophagus and continue until the esophagus is cleared.
11The lower esophageal sphincter is also called the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The LES, located at the esophagogastric junction, is also known as the cardiac sphincter.
12Tone of the LES is increased by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gastrin increases LES tone, helping protect against reflux, whereas VIP, fatty foods, and caffeine all tend to relax the LES.
13A food bolus becomes lodged within the esophagus. Additional peristaltic waves are generated until the bolus reaches the stomach. These waves are called:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — When a bolus lingers, local esophageal distension triggers secondary peristaltic waves that continue until the bolus is cleared into the stomach.
14Which of the following decreases LES tone?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Chocolate (along with fatty foods, alcohol, and caffeine) relaxes the LES and lowers its tone, predisposing to reflux.
15Gastric reflux is prevented by all EXCEPT:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — A relaxed LES tone would promote, not prevent, reflux — the other three factors are normal anti-reflux mechanisms.
16Dysphagia means:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Dysphagia refers to difficulty swallowing, as opposed to odynophagia (painful swallowing).
17A patient complains of recurrent heartburn after meals. Examination reveals reduced tone of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). Which factor normally increases LES tone?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Gastrin normally raises LES tone; the other listed factors (VIP, chocolate, caffeine) all relax the LES and would worsen reflux.
18Achalasia results mainly from deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Achalasia is caused by loss of inhibitory neurons releasing NO and VIP, so the LES fails to relax normally during swallowing.
19A patient with congenital absence of inhibitory neurons in the lower esophagus develops marked esophageal dilatation. The diagnosis is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Congenital absence of inhibitory (NO/VIP) neurons causing a persistently contracted LES and proximal dilatation is the classic picture of achalasia.
20Which gastric cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Parietal cells secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is essential for vitamin B12 absorption.
21Chief cells secrete:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor that is converted to pepsin in the acidic gastric environment.
22A 62-year-old patient presents with fatigue, pallor, glossitis, and numbness in the hands and feet. Laboratory investigations reveal a macrocytic anemia with low serum vitamin B12 levels. Further evaluation suggests autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells. The patient's anemia is most likely due to a deficiency of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells removes the source of intrinsic factor, impairing B12 absorption and causing pernicious (macrocytic) anemia.
23Acetylcholine stimulates HCl secretion through:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Acetylcholine released from vagal/enteric neurons acts on M3 muscarinic receptors on parietal cells to stimulate acid secretion.
24Which drug blocks histamine-stimulated gastric acid secretion?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Cimetidine is an H2-receptor antagonist that specifically blocks histamine-stimulated acid secretion by parietal cells.
25Gastrin stimulates acid secretion by acting on:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gastrin acts on CCK-B (CCK2/gastrin) receptors on parietal cells and ECL cells, the latter releasing histamine to amplify acid secretion.
26Postprandial alkaline tide is due to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — As parietal cells secrete H+ into the lumen, bicarbonate generated intracellularly diffuses into the blood, producing the transient postprandial alkaline tide.
27The optimum pH for pepsin activity is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Pepsin works best in the strongly acidic environment of the stomach, with an optimum pH of about 1.8–3.5.
28Gastric lipase acts mainly on:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gastric lipase preferentially hydrolyzes short- and medium-chain triglycerides, contributing modestly to overall fat digestion before pancreatic lipase takes over.
29The thick alkaline mucus protecting gastric mucosa is secreted by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Surface mucous (epithelial) cells secrete the protective alkaline mucus layer that shields the gastric lining from acid and pepsin.
30Gastrin is secreted mainly from:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gastrin is produced chiefly by G cells located in the pyloric antrum mucosa.
31Which hormone increases LES tone?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gastrin increases LES tone, while secretin, VIP, and GIP all tend to decrease it.
32A patient with peptic ulcer disease is treated with cimetidine. The drug decreases gastric acid secretion by blocking the action of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Cimetidine is an H2-receptor blocker, so it works by inhibiting histamine's action on parietal cell H2 receptors.
33Prostaglandin E₂ protects the stomach by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — PGE2 is cytoprotective: it stimulates mucus and bicarbonate secretion while inhibiting acid secretion, preserving the mucosal barrier.
34The neurotransmitter responsible for receptive relaxation is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Receptive relaxation of the gastric fundus/body is mediated mainly by the inhibitory neurotransmitters VIP and NO via vago-vagal reflexes.
35Gastric peristalsis begins mainly at the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Peristaltic contractions of the stomach are initiated by pacemaker activity around the middle/greater curvature of the body and sweep toward the antrum.
36Hunger contractions are triggered mainly by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Low blood glucose (hypoglycemia) is the principal stimulus for strong, rhythmic hunger contractions of the empty stomach.
37Hunger contractions can be abolished by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Because hunger contractions depend on vagal cholinergic drive, they can be abolished by atropine or by vagotomy.
38Parasympathetic stimulation of the stomach is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Vagal (parasympathetic) input to the stomach is excitatory and cholinergic, increasing motility and secretion.
39Sympathetic stimulation of gastric motility is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Sympathetic activity generally inhibits gastric motility and secretion, opposing the excitatory parasympathetic effect.
40The slowest gastric emptying occurs with:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Fatty meals trigger CCK and enterogastric inhibitory reflexes that slow gastric emptying more than carbohydrates, proteins, or water.
41Moderate gastric distension increases emptying mainly through:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Distension of the stomach activates a vago-vagal reflex and stimulates gastrin release, both of which enhance antral motility and emptying.
42A medical student experiences acute emotional stress while fasting (interdigestive period). Under these conditions, there would be an increase in the secretion of which of the following:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Emotional stress increases vagal activity, stimulating secretion of acidic, pepsin-rich gastric juice even in the fasting state.
43A healthy volunteer swallows a large meal. The fundus and body of the stomach relax to accommodate the incoming food without a significant rise in intragastric pressure. This response is known as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — This vago-vagally mediated relaxation of the proximal stomach that accommodates a meal without raising pressure is receptive relaxation.
44Gastric emptying is accelerated by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Alcohol tends to speed up gastric emptying, whereas atropine, adrenergic drugs, and smoking generally slow gastric motility.
45A 45-year-old male presents to the clinic with persistent early satiety, upper abdominal bloating, and nausea. Which of the following medications is most likely contributing to his symptoms by causing delayed gastric emptying?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Atropine blocks cholinergic stimulation of gastric smooth muscle, reducing motility and delaying emptying — producing gastroparesis-like symptoms.
46The vomiting center is located in the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The vomiting center is located in the medulla oblongata, where it integrates input from the CTZ and other afferents to coordinate the vomiting reflex.
47The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) is located:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The CTZ lies in the area postrema near the floor of the fourth ventricle, outside the blood–brain barrier, allowing it to detect circulating emetic substances.
48Motion sickness induces vomiting mainly through:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Vestibular signals from motion sickness reach the vomiting center largely via stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
49Which cranial nerve is NOT involved in vomiting?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — The optic nerve carries only visual information and plays no direct motor or sensory role in the vomiting reflex, unlike the trigeminal, facial, and glossopharyngeal nerves.
50During retching, the lower esophageal sphincter is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — During retching the LES remains contracted (closed), preventing actual expulsion of gastric contents until true vomiting occurs.
51During actual vomiting, the stomach is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The stomach itself stays passive and relaxed during vomiting; expulsion is driven by contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles, not gastric peristalsis.
52During vomiting, aspiration is prevented by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Elevation of the soft palate closes off the nasopharynx and closure of the glottis protects the airway, preventing aspiration of vomitus.
53Tetany after prolonged vomiting occurs mainly due to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Loss of gastric acid causes metabolic alkalosis; the resulting alkalemia increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionized calcium and provoking tetany.
54A 45-year-old patient presents with a 3-day history of persistent vomiting. Laboratory results are most likely to show which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Loss of gastric HCl and volume contraction trigger secondary hyperaldosteronism, which promotes renal potassium wasting and hypokalemia.
55Which hormone is responsible for the fasting "contractions" of the stomach?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Motilin is released cyclically during fasting and drives the migrating motor complex responsible for interdigestive (hunger) contractions.
56A patient undergoes vagotomy. Which gastric activity is abolished?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Vagotomy removes the cholinergic drive needed for hunger contractions, though basic slow waves (BER) and some acid secretion persist via local/hormonal mechanisms.
57Excess duodenal acidity delays gastric emptying by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Acid in the duodenum triggers both a neural enterogastric reflex and release of inhibitory hormones (e.g., secretin), together slowing gastric emptying.
58Gastric emptying of a mixed meal normally takes approximately:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — A typical mixed meal takes roughly 3 hours to empty from the stomach, though fatty meals can take longer.
59A patient experiences powerful colonic contractions shortly after breakfast. These contractions are known as:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Mass movements are strong, propulsive colonic contractions that often occur after meals, frequently triggered by the gastrocolic reflex.
60The predominant movement responsible for water and electrolyte absorption in the colon is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Slow haustral (segmenting) contractions mix colonic contents and prolong their contact with the mucosa, favoring water and electrolyte absorption.
61A microbiologist studies beneficial bacterial actions in the colon. Which vitamin is synthesized by colonic bacteria?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Colonic bacterial flora synthesize vitamin K, an important supplementary source to dietary intake.
62A patient receives prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics resulting in loss of normal colonic flora. Which function is likely impaired?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Destruction of normal colonic bacteria by broad-spectrum antibiotics reduces bacterial vitamin K synthesis, which can predispose to bleeding.
63A patient develops damage to the pudendal nerve. Which structure loses voluntary control?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control via the pudendal nerve, so pudendal nerve damage impairs voluntary control of defecation.
64The involuntary defecation center is located mainly in:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The basic (involuntary) spinal defecation reflex center resides in the sacral segments S2–S4.
65A 24-year-old man voluntarily suppresses the urge to defecate while attending a long examination. Several hours later, the urge disappears temporarily. Which physiological event is most responsible for postponement of defecation?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Voluntary suppression works through cortical inhibition of the sacral defecation center, allowing the rectum to relax and the internal sphincter to stay contracted, temporarily abolishing the urge.
66Completion of defecation requires:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Even after the internal sphincter relaxes reflexively, defecation is only completed once the external anal sphincter is voluntarily relaxed.
67The main stimulus for pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Secretin, released in response to duodenal acid, is the principal stimulus for pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion.
68Pancreatic enzymatic secretion is produced by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Digestive enzymes of the exocrine pancreas are synthesized and secreted by acinar cells, while duct cells contribute the bicarbonate-rich fluid.
69The principal stimulant of acinar enzyme secretion is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — CCK (cholecystokinin-pancreozymin) is the main hormonal stimulant of enzyme-rich secretion from pancreatic acinar cells.
70Acid tide in pancreatic secretion refers to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — As ductal cells secrete bicarbonate into the pancreatic juice, H+ is generated and released into the pancreatic venous blood, producing the acid tide — the mirror image of the gastric alkaline tide.
71A patient with obstruction of the pancreatic duct is most likely to develop impaired digestion of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Loss of pancreatic lipase and proteases due to ductal obstruction chiefly impairs digestion of fats and proteins.
72What is the primary function of the bicarbonate-rich fluid secreted by the pancreatic ductal cells?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Pancreatic ductal bicarbonate neutralizes acidic gastric chyme as it enters the duodenum, protecting the mucosa and creating optimal pH for pancreatic enzymes.
73A healthy person consumes a meal rich in fats. Which hormone will increase the most to stimulate pancreatic enzyme secretion?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Fat and protein in the duodenum strongly stimulate CCK release, which in turn drives pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion.
74A patient develops a pancreatic duct obstruction due to a tumor of the head of the pancreas. Which pancreatic secretion would decrease most directly?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Duct obstruction directly blocks delivery of pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum, regardless of how much is produced upstream.
75A patient has excessive gastric acid secretion due to a gastrinoma. Which pancreatic response helps protect the duodenal mucosa?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — High duodenal acid load stimulates secretin-driven pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, which neutralizes the acid and protects the mucosa.
76Which process releases glucose from liver glycogen stores?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Glycogenolysis is the breakdown of stored glycogen to release glucose, helping maintain blood glucose between meals.
77Which plasma protein is NOT synthesized by the liver?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Gamma globulins (antibodies) are produced by plasma cells of the immune system, not by hepatocytes, unlike albumin, fibrinogen, and prothrombin.
78Which of the following is a function of liver fat metabolism?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The liver is the major site of endogenous cholesterol synthesis as part of its lipid metabolic functions.
79The liver stores iron mainly in the form of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Iron is stored in hepatocytes predominantly bound to ferritin, the principal intracellular iron-storage protein.
80Vitamin K is required for hepatic synthesis of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, enabling their calcium-dependent activity.
81Approximately how much blood is stored in the liver?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — The liver normally holds roughly 450 mL of blood, acting as a blood reservoir that can shift volume to the circulation when needed.
82After 24 hours of fasting, maintenance of blood glucose is primarily achieved by the liver through:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — In the first day of fasting, hepatic glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) is the main source of blood glucose; gluconeogenesis becomes dominant later.
83A patient develops prolonged bleeding due to severe liver disease. Which clotting factors are most likely reduced because of impaired vitamin K-dependent synthesis?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Severe liver disease impairs vitamin K-dependent synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X, prolonging clotting times.
84A 55-year-old man with advanced liver disease develops confusion and altered mental status. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated blood ammonia levels. Which hepatic function normally prevents this complication?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The liver normally detoxifies ammonia by converting it to urea via the urea cycle; failure of this function in liver disease leads to hyperammonemia and hepatic encephalopathy.
85Acidification of bile in the gallbladder helps prevent:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — A mildly acidic bile environment keeps calcium salts more soluble, reducing the likelihood of calcium bilirubinate or calcium carbonate stone formation.
86Bile pigment stones are mainly composed of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Pigment gallstones are composed primarily of calcium bilirubinate, formed from unconjugated bilirubin and calcium.
87The most potent choleretic factor is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Bile salts themselves are the most potent choleretics — their return to the liver via enterohepatic circulation strongly stimulates further bile secretion.
88A 40-year-old woman eats a fatty meal and shortly afterward her gallbladder contracts while the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, allowing bile to enter the duodenum. Which hormone is primarily responsible for this response?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — CCK, released in response to fat and protein in the duodenum, causes gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation to deliver bile.
89Surgical resection of the terminal ileum is most likely to cause:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — The terminal ileum is the main site of active bile salt reabsorption; its resection interrupts enterohepatic circulation and decreases bile salt reabsorption.
90A patient with terminal ileal disease develops steatorrhea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins despite normal pancreatic function. The symptoms are mainly due to impaired ability of bile salts to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Loss of the bile salt pool from ileal disease impairs micelle formation, which is required for solubilizing and absorbing dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins.
91Trypsinogen is activated initially by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Enterokinase (enteropeptidase), located on the duodenal brush border, converts trypsinogen to active trypsin, which then activates other proenzymes.
92Secretin is released mainly in response to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Secretin is released by S cells of the duodenum chiefly in response to acidic chyme entering from the stomach.
93Which hormone causes gallbladder contraction?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — CCK-PZ (cholecystokinin-pancreozymin) is the principal hormone causing gallbladder contraction in response to fat in the duodenum.
94A patient with terminal ileal disease develops steatorrhea. The defect is most directly related to impaired:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Disease of the terminal ileum disrupts bile salt reabsorption, reducing the bile salt pool available for micelle formation and fat absorption.
95A patient presents complete obstruction of the common bile duct. Formation of bilirubin continues normally, but its passage into the intestine is blocked. Which substance will be markedly reduced in the feces?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Without bile reaching the intestine, bacterial conversion of bilirubin to urobilinogen and then stercobilin cannot occur, so fecal stercobilin (the pigment giving stool its color) is markedly reduced, producing pale (acholic) stools.
96A patient has been fasting for 48 hours. Which hormonal pattern is expected?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Prolonged fasting lowers blood glucose, suppressing insulin and raising glucagon to promote glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and lipolysis.
97A starving patient develops ketonemia. The primary source of ketone body production is:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — During starvation, accelerated β-oxidation of fatty acids in the liver generates excess acetyl-CoA, which is converted to ketone bodies.
98A prolonged starvation state is associated with:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Increased ketone body production during prolonged starvation leads to their excretion in urine, i.e., ketonuria.
99A 32-year-old woman with obesity starts a weight reduction program. After significant weight loss, she experiences increased hunger due to activation of the feeding center in the hypothalamus. Which physiological stimulus is most closely associated with activation of the feeding center and hunger contractions?
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Falling blood glucose (relative hypoglycemia) activates the hypothalamic feeding (hunger) center and promotes hunger contractions.
100A hypothalamic lesion produces excessive food intake and weight gain. The lesion most likely affects the:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Damage to the satiety (feeding-inhibition) center, such as the ventromedial hypothalamus, removes the brake on feeding behavior, causing overeating and weight gain.
101Which cardiovascular complication is commonly associated with obesity?
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — Obesity is strongly associated with dyslipidemia and accelerated atherosclerosis, raising cardiovascular risk.
102A physician advises an obese patient to consume food rich in cellulose, vegetables, salads, and fruits with reduced fat intake. This recommendation aims primarily to:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — High-fiber, low-fat foods are bulky and lower in calories, helping reduce overall energy (caloric) intake for weight management.
✍️Physiology Written›

1 — Describe Swallowing (Deglutition) Reflex

  • Receptor: oropharynx (tonsillar pillars)
  • Afferent: glossopharyngeal nerve
  • Center: medulla oblongata (swallowing center)
  • Efferent: motor fibers of cranial nerves V, IX, X, XII
  • Response: series of reflexes → prevent food entry into air passages:
  • • Elevation of soft palate → closure of nasal cavity
  • • Palatopharyngeal folds approximation → small particles pass & large particles not
  • • Closure of glottis
  • • Inhibition of breathing → relaxation of pharyngoesophageal sphincter → rapid pharyngeal peristalsis → forces food into relaxed upper esophagus

2 — Describe the Esophageal Phase of Swallowing

  • Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES):
  • → Normally: closed by striated muscle tone; prevents air from entering stomach
  • → During swallowing: relaxes to allow food passage, then closes immediately
  • Traveling along the esophagus:
  • 1ry peristaltic waves: start at the upper end — pharyngeal peristalsis continuation; velocity 2–4 cm/sec
  • 2ry peristaltic waves: triggered by presence of a bolus in esophagus; repeated until bolus is driven into stomach
  • → Upper half: coordinated by vago-vagal reflex
  • → Lower half: coordinated by local enteric reflex
  • Lower esophageal sphincter (LES) — cardiac sphincter:
  • → Maintains high resting tone & prevents reflux of gastric content into esophagus
  • → Relaxed when bolus reaches it with some delay
  • → Tone increased by Gastrin hormone & local nerve plexuses
  • → Tone decreased by VIP secretion & fats, chocolate & coffee

3 — Describe the Mechanism of Gastric Hydrochloric Acid Secretion

  • Inside the cell: CO₂ + H₂O → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻
  • To the lumen: H⁺ (via H⁺/K⁺ pump) + Cl⁻ + H₂O = HCl
  • To the blood: HCO₃⁻ enters blood → increases pH (Alkaline tide)

4 — Explain Gastric Enzymes Secretion

  • - Pepsinogens (I & II)
  • - Gelatinase
  • - Gastric lipase
  • - Amylase
  • - Rennin

5 — Describe the Control of Gastric Secretion (Important)

  • Cephalic phase (30%): activated by conditioned & unconditioned reflexes. Conditioned reflex: psychic stimulation of cerebral cortex, centers of amygdala & hypothalamus stimulate vagal center. Unconditioned reflex: direct contact of food stimulates taste buds → afferent to vagal center
  • → Vagal nuclei stimulate gastric secretion by: 1. Direct stimulation of gastric glands (ACh). 2. Release of gastrin hormone (Gastrin RP)
  • → This phase is increased by anxiety and decreased in depression
  • Gastric phase (60%): presence of food in stomach → increases gastric secretion by mechanical, chemical, neural stimuli:
  • 1. Gastrin secretion (direct stimuli as alcohol, polypeptides & caffeine, or via local & vago-vagal reflex)
  • 2. Local nerve plexus: distension or polypeptides stimulate Meissner's plexus → increases secretion
  • 3. Vago-vagal long reflex: food in stomach → afferent vagus to vagal center & efferent vagal increases gastric secretion, so decreased by atropine
  • Intestinal phase (10%): food in duodenum → small increase in stomach secretion of gastric juice, because of small amounts of gastrin released by duodenal mucosa
  • Enterogastric inhibition (duodenal feedback on gastric secretion):
  • → Nervous (enterogastric reflex): stimulated by presence of acid, fats, or hyperosmotic solution in duodenum, or distention of duodenum; conducted via local, ganglionic, vago-vagal reflex → decreases gastric secretion and motility, protects duodenum from over-distention
  • → Hormonal (enterogastric hormones): presence of fats, acid, protein products, hyperosmotic or hypo-osmotic fluids → release of 4 hormones from duodenum (CCK, secretin, GIP & VIP) → negative inhibition of gastric secretion and motility

6 — Describe the Motility of the Large Intestine (Important)

  • 1- Mixing segmenting movement:
  • → For H₂O and ions absorption
  • → Large intestine has outer muscular 3 bands (teniae coli) with contraction of circular muscle layer
  • 2- Peristaltic (propulsive) movements:
  • → Weak peristalsis movements: colon is able to restore its contents for days; propels chyme from cecum to transverse colon
  • → Antiperistalsis: occurs from transverse to ascending colon to complete water absorption
  • → Mass movements: see next topic

7 — Describe Mass Movements and their Physiological Importance (Important)

  • Definition: strong peristaltic contractions in which a segment of colon (20–25 cm) contracts as one unit, pushing its contents en masse into the rectum
  • Initiated by: gastrocolic and duodenocolic reflex — presence of food in stomach and duodenum → reflex colonic contraction, partly mediated by gastrin → increases colonic motility
  • Pathways: local enteric reflex or prevertebral ganglionic reflex
  • Physiological importance: propels faecal matter from the transverse colon to the sigmoid colon and rectum

8 — Describe the Functions of the Large Intestine

  • 1. Absorption of water, electrolytes, vitamins, drugs:
  • • Helps form solid stool and maintain the body's fluid and electrolyte balance
  • • Contributes to overall nutritional status
  • 2. Storage and evacuation of stool: stores the feces until they are excreted through the rectum during defecation
  • 3. Bacterial action: see next topic
  • 4. Secretion of alkaline mucus:
  • → High alkaline (pH = 8) to protect the mucosa from acids
  • → Emotional stress → stimulates pelvic nerve → increases mucus secretion & motility

9 — Describe the Bacterial Actions on Large Intestine (Beneficial or Harmful)

  • Useful (beneficial) bacteria:
  • → Synthesis of vit. K, thiamine, biotin & folic acid
  • → Prevention of cecal enlargement via digesting macromolecules
  • → Stimulate lymphocytes to secrete IgA & IgM
  • Harmful bacteria:
  • → Increase ammonia in blood & hypercholesterolemia
  • → Utilize vit B12 and ascorbic acid
  • → Produce histamine & serotonin

10 — Describe Defecation Reflex (Important)

  • 1. Preparatory reflexes:
  • → Gastro-colic reflex: distention of stomach → reflex contraction of the colon
  • → Duodeno-colic reflex: distention of duodenum → reflex contraction of the colon
  • 2. Intrinsic defecation reflex: distension of rectum → weak peristaltic waves in colon & relaxation of internal anal sphincter
  • 3. Spinal defecation reflex:
  • → Stimulus: distension of the rectum
  • → Receptor: mechanoreceptors
  • → Afferent: pelvic nerve and pudendal nerve
  • → Center: L.H.C of S2, S3, S4 & A.H.C of S2, S3, S4
  • → Efferent: pelvic nerve & pudendal nerve
  • → Response — Pelvic N: wall contraction & internal anal sphincter relaxation; Pudendal N: relaxation of external anal sphincter

11 — Discuss Voluntary Control of Defecation (Important)

  • 1- If conditions are suitable: cerebral cortex sends excitatory impulses → activates defecation center in spinal cord → more peristalsis and relaxation of anal sphincters; the act is facilitated by straining → increases intra-abdominal pressure and squeezes the rectum
  • 2- If conditions are unsuitable: cerebral cortex sends inhibitory impulses → inhibits defecation center with rectal wall relaxation & internal sphincter contraction by sympathetic effect
  • The external anal sphincter contracts voluntarily via pyramidal fibers → prevents defecation

12 — Describe the Mechanism of Secretion of Aqueous Alkaline Pancreatic Juice (Important)

  • 1- CO₂ from blood diffuses to interior of duct and, by carbonic anhydrase, combines with water to form H₂CO₃
  • 2- Carbonic acid dissociates into HCO₃⁻ and H⁺
  • 3- HCO₃⁻ is exchanged for Cl⁻ by 2ry active transport through luminal border into lumen of duct; the Cl⁻ is recycled back into lumen by chloride channels
  • 4- H⁺ is pumped out to plasma in exchange for sodium, which is pumped into the cell then diffuses to lumen
  • 5- Na⁺ enters the cell
  • 6- Na⁺ & HCO₃⁻ move from blood into duct lumen → creates osmotic pressure gradient → osmosis of water also into pancreatic duct → forming isosmotic bicarbonate solution

13 — Discuss the Control of Pancreatic Secretion (Important)

  • I. Nervous — 3 phases:
  • 1) Cephalic phase: conditioned & unconditioned reflexes → vagal stimulation of enzymatic secretion from acini after a meal; little secretion flows through pancreatic ducts into the intestine because only small amounts of water, electrolytes & enzymes are secreted
  • 2) Gastric phase: after a meal, only small amounts reach the duodenum because of continued lack of significant fluid secretion
  • 3) Intestinal phase: gastric chyme enters duodenum, pancreatic secretion becomes copious in response to secretin
  • II. Hormonal:
  • → Secretin: increases aqueous alkaline secretion from ducts
  • → CCK-PZ: increases enzymatic secretion from acini (70–80% of total secretion after a meal)

14 — Compare the Actions of Secretin and Cholecystokinin (CCK) on Pancreatic Secretion

CCKSecretin
Increases secretion of enzymesIncreases secretion of alkaline juice
Potentiates the effects of secretin on HCO₃⁻ secretionIncreases insulin hormone
Increases insulin hormone
Trophic effect

15 — Describe Pancreatic Enzyme Secretion

  • • Pancreatic amylase: starch, glycogen → maltose
  • • Pancreatic lipolytic enzymes: lipase & phospholipase
  • → Triglycerides: FFA & monoglyceride
  • → Phospholipase A: acts on lecithin → lysolecithin
  • → Cholesterol esterase: hydrolysis of cholesterol esters
  • • Proteolytic enzymes:
  • → Endopeptidases: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and proelastase
  • → Exopeptidases: procarboxypeptidases
  • • Pancreatic nucleases: ribonuclease & deoxyribonuclease, act on RNA and DNA → nucleotides

16 — Define Obesity and Discuss its Causes (Important)

  • Definition: deposition of excess stored fat in the body — more than 20% of body weight in male, more than 25% in female
  • Caused by increased food intake over energy expenditure
  • 1- Hyperphagia: direct cause
  • → Absolute hyperphagia: increased food intake
  • → Relative hyperphagia: decreased energy output with normal amount of food intake
  • Hyperphagia may be caused by:
  • 1- Psychogenic obesity: severe → early in first few years of life; increased number of fat cells & increased fat content inside fat cells (hyperplasia and hypertrophy of fat cells)
  • 2- Hypothalamic abnormalities: not severe → in adult; increased fat content inside fat cells without increase in number (hypertrophy of the existing fat cells)

17 — Define Starvation and Discuss its Causes and General Effects (Important)

  • Definition: severe deficiency in caloric energy intake, either partial or complete, for a long time; water intake is maintained
  • Causes:
  • → Absence of food
  • → Coma
  • → Surgical operation
  • → Lesion in feeding center in hypothalamus
  • → Anorexia nervosa
  • Body depends on its own stored food during starvation → 60 days till death
  • Prolonged starvation (>30 days) → death from myocardial infarction, pneumonia, or organ failure
  • General effects:
  • 1. Mental depression
  • 2. Reduced glandular activity
  • 3. General weakness
  • 4. Loss of body weight and negative nitrogen balance
  • 5. Reduced power of regeneration
  • 6. Decreased resistance to infection
  • 7. Decreased cardiovascular system activity

18 — Compare Simple Starvation and Stress Starvation (Important)

Short starvation (< 72 h)Prolonged starvation (> 72 h)
Decreased insulin & increased glucagon and catecholamineFurther decrease in insulin
Increased glycogenolysis & lipolysisGlycogen stores depletion
Hydrolysis of TAG in adipose tissue releases FFA & glycerolIncreased gluconeogenesis
Increased gluconeogenesisIncreased β-oxidation of fatty acids & ketogenesis
Increased metabolic rate → decreased after 2 daysAdaptation of brain to using ketones as fuel
Decreased protein catabolism
Decreased energy expenditure/activity
  • Stress starvation: starvation plus a stress condition like:
  • • Burns
  • • Necrosis
  • • Severe infection and sepsis
  • • Penetrating and blunt injury
  • • Tumors
  • • Radiation
  • • Exposure to allergens
  • • Chronic inflammatory diseases
  • • Environmental pollutants
1Small Intestine›

Wall Layers — Standard 4 Layers

  • 1. Mucosa — Epithelium + Lamina propria + Muscularis mucosae
  • 2. Submucosa — Dense irregular CT + Meissner's plexus
  • 3. Muscularis externa (musculosa) — Inner circular + Outer longitudinal + Auerbach's plexus between them
  • 4. Serosa — Thin loose CT covered by mesothelium (squamous cells)

1. Mucosa — Epithelium Cell Types

  • a. Columnar absorptive cells (Enterocytes) — MOST ABUNDANT:
  • LM: Tall columnar; basal oval nucleus; luminal border is acidophilic and STRIATED (brush border = abundant microvilli)
  • EM: Abundant microvilli on apical surface (each 2μm long, 80nm diameter); glycocalyx coating with enzymes; lateral junctional complexes (zonula occludens, adherens, desmosomes); abundant elongated mitochondria, Golgi, SER, RER, lysosomes
  • Function: Absorption of water, nutrients (CHO, FA, AA); secrete enzymes; tight junctions seal intercellular spaces
  • b. Goblet cells:
  • LM: Flask-shaped; basal flat dark nucleus; expanded pale apical part (mucin granules) + narrow basophilic base
  • EM: Apical part full of electron-lucent mucinogen granules; some apical microvilli; basal RER + Golgi
  • Function: Secrete mucus → lubricates + protects mucosa
  • Number INCREASES steadily: duodenum (few) → jejunum (more) → ileum (abundant) → colon (most)
  • c. Enteroendocrine cells:
  • Mainly at crypt bases, few in villi; appear CLEAR in H&E; black granules in Ag-stained sections; types distinguished by immunohistochemistry
  • EM: Peptide-hormone secreting cells; apical microvilli; basal granules

Enteroendocrine Cell Types Table

  • A cells: Glucagon → stimulates glycogenolysis in hepatocytes
  • D cells: Somatostatin → inhibits release of other hormones
  • EC cells: Serotonin → increases peristaltic movement
  • G cells: Gastrin → stimulates HCl secretion
  • I cells: Cholecystokinin (CCK) → stimulates pancreatic enzymes + gallbladder contraction
  • K cells: GIP (Gastric inhibitory peptide) → inhibits HCl secretion
  • Mo cells: Motilin → increases intestinal peristalsis

Enteroendocrine Cell Types Table (Continued)

  • d. Paneth cells:
  • LM: Large pyramidal/columnar cells at BASE of crypts of Lieberkühn only; basal BASOPHILIC cytoplasm + large ACIDOPHILIC apical zymogen granules
  • EM: Extensive RER, prominent Golgi, many mitochondria, numerous electron-dense apical granules → typical protein-secreting cell
  • Function: (1) Major source of LYSOZYME (antibacterial enzyme); (2) Secrete α-defensin + TNF-α; (3) Regulate normal bacterial flora of intestine
  • e. Caveolated cells (Tuft cells): Rare; wide base + narrow apex; rounded nucleus; microvilli; may be seen in stomach and LI too
  • f. M-cells (Microfold cells): Antigen-transporting cells; dome-shaped; large basal invaginations enclosing lymphocytes; present over Peyer's patches (ileum); phagocytose and transport antigens from intestinal lumen to macrophages/lymphocytes → initiate immune response
  • g. Stem cells: At crypt base; regenerate all epithelial cell types continuously

1. Mucosa — Lamina Propria

  • Composition: Loose CT with fibroblasts, lymphocytes, eosinophils, macrophages
  • Contents:
  • → Core of villi (connective tissue stroma)
  • → Central lacteal (blind-end lymphatic vessel) — for fat absorption
  • → Network of blood capillaries + fenestrated venules
  • → Few smooth muscle fibres from muscularis mucosae → extend up into villi
  • → Crypts of Lieberkühn

Crypts of Lieberkühn (Intestinal Glands)

  • Definition: Simple tubular glands in lamina propria between the bases of villi
  • Upper half lining: Columnar absorptive cells + goblet cells
  • Lower half lining: Stem cells + goblet cells + Paneth cells + enteroendocrine cells + M cells + caveolated cells
  • Function: Site of cell renewal (new cells form here and migrate up to villi); secrete enzymes and mucus

Muscularis Mucosae

  • Composed of: Inner CIRCULAR + Outer LONGITUDINAL smooth muscle layers
  • Muscle fibres extend from inner circular layer into the core of villi → responsible for RHYTHMIC MOVEMENT OF VILLI (villous pump) → important for absorption

2. Submucosa

  • Dense irregular CT rich in lymphatics and vascular supply
  • Contains Meissner's (submucosal) plexus — autonomic parasympathetic, controls secretion
  • DUODENUM ONLY: Brunner's glands in submucosa
  • ILEUM ONLY: Peyer's patches in submucosa

Brunner's Glands (Duodenum Submucosa ONLY)

  • Branched tubuloalveolar glands
  • Ducts open into BASE of crypts of Lieberkühn or into intervillar space
  • Cells: well-developed RER, Golgi, mitochondria, dense secretory granules
  • Secretions:
  • 1. ALKALINE MUCUS → neutralizes acidic chyme → protects duodenal mucosa
  • 2. UROGASTRONE (EGF) → inhibits gastric HCl secretion + increases mitotic activity of epithelial cells

Peyer's Patches (Ileum Submucosa ONLY)

  • Aggregates of lymphoid nodules opposite the attachment of mesentery (ANTI-MESENTERIC border)
  • Present in lamina propria + penetrate muscularis mucosae → appear in submucosa
  • Each nodule: pale germinal center with lymphoblasts, T and B lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells
  • Villi OVER Peyer's patches: short or absent; absorptive columnar cells replaced by M cells
  • Function: immune surveillance of intestinal contents (part of MALT)

Microvilli (Brush Border) — Detailed Structure

  • Finger-like projections from apical surface of enterocytes
  • In longitudinal sections: cylindrical processes (2μm long, 80nm diameter)
  • Center contains ACTIN FILAMENTS — tips attached to covering cell membrane; bases attached to terminal web
  • Actin filaments interconnected and to cell membrane by FIMBRIN protein
  • Covering cell membrane has GLYCOCALYX (carbohydrate coat with digestive enzymes)
  • Function: Increase surface area 30-fold; absorption of water, nutrients; secrete digestive enzymes

Surface Area Amplification — Summary

  • 1. Plicae circulares (Valves of Kerckring): Circular mucosal folds WITH submucosal cores; permanent (present even when distended); most numerous in UPPER SI; INCREASE SURFACE AREA × 3
  • 2. Intestinal villi: Finger-like mucosal projections ~1 mm long; covered by epithelium; core of lamina propria with lacteal + capillaries; INCREASE SURFACE AREA × 10
  • 3. Microvilli: Minute cell membrane projections; INCREASE SURFACE AREA × 30
  • TOTAL AMPLIFICATION: ~ ×200 (3 × 10 × 30 = ×900, but actual functional = ~×200)

Intestinal Villi — Detailed Structure

  • Light microscope: finger-like mucosal projections
  • Core (stroma) of lamina propria contains:
  • → Central blind-end LACTEAL (lymphatic) — absorbs chylomicrons/fat
  • → Network of blood capillaries
  • → Few smooth muscle fibres
  • Covered by: columnar absorptive cells + goblet cells + enteroendocrine cells + stem cells
FeatureDuodenumJejunumIleum
Villi shapeBroad, leaf-shapedNarrow, short, tongue-shapedFewer and narrow, shorter
Goblet cellsFewMoreAbundant
Brunner's glandsPRESENT in submucosaAbsentAbsent
Peyer's patchesAbsentAbsentPRESENT (antimesenteric)
Serosa/adventitiaAdventitia (retroperitoneal)SerosaSerosa
📝 Practice MCQs 10 Questions
1Which cells at the BASE of crypts of Lieberkühn provide innate immunity by secreting lysozyme and α-defensin?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Paneth cells are located at the BASE of crypts; they have large acidophilic apical zymogen granules and secrete: lysozyme (antibacterial), α-defensin, and TNF-α → regulate intestinal flora and innate immunity.
2Brunner's glands are found in the SUBMUCOSA of which segment?
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Brunner's glands are in the SUBMUCOSA of the DUODENUM ONLY. They secrete alkaline mucus (to neutralize acidic chyme) and urogastrone (EGF). This is the key histological feature distinguishing duodenum from other SI segments.
3Plicae circulares increase absorptive surface area by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Plicae circulares (Valves of Kerckring) × 3. Villi × 10. Microvilli × 30. Total amplification ≈ ×200.
4Peyer's patches are located in the wall of:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Peyer's patches are aggregates of lymphoid nodules in the ILEUM, located in the lamina propria and penetrating through the muscularis mucosae into the SUBMUCOSA.
5Fat absorbed in the small intestine enters:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Long-chain fatty acids → re-esterified → chylomicrons → enter LACTEALS (central lymphatics in villi) → lymph → thoracic duct → systemic circulation.
6Urogastrone secreted by Brunner's glands:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Urogastrone (= EGF, epidermal growth factor) secreted by Brunner's glands: (1) inhibits gastric HCl secretion; (2) increases mitotic activity of intestinal epithelial cells → promotes mucosal renewal.
7M cells (Microfold cells) are located:
✅ Show Answer
✅ B — M cells are dome-shaped antigen-transporting cells found between epithelial cells overlying lymphoid nodules (Peyer's patches in ileum). They phagocytose and transport antigens to macrophages/lymphocytes.
8The actin filaments in microvilli are held together by:
✅ Show Answer
✅ D — Microvilli actin filaments are interconnected to each other and to the surrounding cell membrane by FIMBRIN protein. The bases attach to the terminal web.
9Muscularis mucosae fibres extending into villi are responsible for:
✅ Show Answer
✅ C — Fibres from the inner circular layer of muscularis mucosae extend up into the core of each villus → rhythmic villous pumping movement → squeezes lymph out of lacteals → aids absorption.
10Goblet cell number in the small intestine:
✅ Show Answer
✅ A — Goblet cells INCREASE from duodenum (few) → jejunum (more) → ileum (abundant). This pattern continues into the colon. More mucus is needed as contents become more solid.
2Large Intestine›

Overview — Key Features

  • Large intestine = cecum + colon (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid) + rectum
  • Function: Completes absorption (water + Na⁺); secretes mucus; contains bacterial flora; eliminates feces
  • Formed of the standard 4 layers

1. Mucosa — Key Differences from Small Intestine

  • NO VILLI — this is the MOST IMPORTANT distinguishing feature
  • NO plicae circulares
  • Has DEEP, STRAIGHT, LONG CRYPTS (relatively numerous)
  • Its whole thickness is occupied by numerous STRAIGHT INTESTINAL GLANDS

1a. Mucosa — Epithelium

  • Crypts are lined by 4 cell types:
  • 1. Absorptive columnar cells: Absorb water and electrolytes; fewer microvilli than SI
  • 2. Numerous goblet cells: INCREASE in number from cecum → sigmoid colon (most numerous); secrete abundant protective mucus
  • 3. Few enteroendocrine cells
  • 4. Some basal stem cells
  • N.B: NO Paneth cells in large intestine (only in SI)

1b. Mucosa — Lamina Propria

  • Loose CT containing simple tubular intestinal glands (crypts)
  • Rich in lymphocytes which frequently aggregate to form SOLITARY LYMPHOID NODULES

1c. Muscularis Mucosae

  • Outer longitudinal + Inner circular layers of smooth muscle

2. Submucosa

  • Resembles small intestine EXCEPT:
  • LACKS submucosal glands (no Brunner's glands — only in duodenum)

3. Muscularis Externa — TAENIAE COLI (Key Feature)

  • Inner circular layer: Complete, similar to SI
  • Outer longitudinal layer: Arranged as THREE LONGITUDINAL BANDS = TAENIAE COLI
  • These thickenings are shorter than the bowel wall → remaining wall SACCULATES → HAUSTRA (haustrations)
  • Auerbach's myenteric plexus present between the two layers

4. Serosa

  • Retroperitoneal segments of colon and rectum covered by ADVENTITIA
  • Remainder covered by SEROSA
  • Connective tissue of serosa is rich in fat cells → form pouches = APPENDICES EPIPLOICAE

Functions of Large Intestine (Histological Basis)

  • 1. Abundant mucus secretion (by goblet cells) → lubricates lumen → facilitates compaction and passage of feces
  • 2. Contains digestive enzymes received from small intestine
  • 3. Water and electrolyte absorption by lining columnar cells
  • 4. Contains bacterial flora → produce RIBOFLAVIN, THIAMIN, VITAMIN B12, VITAMIN K
